$$ \phi(\mu_{0})-\phi(\mu_{T})=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}(x)|^{2}\,\mu_{t}(\mathrm{d}x)\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

∎

#### Theorem 2.26 (Every gradient flow is optimal solution).

Suppose $v$ satisfies Property (Cal) in Definition 2.22 with its metric slope $|\partial v|$ being a strong upper gradient on set $\{\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E):v(\mu)<\infty\}$ . Assume $v$ satisfies the HJB equation (2.18). Then, for any curve of maximal slope $(\mu_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ with initial distribution $\mu$ , the pair $(\bm{\mu},\alpha^{\star})$ with $\alpha_{t}^{\star}:=-\zeta_{t}$ (given by (Cal)) is an optimal solution of

$$ \inf_{(\bm{\tilde{\mu}},\tilde{\alpha})\in{\mathcal{A}}_{0}(\mu)}\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}\!\Big(\int_{E}\tfrac{1}{2}|\tilde{\alpha}_{t}(x)|^{2}\,\tilde{\mu}_{t}(\mathrm{d}x)+\ell(\tilde{\mu}_{t})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t,\qquad\partial_{t}\tilde{\mu}_{t}+\nabla\!\cdot(\tilde{\mu}_{t}\tilde{\alpha}_{t})=0,\ \tilde{\mu}_{0}=\mu, $$

and all such optimal pairs achieve the same value $J=v(\mu_{0})$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\bm{\mu}=(\mu_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ be a curve of maximal slope and for every $t\geq 0$ , choose $(\zeta_{t},\alpha_{t})$ from (Cal). By Young’s inequality and (CR),

$$ -\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}v(\mu_{t})=\int_{E}\zeta_{t}\!\cdot\!\alpha_{t}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\|\zeta_{t}\|_{L^{2}(\mu_{t})}^{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\!\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}=\tfrac{1}{2}|\partial v|(\mu_{t})^{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}|\mu^{\prime}|(t)^{2}, $$

with equality since $\bm{\mu}$ is a curve of maximal slope. Hence $\alpha_{t}=-\zeta_{t}$ a.e. and $\tfrac{1}{2}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,|\partial v|(\mu_{t})^{2}$ . Using HJB equation (2.18) with $\epsilon=0$ ,

$$ \int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}+\ell(\mu_{t})=v(\mu_{t})-\partial_{t}v(\mu_{t}). $$

Multiplying by $e^{-t}$ and integrating on $[0,\infty)$ , the discounted boundary term vanishes and the cost equals $v(\mu)$ . Thus $(\bm{\mu},\alpha^{\star})$ is optimal and the value is unique. ∎

## 3 Early Stopping Formulation

### 3.1 An endpoint formulation from DPP

For every $\epsilon\geq 0$ , $T>0$ and $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ , we denote the reachable sets by

$$ {\mathcal{T}}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu):=\begin{cases}\{\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E):\text{exists}\,(\alpha,\,\bm{\mu}^{\alpha})\text{ satisfying}\penalty\ \eqref{eq:controlledSDE},\text{ s.t. }\mu^{\alpha}_{T}=\nu\},\qquad\epsilon>0,\\
\{\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E):\text{exists}\,(\alpha,\,\bm{\mu}^{\alpha})\text{ satisfying}\penalty\ \eqref{eq:continuity_eq},\text{ s.t. }\mu^{\alpha}_{T}=\nu\},\qquad\epsilon=0.\end{cases} $$

When $\epsilon=0$ , we may omit the dependence on $\epsilon$ , and write ${\mathcal{T}}_{T}(\mu)$ for ${\mathcal{T}}_{T,0}(\mu)$ .

#### Remark 3.1.

Characterizations of the reachable sets are known in the literature, from either the Schrödinger bridge theory or the optimal transport theory. We recall some results here.

- • When $\epsilon>0$ , for every $\mu,\nu$ such that ${\mathcal{H}}(\mu|\ \textit{Leb})<\infty$ and ${\mathcal{H}}(\nu|\ \textit{Leb})<\infty$ , there exists $\alpha\in{\mathcal{A}}$ such that $\nu\in{\mathcal{T}}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu)$ for every $T>0,\epsilon>0$ . See (Léonard, 2014, Theorem 2.12).

- • When $\epsilon=0$ , for every given $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ and every $\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ , there exists $\alpha\in{\mathcal{A}}$ such that $\nu\in{\mathcal{T}}_{T,0}(\mu)$ . Moreover, there exists $\alpha^{*}\in{\mathcal{A}}$ such that $\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\mathrm{d}\mu^{\alpha}_{t}\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t=\frac{1}{2T}{\mathcal{W}}_{2}^{2}(\mu,\nu)$ . See (Santambrogio, 2015, Theorem 5.27).

For every $\mu,\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ , we denote the pair of the curve and the corresponding controls that transport $\mu$ to $\nu$ by

$$ {\mathcal{A}}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu,\nu):=\begin{cases}\{(\bm{\mu},\alpha)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{\epsilon}(\mu):\exists\,\bm{\mu}\in AC^{2}([0,T])\textit{ s.t. }(\bm{\mu},\alpha)\text{ satisfies}\penalty\ \eqref{eq:controlledSDE},\,\mu_{0}=\mu,\,\mu_{T}=\nu\},\quad\epsilon>0,\\
\{(\bm{\mu},\alpha)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{\epsilon}(\mu):\exists\,\bm{\mu}\in AC^{2}([0,T])\textit{ s.t. }(\bm{\mu},\alpha)\text{ satisfies}\penalty\ \eqref{eq:continuity_eq},\,\mu_{0}=\mu,\,\mu_{T}=\nu\},\quad\epsilon=0.\end{cases} $$

If $\nu\notin{\mathcal{T}}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu)$ , then ${\mathcal{A}}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu,\nu)=\emptyset$ . For $\nu\in{\mathcal{T}}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu)$ , we define the discounted energy as

$$ d_{T,\epsilon}^{2}(\mu,\nu):=\inf\Big\{\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|\alpha_{t}\|^{2}+\ell_{\epsilon}(\mu_{t})\Big)\mathrm{d}t:\ \partial_{t}\mu_{t}=-\nabla_{x}\cdot(\mu_{t}\alpha_{t})+\tfrac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\Delta_{x}\mu_{t},\mu_{0}=\mu,\mu_{T}=\nu\ \Big\}. $$

We recall from Proposition 2.15 that the optimal value function $v$ of (2.12) satisfies the dynamic programming principle 2.15. Next we show an equivalent endpoint formulation from the dynamic programming principle.

#### Proposition 3.2 (Endpoint formulation from DPP).

For every $T>0$ , $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ and $\epsilon\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle v_{\epsilon}(\mu)=\inf_{\nu\in\mathcal{T}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu)}\Big\{\,d_{T,\epsilon}^{2}(\mu,\nu)+e^{-T}v_{\epsilon}(\nu)\,\Big\}. $$

#### Proof.

Fix $T>0$ and $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(E)$ . By Proposition 2.15,

$$ v_{\epsilon}(\mu)=\inf_{(\bm{\mu},\alpha)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu)}\Big\{\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|\alpha_{t}\|^{2}+\ell(\mu_{t})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t+e^{-T}v_{\epsilon}(\mu_{T})\Big\}. $$

For any admissible pair $(\bm{\mu},\alpha)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{\epsilon}(\mu)$ , set $\nu:=\mu_{T}\in\mathcal{T}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu_{0})$ . Then, by definition,

$$ \int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|\alpha_{t}\|^{2}+\ell(\mu_{t})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t\;\geq\;d_{T,\epsilon}^{2}(\mu,\nu). $$

Adding $e^{-T}v_{\epsilon}(\nu)$ on both sides, and taking the infimum over ${\mathcal{A}}_{\epsilon}(\mu)$ , yields

$$ v_{\epsilon}(\mu)\;\geq\;\inf_{\nu\in{\mathcal{T}}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu)}\Big\{d_{T,\epsilon}^{2}(\mu_{0},\nu)+e^{-T}v_{\epsilon}(\nu)\Big\}. $$

Conversely, let $\nu\in\mathcal{T}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu)$ be arbitrary. By definition of the reachable set, there exists an admissible pair $(\bm{\mu},\alpha)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{\epsilon}(\mu)$ on $[0,T]$ with initial distribution $\mu$ and with $\mu_{T}=\nu$ . Plugging this pair into the dynamic programming identity gives

$$ v_{\epsilon}(\mu)\;\leq\;\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|\alpha_{t}\|^{2}+\ell(\mu_{t})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t+e^{-T}v_{\epsilon}(\nu). $$

Taking the infimum over all admissible $(\bm{\mu},\alpha)$ with the same endpoints $(\mu,\nu)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{\epsilon}(\mu)$ yields

$$ v_{\epsilon}(\mu)\;\leq\;d_{T,\epsilon}^{2}(\mu,\nu)+e^{-T}v_{\epsilon}(\nu). $$

Since $\nu\in\mathcal{T}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu)$ is arbitrary, we obtain

$$ v_{\epsilon}(\mu_{0})=\inf_{\nu\in\mathcal{T}_{T,\epsilon}(\mu)}\Big\{d_{T,\epsilon}^{2}(\mu,\nu)+e^{-T}v_{\epsilon}(\nu)\Big\}. $$

This is the desired endpoint formulation. ∎

#### Theorem 3.3 ( $\Gamma$ -convergence with endpoint formulations).

Fix $V\in{\mathcal{C}}_{quad}$ and $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ . For every $T>0$ , as $\varepsilon\to 0$ , the functional $\nu\mapsto d_{T,\varepsilon}^{2}(\mu,\nu)+e^{-T}V(\nu)$ $\Gamma$ -converges (in ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ ) to $\nu\mapsto d_{T,0}^{2}(\mu,\nu)+e^{-T}V(\nu)$ . In particular, minimizers $\nu_{\varepsilon,T}$ converge (along subsequences) to minimizers of the limit functional.

The proof is postponed to Appendix B.

### 3.2 An endpoint formulation from curves of maximal slope

In this section, we focus on the deterministic case and set $\epsilon=0$ , and omit the dependence on $\epsilon$ . Recall from Definition 2.3 and Definition 2.4 the concepts of upper gradient and curve of maximal slope. Recall that in Proposition 2.20, we show that

$$ G(\mu):=\sqrt{2\left(\ell(\mu)-v_{0}(\mu)\right)}\geq 0 $$

is an upper gradient of $v$ . For every $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ and $\nu\in{\mathcal{T}}_{T}(\mu)$ , we define the Finsler metric

$$ \displaystyle d_{G}(\mu,\nu) \displaystyle:=\inf_{\bm{\mu}\in{\mathcal{A}}_{1,0}(\mu,\nu)}\left\{\int_{0}^{1}|\mu^{\prime}|(t)G(\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\right\}, $$

and the energy

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu):=\inf\left\{\int_{0}^{T}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}|\eta^{\prime}|^{2}(t)+\tfrac{1}{2}G(\eta_{t})^{2}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t:\ \eta\in AC_{2}([0,T];\mathcal{P}_{2}(E)),\ \eta_{0}=\mu,\ \eta_{T}=\nu\right\}. $$

#### Remark 3.4.

This action energy is different from the previous discounted energy with different running cost function. There is no discount factor. Moreover, $d_{G}$ does not depend on the choice of integrated time horizon.

We first restate some standard results of the time and length reparameterization of curves. The following lemma can be found in Rossi et al. (2019).

#### Lemma 3.5 (Length and time reparameterization).

Fix $0\leq s<t$ . Let $\omega:{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)\to[0,\infty)$ be a Borel function, and let $\bm{\mu}\in AC([s,t];{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E))$ . If $L:=\int_{s}^{t}\frac{|\mu^{\prime}|(r)}{\omega(\mu_{r})}\mathrm{d}r<\infty$ , then the reparametrized curve $\bm{\mu}_{\omega}:[0,L]\to{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ with

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{\omega}(r):=\mu(\kappa_{\omega}(r)),\qquad\kappa_{\omega}(r):=\inf\left\{p\in[s,t]:\int_{s}^{p}\frac{|\mu^{\prime}|(\tau)}{\omega(\mu(\tau))}\mathrm{d}\tau=r\right\},\qquad r\in[0,L], $$

satisfies

$$ \bm{\mu}_{\omega}\in AC([0,L];{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)),\quad\mu_{\omega}(0)=\mu_{s},\quad\mu_{\omega}(L)=\mu_{t},\quad\omega(\mu_{\omega}(r))=|\mu^{\prime}_{\omega}|(r)\quad\textit{a.e. }r\in[0,L]. $$

If additionally $\int_{s}^{t}|\mu^{\prime}|(r)\omega(\mu_{r})\,\mathrm{d}r<\infty$ , we have $\bm{\mu}_{\omega}\in AC^{2}([0,L];{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E))$ and

$$ \int_{0}^{L}|\mu_{\omega}^{\prime}|^{2}(r)\,\mathrm{d}r=\int_{0}^{L}\omega(\mu_{\omega}(r))^{2}\,\mathrm{d}r=\int_{s}^{t}|\mu^{\prime}|(r)\omega(\mu_{r})\,\mathrm{d}r<\infty. $$

#### Proposition 3.6 (Basic properties of $d_{G}$ ).

For every $\mu,\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ , we have the following:

- (i) $d_{G}(\mu,\nu)\geq 0$ and $d_{G}(\mu,\nu)=d_{G}(\nu,\mu)$ .

- (ii) $d_{G}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1})+d_{G}(\mu^{1},\mu^{2})\geq d_{G}(\mu^{0},\mu^{2})\hskip 11.38092pt\forall\,\mu^{0},\mu^{1},\mu^{2}\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ .

- (iii) $d_{G}(\mu,\nu)=\inf_{T>0}{\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)$ .

In general, $d_{G}$ is a pseudo-distance on ${\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ .

The proof is postponed to Appendix C. Similar to Proposition 3.2, curves of maximal slope provide another form of endpoint formulation. Recall that $G$ is a strong upper gradient of $v_{0}$ .

#### Proposition 3.7 (Endpoint formulation from curves of maximal slope).

Fix $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ . Assume there exists a curve of maximal slope $\eta\in AC^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,\infty);\mathcal{P}_{2}(E))$ for $v_{0}$ with respect to $G$ such that $\eta_{0}=\mu$ , then for every $T>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle v_{0}(\mu)=\inf_{\nu\in{\mathcal{T}}_{T}(\mu)}\left\{{\mathcal{E}}^{T}_{G}(\mu,\nu)+v_{0}(\nu)\right\}. $$

Moreover, the infimum is attained at $\nu=\eta_{T}$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(E)$ and any curve $\rho\in AC_{2}([0,T])$ with $\rho_{0}=\mu$ and $\rho_{T}=\nu$ . Since $G$ is a strong upper gradient, we have

$$ v_{0}(\mu)-v_{0}(\nu)\ \leq\ \int_{0}^{T}G(\rho_{t})\,|\rho^{\prime}|(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\int_{0}^{T}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}|\rho^{\prime}|^{2}(t)+\tfrac{1}{2}G(\rho_{t})^{2}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Taking the infimum over all such $\eta$ yields

$$ v_{0}(\mu)\ \leq\ v_{0}(\nu)+\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu),\qquad\forall\,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(E). $$

In particular,

$$ v_{0}(\mu)\ \leq\ \inf_{\nu}\Big\{v_{0}(\nu)+\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\Big\}. $$

Now let $\eta$ be a curve of maximal slope for $v_{0}$ with respect to $G$ such that $\eta_{0}=\mu$ . Since $\eta\in AC^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,\infty);\mathcal{P}_{2}(E))$ , its endpoint $\eta_{T}$ belongs to $\mathcal{T}_{T}(\mu)$ . Moreover, by the defining identity of a curve of maximal slope,

$$ -\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}v_{0}(\eta_{t})=|\eta^{\prime}|^{2}(t)=G(\eta_{t})^{2}\qquad\text{for a.e. }t\in(0,T). $$

Integrating from $0$ to $T$ , we obtain

$$ v_{0}(\mu)-v_{0}(\eta_{T})=\int_{0}^{T}G(\eta_{t})^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{T}\Big(\frac{1}{2}|\eta^{\prime}|^{2}(t)+\frac{1}{2}G(\eta_{t})^{2}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Therefore,

$$ {\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\eta_{T})\leq\int_{0}^{T}\Big(\frac{1}{2}|\eta^{\prime}|^{2}(t)+\frac{1}{2}G(\eta_{t})^{2}\Big)\,dt=v_{0}(\mu)-v_{0}(\eta_{T}). $$

Hence,

$$ \inf_{\nu}\Big\{v_{0}(\nu)+\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\Big\}\leq v_{0}(\eta_{T})+\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\eta_{T})\leq v_{0}(\mu). $$

Combining (3.8) and (3.9) gives

$$ \inf_{\nu}\Big\{v_{0}(\nu)+\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\Big\}=v_{0}(\mu). $$

Moreover, (3.9) shows that the infimum is achieved at $\nu=\eta_{T}$ , which is exactly (3.6). ∎

## 4 Early Stopping and Implicit Regularization

It is widely observed and analyzed that overparametrized neural networks can overcome overfitting and generalize well (Zhang et al., 2017; Belkin et al., 2019; Neyshabur et al., 2017). One explanation is through implicit regularization of gradient-descent-based training algorithms, see Neyshabur et al. (2014); Heiss et al. (2019). It is shown that in the training process of large neural networks, by stopping early (compared to training for infinite time), the trained parameters belong to a set of “regularized” local minima. In this section, we apply the previous McKean–Vlasov control formulation for gradient flows in overparametrized neural networks, and provide a theoretical analysis of this interesting phenomenon.

### 4.1 Mean field formulation of neural network

From now on, let $E:=\Theta:=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}$ denote the space of parameters, with coordinates $\theta:=(w,a,b)$ . In a one-hidden layer fully-connected neural network with $N$ hidden neurons, with nonlinear activation function $\sigma:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ , the output of the neural network can be represented by

$$ \displaystyle f_{N}(x):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\sigma(a_{i}\cdot x+b_{i}),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, $$

where $\{\theta_{i}:=(w_{i},a_{i},b_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ denote the trainable parameters. When the neural network is wide enough, its output can be well-approximated by its mean field formulation. With the same activation function $\sigma$ , the mean field formulation of infinite neural network is defined as

$$ \displaystyle f_{\mu}(x):=\int_{\Theta}w\,\sigma(a\cdot x+b)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}w,\mathrm{d}a,\mathrm{d}b),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, $$

where $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta)$ is the trainable parameter.

For a given loss function $\tilde{L}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ and training data set $\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{M}$ , the empirical loss functional for the mean field neural network is

$$ \displaystyle L(\mu):=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{k=1}^{M}\tilde{L}(f_{\mu}(x_{k})-\,y_{k}). $$

Hence, $L$ is a function on ${\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta)$ . Without loss of generality, we assume that $\min_{\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta)}L(\mu)=0$ . A common choice of the loss function is the quadratic loss function.

In the setting of finite neural networks, the parameters are trained via gradient descent-based algorithms. In the mean field formulation, the analogous formulation is via gradient flow of the loss functional $L$ .

#### Assumption 4.1.

- (i) $\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}$ are bounded and $\sigma$ is Lipschitz, i.e. there exists a constant $S_{0}\geq 0$ such that

$$ |\sigma(z)-\sigma(z^{\prime})|\leq S_{0}|z-z^{\prime}|,\quad|\sigma(z)|\leq S_{0},\quad|\sigma^{\prime}(z)|\leq S_{0},\quad\forall\,z,z^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}. $$

- (ii) $R:=\max_{1\leq k\leq M}\|x_{k}\|<\infty$ .

- (iii) $\tilde{L}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\,\in{\mathcal{C}}^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ and is convex. There exists a constant $\beta>0$ such that

$$ |\tilde{L}^{\prime}(r)-\tilde{L}^{\prime}(s)|\leq\beta|r-s|.\quad\forall\,r,s\in\mathbb{R}. $$

- (iv) $\min_{r\in\mathbb{R}}\tilde{L}(r)=0$ .

#### Remark 4.2.

With the above assumptions, for every $r\in\mathbb{R}$ , $(\tilde{L}^{\prime}(r))^{2}\leq 2\beta\ \tilde{L}(r)$ .

#### Remark 4.3.

The boundedness assumption on the activation function $\sigma$ can be relaxed to linear growth condition, as long as we assume that $\mu$ has finite fourth moment, i.e. $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{4}(\Theta)$ .

#### Lemma 4.4.

Under Assumption 4.1, there exists a constant $C_{G}>0$ , depending on all the coefficients in Assumption 4.1, such that

$$ G^{2}(\mu)\leq C_{G}\ L(\mu)\ (1+m_{2}(\mu)),\qquad\forall\,\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta). $$

Moreover, the functional $G^{2}:\mathcal{P}_{2}(\Theta)\to[0,\infty]$ is lower semicontinuous with respect to ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ , i.e. for any $\mu_{n}\to\mu$ in ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ ,

$$ G(\mu)^{2}\ \leq\ \liminf_{n\to\infty}G(\mu_{n})^{2}. $$

#### Corollary 4.5.

For every $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta)$ , the map $\nu\mapsto{\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)$ is lower semicontinuous in ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ .

The proofs are postponed to Appendix C.

#### Remark 4.6 (Bounded approximation of ReLU).

For simplicity we assume bounded activations, and extensions to ReLU require moment conditions. To retain the quadratic-growth framework on ${\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta)$ , we can work with a bounded approximation of ReLU. A convenient choice is the clipped ReLU

$$ \sigma_{M}(z):=\min\{M,\max\{0,z\}\},\qquad M>0, $$

which is bounded by $M$ and $1$ –Lipschitz. All results stated under bounded activation apply to $\sigma_{M}$ for each fixed $M$ . Moreover, $\sigma_{M}(z)\uparrow\max\{0,z\}$ pointwise as $M\to\infty$ .

#### Definition 4.7.

For every given initialization $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta)$ , every training dynamic of $L$ starting from $\mu$ is a curve of maximal slope of $L$ in Definition 2.4. We also call it the gradient flow of $L$ .

From Theorem 2.18, for every $\epsilon\geq 0$ , the loss functional $L$ admits a McKean–Vlasov control formulation (2.12), with running cost identified in (2.20).

### 4.2 Implicit regularization under infinite training time

In this section, we aim to provide a mathematical formulation and solution of the open question:

Will implicit regularization vanish under infinite training time horizon? In other words, if the gradient descent algorithm converges, does it converge to the global minimizer with minimal “complexity”?

#### Theorem 4.8 (Nonvanishing selection).

If a gradient flow of $L$ converges to $\mu_{\infty}$ in ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ as $T\to\infty$ , with initial distribution $\mu$ , and $\mu_{\infty}\in\arg\min_{\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta)}L(\nu)$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{\infty}\in\arg\min\Big\{d_{G}(\mu,\nu):\ \nu\in\arg\min L\Big\}. $$

#### Remark 4.9.

Theorem 4.8 indicates that, even without early stopping, under the mean field formulation of neural networks, if the gradient flow converges, it converges to a global minimizer of the loss function $L$ which minimizes the weighted distance with respect to the initial distribution. The weight only depends on the choice of the loss function $L$ .

#### Remark 4.10.

From the result in Chizat and Bach (2018), we have that, if

$$ \Phi(\theta,x):=w\sigma(a\cdot x+b) $$

is 2-homogeneous (i.e. $\Phi(\lambda\theta)=\lambda^{2}\Phi(\theta)$ for any $\lambda>0$ ), the initial distribution $\mu$ has full support on $\Theta$ , and the gradient flow converges to a limit measure, then the limit must be a global minimizer.

To prove Theorem 4.8, we first state the following lemma, which can be regarded as the limiting behavior of ${\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}$ in (3.5) as $T\to\infty$ .

#### Lemma 4.11.

For every $\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta)$ such that $G(\nu)=0$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\downarrow d_{G}(\mu,\nu)\quad\text{as }\,T\to\infty,\qquad\forall\,\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta). $$

#### Proof.

For every curve $\eta\in{\mathcal{A}}_{T,0}(\mu,\nu)$ , we have

$$ \int_{0}^{T}G(\eta_{t})\,|\eta^{\prime}|(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\int_{0}^{T}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}|\eta^{\prime}|^{2}(t)+\tfrac{1}{2}G(\eta_{t})^{2}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Taking the infimum over ${\mathcal{A}}_{T,0}(\mu,\nu)$ yields

$$ \inf_{\eta\in{\mathcal{A}}_{T,0}(\mu,\nu)}\int_{0}^{T}G(\eta_{t})\,|\eta^{\prime}|(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\ \leq\ \mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu). $$

Using Lemma 3.5, we reparametrize $\eta\in{\mathcal{A}}_{T,0}(\mu,\nu)$ to $\tilde{\eta}\in{\mathcal{A}}_{1,0}(\mu,\nu)$ via $\tilde{\eta}_{s}:=\eta_{Ts}$ for $s\in[0,1]$ . Then

$$ \int_{0}^{T}G(\eta_{t})|\eta^{\prime}|(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{1}G(\tilde{\eta}_{s})\,|\tilde{\eta}^{\prime}|(s)\,\mathrm{d}s. $$

Taking the infimum on the left hand side, we have

$$ d_{G}(\mu,\nu)\leq{\mathcal{E}}^{T}_{G}(\mu,\nu),\qquad\forall\,T>0. $$

Fix $\varepsilon>0$ . From Proposition 3.6(iii), there exist $S>0$ and a curve $\gamma\in{\mathcal{A}}_{S,0}(\mu,\nu)$ such that

$$ \int_{0}^{S}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}|\gamma^{\prime}|^{2}(t)+\tfrac{1}{2}G(\gamma_{t})^{2}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq d_{G}(\mu,\nu)+\varepsilon. $$

For any $T\geq S$ , define the concatenation

$$ \eta^{T}_{t}=\begin{cases}\gamma_{t},&0\leq t\leq S,\\
\nu,&S<t\leq T.\end{cases} $$

Since $\eta^{T}$ is constant on $(S,T]$ , we have $|(\eta^{T})^{\prime}|(t)=0$ there. Moreover $G(\nu)=0$ implies $G(\eta^{T}_{t})=0$ on $(S,T]$ . Then, for all $T\geq S$ ,

$$ {\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\leq\int_{0}^{T}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}|(\eta^{T})^{\prime}|^{2}(t)+\tfrac{1}{2}G(\eta^{T}_{t})^{2}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{S}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}|\gamma^{\prime}|^{2}(t)+\tfrac{1}{2}G(\gamma_{t})^{2}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq d_{G}(\mu,\nu)+\varepsilon. $$

Hence $\limsup_{T\to\infty}{\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\leq d_{G}(\mu,\nu)$ . This construction also indicates that, for every $0<T_{1}<T_{2}$ , we have ${\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T_{2}}(\mu,\nu)\ \leq\ {\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T_{1}}(\mu,\nu)$ . Combined with the fact that $d_{G}(\mu,\nu)\leq\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)$ for all $T>0$ , we conclude. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 4.8.

We first show that $G(\mu_{\infty})=0$ and $\mu_{\infty}\in\arg\min L$ . In Proposition 3.7, taking $v_{0}=L$ , we have, for every $T>0$ ,

$$ L(\mu)-L(\mu_{T})=\int_{0}^{T}G(\mu_{t})^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t, $$

where we used $\|\alpha_{t}\|_{L^{2}(\mu_{t})}=|\partial L|(\mu_{t})=G(\mu_{t})$ , and $G$ is an upper gradient of $L$ . Since $L$ is nonnegative and continuous, taking $T\to\infty$ yields

$$ \int_{0}^{\infty}G(\mu_{t})^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t=L(\mu)-\lim_{T\to\infty}L(\mu_{T})<\infty. $$

Hence there exists a sequence $T_{n}\to\infty$ such that $G(\mu_{T_{n}})\to 0$ . Since ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\mu_{T_{n}},\mu_{\infty})\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ , together with the lower semicontinuity of $G$ from Lemma 4.4, we obtain

$$ G(\mu_{\infty})\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}G(\mu_{T_{n}})=0, $$

which implies that $G(\mu_{\infty})=0$ .

Now fix $T>0$ . From Proposition 3.7, along every curve of maximal slope $\bm{\mu}\in{\mathcal{A}}_{T,0}(\mu)$ ,

$$ \mu_{T}\in\arg\min_{\nu}\Big\{L(\nu)+\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\Big\}. $$

Fix any $\bar{\mu}\in\arg\min L$ . From (4.5) we have, for every $T>0$ ,

$$ L(\mu_{T})+\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\mu_{T})\leq L(\bar{\mu})+\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\bar{\mu}). $$

Since $L(\mu_{T})\geq L(\bar{\mu})$ , dropping the $L$ term leads to

$$ \mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\mu_{T})\leq\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\bar{\mu}),\qquad\forall\,T>0. $$

Sending $T$ to infinity, from Lemma 4.11 we have

$$ \mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\mu_{\infty})\downarrow d_{G}(\mu,\mu_{\infty}),\qquad\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\bar{\mu})\downarrow d_{G}(\mu,\bar{\mu}). $$

Moreover, for each fixed $T>0$ , from Corollary 4.5, the map $\nu\mapsto\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)$ is lower semicontinuous in ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ , hence using $\mu_{T}\to\mu_{\infty}$ we have

$$ \mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu_{,}\mu_{\infty})\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\mu_{T_{n}})\qquad\text{for any }T_{n}\to\infty. $$

Choosing $T_{n}=n$ and combining with (4.7) yields, for each fixed $T$ ,

$$ \mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\mu_{\infty})\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\mu_{n})\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\bar{\mu})=d_{G}(\mu,\bar{\mu}), $$

where the last equality uses Lemma 4.11 and $G(\bar{\mu})=0$ .

Finally, letting $T\to\infty$ on the left hand side, we get

$$ d_{G}(\mu,\mu_{\infty})\leq d_{G}(\mu,\bar{\mu}). $$

Since $\bar{\mu}\in\arg\min L$ is arbitrary, this proves (4.1). ∎

### 4.3 Implicit regularization under short-time horizon

In this section, we show how to apply our framework to recover the classical results on the equivalence between early stopping and ridge penalty. We need a further assumption on $L$ .

#### Assumption 4.12 (Growth condition).

There exist constants $A_{0}$ and $A_{1}$ such that, for all $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta)$ ,

$$ L(\mu)\leq A_{0}+A_{1}\,m_{2}(\mu), $$

where $m_{2}(\mu):=\int_{\Theta}|\theta|^{2}\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\theta)$ .

#### Remark 4.13.

If $\tilde{L}$ is quadratic loss, then $L$ satisfies Assumption 4.12. Indeed, one may take

$$ A_{0}:=\frac{2}{M}\sum_{k=1}^{M}|y_{k}|^{2},\qquad A_{1}:=2S_{0}^{2}, $$

where $S_{0}$ is the constant in Assumption 4.1. This follows from the fact that for every $k\in\{1,\dots,M\}$ , by the boundedness of $\sigma$ ,

$$ |f_{\mu}(x_{k})|=\Big|\int_{\Theta}w\,\sigma(\langle a,x_{k}\rangle+b)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\theta)\Big|\leq\int_{\Theta}|w|\,|\sigma(\langle a,x_{k}\rangle+b)|\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\theta)\leq S_{0}\int_{\Theta}|w|\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\theta). $$

From Cauchy–Schwarz,

$$ \int_{\Theta}|w|\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\theta)\leq\Big(\int_{\Theta}|w|^{2}\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\theta)\Big)^{1/2}\leq\Big(\int_{\Theta}|\theta|^{2}\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\theta)\Big)^{1/2}=\sqrt{m_{2}(\mu)}. $$

Combining the previous displays yields

$$ |f_{\mu}(x_{k})|^{2}\leq S_{0}^{2}\,m_{2}(\mu). $$

Finally,

$$ |f_{\mu}(x_{k})-y_{k}|^{2}\leq 2|f_{\mu}(x_{k})|^{2}+2|y_{k}|^{2}\leq 2S_{0}^{2}\,m_{2}(\mu)+2|y_{k}|^{2}. $$

Averaging over $k=1,\dots,M$ gives

$$ L(\mu)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{k=1}^{M}|f_{\mu}(x_{k})-y_{k}|^{2}\leq 2S_{0}^{2}\,m_{2}(\mu)+\frac{2}{M}\sum_{k=1}^{M}|y_{k}|^{2}, $$

which is the desired bound with the stated constants.

We start with an observation on ${\mathcal{E}}^{T}_{G}$ .

#### Lemma 4.14.

For every $\mu,\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta)$ ,

$$ {\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)=\inf_{\eta\in{\mathcal{A}}_{1,0}(\mu,\nu)}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2T}|\eta^{\prime}|^{2}(t)+\frac{T}{2}G^{2}(\eta_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Hence

$$ {\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\geq\frac{1}{2T}{\mathcal{W}}_{2}^{2}(\mu,\nu). $$

The proof follows directly via a change of variables in time. Now denote

$$ \Phi_{T}(\nu):=L(\nu)+\frac{1}{2T}{\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\mu,\nu)^{2}, $$

where $\mu$ is the initial distribution. We will show that, when $T\ll 1$ , along any gradient flow $\bm{\mu}$ of $L$ starting at $\mu$ , $\mu_{T}$ is an $\epsilon(T)$ -minimizer of $\Phi_{T}$ .

#### Lemma 4.15.

Let $\nu_{T}\in\arg\min_{\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta)}\Phi_{T}(\nu)$ , then

$$ m_{2}(\nu_{T})\ \leq\ 2m_{2}(\mu)\ +\ 4T\,L(\mu). $$

The proof can be found in Appendix C.

#### Theorem 4.16.

There exists a constant $C>0$ such that, along every gradient flow of $L$ with initial distribution $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta)$ , for every $T>0$ ,

$$ \inf_{\nu}\Phi_{T}(\nu)\leq\Phi_{T}(\mu_{T})\ \leq\ \inf_{\nu}\Phi_{T}(\nu)+CT\ r(T,\mu), $$

where $r(T,\mu):=\big[1+m_{2}(\mu)+TL(\mu)\big]^{2}$ .

#### Proof.

Since $G^{2}\geq 0$ , for every $\eta\in{\mathcal{A}}_{1,0}(\mu,\nu)$ ,

$$ \int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2T}|\eta^{\prime}|^{2}(t)+\frac{T}{2}G^{2}(\eta_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\geq\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2T}|\eta^{\prime}|^{2}(t)\mathrm{d}t\geq\frac{1}{2T}{\mathcal{W}}_{2}^{2}(\mu,\nu). $$

Taking the infimum over ${\mathcal{A}}_{1,0}(\mu,\nu)$ on the left-hand-side and adding $L(\nu)$ on both sides yields

$$ L(\nu)+{\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\geq L(\nu)+\frac{1}{2T}{\mathcal{W}}_{2}^{2}(\mu,\nu)\geq\Phi_{T}(\nu),\qquad\forall\,\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta). $$

Hence, we obtain

$$ \inf_{\nu}\Phi_{T}(\nu)\leq\inf_{\nu}\{L(\nu)+{\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\}. $$

For every $\nu$ , let $\bm{\mu}\in{\mathcal{A}}_{1,0}(\mu,\nu)$ denote the constant-speed ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ -geodesic between $\mu$ and $\nu$ . Then

$$ \int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2T}|\mu^{\prime}|^{2}(t)\mathrm{d}t=\frac{1}{2T}{\mathcal{W}}_{2}^{2}(\mu,\nu),\qquad{\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\leq\frac{1}{2T}{\mathcal{W}}_{2}^{2}(\mu,\nu)+\frac{T}{2}\int_{0}^{1}G^{2}(\mu_{t})\mathrm{d}t. $$

Take $\nu=\nu_{T}\in\arg\min\Phi_{T}$ and let $\bm{\rho}\in{\mathcal{A}}_{1,0}(\mu,\nu_{T})$ be the corresponding constant speed geodesic. Then we have

$$ \inf_{\nu}\Phi_{T}(\nu)\leq\inf_{\nu}\{L(\nu)+{\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\}\leq\inf_{\nu}\Phi_{T}(\nu)+\frac{T}{2}\int_{0}^{1}G^{2}(\rho_{t})\mathrm{d}t. $$

From Lemma 4.4 and Assumption 4.12,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}G(\rho_{t})^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle\leq C_{G}\int_{0}^{1}L(\rho_{t})\big(1+m_{2}(\rho_{t})\big)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq C_{G}\int_{0}^{1}(A_{0}+A_{1}m_{2}(\rho_{t}))(1+m_{2}(\rho_{t}))\mathrm{d}t. $$

Notice that the second moment $t\mapsto m_{2}(\rho_{t})$ is convex along geodesics. Then, for every $t\in[0,1]$ ,

$$ m_{2}(\rho_{t})\leq(1-t)m_{2}(\mu)+t\,m_{2}(\nu_{T})\leq m_{2}(\mu)+m_{2}(\nu_{T}). $$

Plugging this into (4.10) and letting $C:=C_{G}\max\{A_{0},A_{1}\}$ , we obtain

$$ \frac{T}{2}\int_{0}^{1}G(\rho_{t})^{2}\,dt\leq\frac{CT}{2}\,\left(1+m_{2}(\mu)+m_{2}(\nu_{T})\right)^{2}. $$

By Lemma 4.15, we then have

$$ \frac{T}{2}\int_{0}^{1}G(\rho_{t})^{2}\,dt\leq CT\big[1+m_{2}(\mu)+TL(\mu)\big]^{2}. $$

∎

### 4.4 Stability interpretation of the kinetic energy

In the mean–field control formulation, the dynamic evolves according to

$$ \partial_{t}\mu_{t}+\nabla_{\theta}\!\cdot(\mu_{t}\alpha_{t})=0,\qquad\alpha_{t}=-\nabla_{\theta}\partial_{\mu}L(\mu_{t}), $$

and the kinetic energy

$$ \mathcal{K}(T):=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\|\alpha_{t}\|_{L^{2}(\mu_{t})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t $$

appears naturally in both the Benamou–Brenier formulation of the Wasserstein metric and in the Energy–Dissipation Equality (EDE) $L(\mu_{0})-L(\mu_{T})=\int_{0}^{T}\|\alpha_{t}\|_{L^{2}(\mu_{t})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t.$ Beyond its geometric role, $\mathcal{K}(T)$ admits a direct stability interpretation that connects optimization dynamics with generalization.

#### Algorithmic stability.

For a training dataset $S=\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M}$ and its variant $S^{(i)}$ obtained by replacing $z_{i}$ with an independent copy, let $\bm{\mu}^{S}$ and $\bm{\mu}^{S^{(i)}}$ denote the parameter–law trajectories produced by the algorithm on $S$ and $S^{(i)}$ , respectively. Define the uniform stability at time $T$ by

$$ \mathrm{stab}(T):=\sup_{i\leq M,\,z}\;\big|\ell\big(f_{\mu_{T}^{S}}(x),y\big)-\ell\big(f_{\mu_{T}^{S^{(i)}}}(x),y\big)\big|. $$

We also define the expected generalization gap at time $T$ by

$$ \mathrm{gen}(T):=\mathbb{E}_{S}\Big[{\mathcal{R}}(\mu_{T}^{S})-{\mathcal{R}}_{S}(\mu_{T}^{S})\Big]. $$

By the classical stability theorem of Bousquet and Elisseeff (2002); Hardt et al. (2016), one has

$$ |\mathrm{gen}(T)|\leq\mathrm{stab}(T). $$

#### Remark 4.17.

At a heuristic level, and under smoothness and Lipschitz assumptions, one expects an estimate of the form

$$ \mathrm{stab}(T)\leq C_{\rm gen}{\mathcal{W}}_{2}\big(\mu_{t}^{S},\mu_{t}^{S^{(i)}}\big)\leq\frac{C_{\rm gen}C_{\mathrm{stab}}}{M}\int_{0}^{t}\|\alpha_{s}^{S}\|_{L^{2}(\mu_{s}^{S})}\,\mathrm{d}s, $$

where $C_{\rm gen}$ and $C_{\mathrm{stab}}$ are two constants. Therefore the stability, and hence the generalization gap, are controlled by the path length of the trajectory. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality yields

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\|\alpha_{t}\|_{L^{2}(\mu_{t})}\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\sqrt{T}\,\Big(\int_{0}^{T}\|\alpha_{t}\|_{L^{2}(\mu_{t})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\Big)^{1/2}=\sqrt{2T\,\mathcal{K}(T)}. $$

Consequently, under suitable regularity assumptions,

$$ |\mathrm{gen}(T)|\leq\frac{C_{\mathrm{gen}}C_{\mathrm{stab}}}{M}\sqrt{2T\,\mathcal{K}(T)}. $$

Hence the kinetic energy $\int_{0}^{T}\|\alpha_{t}\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mu_{t})}\,\mathrm{d}t$ quantifies the cumulative sensitivity of the training trajectory to data perturbations: shorter and slower trajectories (that is, trajectories with smaller action) correspond to more stable algorithms and smaller generalization gaps.

#### Interpretation.

In this view, the kinetic term plays two simultaneous roles:

- • Optimization: it measures the metric speed of the mean–field flow and appears in the energy–dissipation identity.

- • Generalization: through stability bounds, it quantifies how much the solution depends on individual data points.

Minimizing $\mathcal{K}(T)$ therefore not only enforces smoother dynamics (implicit regularization), but also enhances the algorithm’s robustness to data perturbations. This provides a rigorous link between the geometry of gradient flows in Wasserstein space and the statistical notion of stability, and corresponds to the statement in Hardt et al. (2016):"If one can achieve low training error quickly on a nonconvex problem with stochastic gradient, our results guarantee that the resulting model generalizes well."

### 4.5 Bounds on moments

#### Proposition 4.18 (Second–moment growth).

Recall that $m_{2}(\mu):=\int_{\Theta}\|\theta\|^{2}\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\theta)$ . Let $\bm{\mu}$ be the closed-loop flow generated by the feedback control $\alpha(\theta,\mu)$ with initial distribution $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ from (2.13). Then, for almost every $T>0$ ,

$$ m_{2}(\mu_{T})\leq e^{T}\,m_{2}(\mu)+\int_{0}^{T}e^{T-t}\|\alpha_{t}\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mu_{t})}\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

If $\bm{\mu}$ is a gradient flow of $L$ , then

$$ m_{2}(\mu_{T})\leq e^{T}\,m_{2}(\mu)+\int_{0}^{T}e^{T-t}G(\mu_{t})^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\leq e^{T}\Big(m_{2}(\mu)+L(\mu)-L(\mu_{T})\Big). $$

#### Proof.

Taking the test function $\varphi(\theta)=|\theta|^{2}$ in the weak formulation of the continuity equation yields

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}m_{2}(\mu_{t})=2\int_{\Theta}\theta\cdot\alpha_{t}(\theta)\,\mu_{t}(\mathrm{d}\theta)\leq m_{2}(\mu_{t})+\int_{\Theta}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mu_{t}(\mathrm{d}\theta),\qquad\text{for a.e.\ }t. $$

By Grönwall inequality, we obtain

$$ m_{2}(\mu_{T})\leq e^{T}\,m_{2}(\mu)+\int_{0}^{T}e^{T-t}\Big(\int_{\Theta}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mu_{t}(\mathrm{d}\theta)\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Along the curves of maximal slope, with minimum control, we have for a.e. $t$ ,

$$ \int_{\Theta}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}\;=\;|\mu^{\prime}|^{2}(t)\;=\;G(\mu_{t})^{2}. $$

Hence,

$$ m_{2}(\mu_{T})\leq e^{T}\,m_{2}(\mu)+\int_{0}^{T}e^{T-t}G(\mu_{t})^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\leq e^{T}\Big(m_{2}(\mu)+L(\mu)-L(\mu_{T})\Big). $$

∎

### 4.6 Interpretations of implicit regularizations

The solution reached by gradient flow minimizes the original loss subject to a dynamical or action cost, measuring the total movement of the particle distribution in parameter space.

Moment bounds show that this action cost controls the parameter complexity of the network. In one sentence: implicit regularization is the preference induced by the training dynamics, not an explicit penalty that selects among many interpolating solutions those with small algorithm–dependent complexity, such as minimum–norm in linear/NTK limits, maximum–margin in separable classification, and small–movement/low–action solutions in the mean–field feature–learning regime.

## 5 Numerical Results

In this section, we test several deterministic diagnostics suggested by the theory in Section 4. First, we examine whether the finite-width training dynamics exhibit the energy–dissipation and complexity-growth patterns predicted by the mean-field formulation. Second, we test a finite-width proxy of Theorem 4.16, which states that for small $T>0$ , with initial distribution $\mu$ , the gradient-flow endpoint $\mu_{T}$ is an approximate minimizer of

$$ \Phi_{T}(\nu)=L(\nu)+\frac{1}{2T}{\mathcal{W}}_{2}^{2}(\mu,\nu). $$

#### Finite-width model and data.

We work with the finite-width approximation of large neural network, where

$$ f_{N}(x)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\,\sigma(a_{i}\cdot x+b_{i}),\qquad\theta_{i}=(w_{i},a_{i},b_{i})\in\Theta=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d+1}, $$

so that the empirical parameter distribution is

$$ \mu_{t}^{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{\theta_{i}^{t}}. $$

Since the analysis in Section 4 assumes bounded activations, in the numerics we use the clipped ReLU

$$ \sigma_{M}(z):=\min\{M,\max\{0,z\}\}, $$

with $M=5$ , consistent with Remark 4.6. The data are generated from a network of the same form with additive Gaussian noise. Training is performed by deterministic full-batch gradient descent.

#### Recorded observables.

Along the trajectory $t\mapsto\mu_{t}^{N}$ , we record the empirical loss $L(\mu_{t}^{N})$ , the second moment

$$ m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{N}):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|\theta_{i}^{t}|^{2}, $$

and the Barron-type surrogates

$$ B_{1}(\mu_{t}^{N}):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|w_{i}^{t}|,\qquad B_{1,1}(\mu_{t}^{N}):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|w_{i}^{t}|\,\|a_{i}^{t}\|. $$

To compare with the energy–dissipation identity, we use the mean-field-scaled discrete kinetic action

$$ \sum_{k}\frac{1}{\Delta t}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|\theta_{i}^{k+1}-\theta_{i}^{k}|^{2}, $$

which is the finite-width approximation of $\int_{0}^{T}\|\alpha_{t}\|_{L^{2}(\mu_{t})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t.$ We also use the identity-coupling displacement proxy

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{W}}_{2,\mathrm{id}}^{2}(\mu_{0}^{N},\mu_{t}^{N}):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|\theta_{i}^{t}-\theta_{i}^{0}|^{2}, $$

and the associated short-time proxy

$$ \widetilde{\Phi}_{t}^{N,\mathrm{id}}:=L(\mu_{t}^{N})+\frac{1}{2t}\widetilde{\mathcal{W}}_{2,\mathrm{id}}^{2}(\mu_{0}^{N},\mu_{t}^{N}),\qquad t>0. $$

#### Deterministic scaling diagnostics.

Figure 1 displays three deterministic diagnostics along a single full-batch run. The left panel compares the loss drop $L(\mu_{0}^{N})-L(\mu_{t}^{N})$ with the cumulative mean-field-scaled kinetic action. The observed parity is close to the diagonal, in agreement with the energy–dissipation interpretation of the gradient-flow dynamics. The middle panel plots the second-moment increment $m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{N})-m_{2}(\mu_{0}^{N})$ against the scale $\sqrt{t}\sqrt{L(\mu_{0}^{N})-L(\mu_{t}^{N})}$ , and the right panel shows the analogous increments for $B_{1}$ and $B_{1,1}$ . In this run, both moment growth and Barron-surrogate growth remain controlled and increase smoothly with the dissipated energy. We interpret this as numerical evidence that, in the deterministic mean-field regime, the loss decrease is accompanied by only moderate growth of parameter complexity, consistent with the implicit-regularization mechanism suggested by Proposition 4.18 and the discussion in Section 4.6.

#### Finite-width proxy for Theorem 4.16.

We also perform a direct finite-width proxy test of the short-time endpoint principle in Theorem 4.16. For each small stopping time $T$ , starting from the same initialization $\mu_{0}^{N}$ , we compare two endpoints:

- 1. the endpoint $\mu_{T}^{N,\mathrm{GF}}$ produced by mean-field-scaled full-batch gradient descent on $L_{N}$ ;

- 2. an approximate minimizer of the empirical identity-coupling proxy

$$ \widetilde{\Phi}_{T}^{N,\mathrm{id}}(\nu):=L_{N}(\nu)+\frac{1}{2T}\widetilde{\mathcal{W}}_{2,\mathrm{id}}^{2}(\mu_{0}^{N},\nu). $$

Figure 2 compares the corresponding displacement proxies from initialization. For small $T$ , the displacement of the gradient-flow endpoint and that of the proxy minimizer are of the same order and remain close. This is the finite-width analogue of the statement that the gradient-flow endpoint is approximately optimal for the regularized short-time variational problem. Since the experiment replaces the exact Wasserstein term by the identity-coupling proxy and computes the minimizer only approximately, we view it as supportive rather than definitive evidence for Theorem 4.16. Nevertheless, it is consistent with the qualitative prediction that, for short stopping times, the endpoint selected by gradient descent is close to the optimizer of a loss-plus-movement functional.

#### Interpretation.

Taken together, the numerical experiments support the following picture. In the deterministic mean-field regime, the gradient-flow trajectory satisfies an energy–dissipation balance and exhibits controlled growth of moments and Barron-type surrogates. In addition, for short stopping times, the endpoint generated by gradient descent is well approximated by the minimizer of a finite-width proxy of the regularized loss functional in Theorem 4.16. These experiments do not constitute a direct computation of ${\mathcal{E}}_{G}^{T}$ , nor a full numerical verification of the continuum theorem, but they do support the variational interpretation of early stopping developed in Sections 3 and 4.

## 6 Conclusion, Limitations and Future Work

We proposed a mathematical framework connecting gradient flows and McKean–Vlasov optimal control to study implicit regularization in overparametrized two-layer neural networks. By reformulating the mean-field training dynamics as a control problem, we obtained a variational principle that characterizes early stopping as a trajectory-selection mechanism: the stopped iterate approximately minimizes the loss penalized by a dynamical cost measuring the total movement of the parameter distribution. We further showed that, even under infinite training time, the gradient flow selects a minimizer closest to the initialization in a data- and loss-dependent pseudo-metric $d_{G}$ , if the gradient flow converges.

Our analysis has several limitations. It is restricted to two-layer networks in the mean-field limit, and extending the framework to deeper architectures remains a substantial open challenge. The implicit regularizer that emerges depends on the loss function and training data through the upper gradient $G$ , making it harder to interpret than classical explicit penalties such as weight decay. Moreover, while we provide non-asymptotic bounds relating the regularization to Wasserstein distances and moment growth, the tightness of these bounds in practical settings is unclear and warrants further investigation. More broadly, this work is primarily theoretical and does not claim to offer immediate practical guidance; we view it as providing a geometric and variational perspective that may prove valuable as the theoretical understanding of neural network training matures.

We see several natural directions for future work. It would be interesting to tighten the connection between $d_{G}$ and function-space complexity measures such as Barron or variation norms, potentially yielding more interpretable characterizations of the inductive bias. As discussed in Section 1.1, a particularly promising direction is to leverage such connections to obtain a more fine-grained understanding of implicit regularization in terms of feature learning, building on recent work relating parameter norms to properties of the learned function.

## Appendix A A Counter Example

Let $E:=\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , and consider $({\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),{\mathcal{W}}_{2})$ . Let $\eta\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ be a smooth cutoff with $\eta\equiv 1$ on $[-1,1]$ , $\eta\equiv 0$ on $\mathbb{R}\setminus[-2,2]$ , and $0\leq\eta\leq 1$ . Define

$$ f(x,y):=y\,\eta(y)\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),\qquad S(\mu):=\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}f\,\mathrm{d}\mu,\qquad\kappa(\mu):=\Big(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|\nabla f|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu\Big)^{1/2}. $$

Set a piecewise-linear (kinked) scalar nonlinearity

$$ h(z):=az+|z|,\qquad a>1, $$

and the value functional

$$ v(\mu):=h(S(\mu))=a\,S(\mu)+|S(\mu)|. $$

Note that $v$ is proper, l.s.c., Lipschitz on ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ -balls (since $S$ is Lipschitz via Benamou–Brenier and $f\in C_{c}^{\infty}$ ), but not $C^{1}$ at $S=0$ .

Relaxed slope and viscosity HJB. The metric subdifferential in the $S$ -direction at $\mu$ is the interval

$$ \partial h(S(\mu))=\begin{cases}\{a+1\},&S(\mu)>0,\\
[a-1,a+1],&S(\mu)=0,\\
\{a-1\},&S(\mu)<0,\end{cases} $$

so the relaxed slope of $v$ at $\mu$ is

$$ |\partial^{-}v|(\mu)\;=\;\min_{s\in\partial h(S(\mu))}\,|s|\,\kappa(\mu)\;=\;\begin{cases}(a+1)\,\kappa(\mu),&S(\mu)>0,\\
(a-1)\,\kappa(\mu),&S(\mu)=0,\\
(a-1)\,\kappa(\mu),&S(\mu)<0.\end{cases} $$

Define the running cost by the viscosity HJB identity with the relaxed slope,

$$ \ell(\mu):=v(\mu)+\tfrac{1}{2}\,|\partial^{-}v|(\mu)^{2}. $$

Then $v$ is a viscosity solution of

$$ v(\mu)+\tfrac{1}{2}\,|\partial^{-}v|(\mu)^{2}=\ell(\mu) $$

on $\mathcal{P}_{2}$ (test functionals touch $S(\cdot)$ in the direction of minimal subgradient).

Initial condition at the kink. Pick $\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}$ such that $S(\mu_{0})=0$ and $\kappa(\mu_{0})>0$ (e.g., any compactly supported law with zero $f$ -moment but nontrivial mass in $\{|\nabla f|>0\}$ ). At $S=0$ the subgradient set is the whole interval $[a-1,a+1]$ with minimal element $s_{\min}=a-1>0$ and other larger elements $s\in(s_{\min},a+1]$ .

Two distinct gradient flows (curves of maximal slope). From Ambrosio et al. [2008], with the relaxed slope, one may construct (locally in time) curves of maximal slope $\mu^{(s)}_{t}$ calibrated by a constant subgradient choice $s\in[a-1,a+1]$ at $t=0$ , i.e.

$$ -\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}v(\mu^{(s)}_{t})=\frac{1}{2}\,|\partial^{-}v|(\mu^{(s)}_{t})^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\,|\mu^{(s)}{}^{\prime}|(t)^{2},\qquad|\partial^{-}v|(\mu^{(s)}_{t})=s\,\kappa(\mu^{(s)}_{t}), $$

and (by equality in Cauchy–Schwarz/Young for the relaxed slope)

$$ |\mu^{(s)}{}^{\prime}|(t)=s\,\kappa(\mu^{(s)}_{t}). $$

In particular, for the two choices

$$ s_{\min}=a-1\qquad\text{and}\qquad s_{\max}=a+1, $$

we obtain two gradient flows $\mu^{(\min)}$ and $\mu^{(\max)}$ starting from the same $\mu_{0}$ and satisfying the curves of maximal slope definition with the relaxed slope.

Control costs and non-optimality of the larger- $s$ flow. Let $\alpha^{(s)}_{t}$ be any velocity field realizing the metric speed: $|\mu^{(s)}{}^{\prime}|(t)^{2}=\int|\alpha^{(s)}_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu^{(s)}_{t}$ . Along $\mu^{(s)}$ the discounted control cost reads

$$ J(\mu^{(s)},\alpha^{(s)})=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}\Big(\int|\alpha^{(s)}_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu^{(s)}_{t}+\ell(\mu^{(s)}_{t})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Using the viscosity HJB (with $|\partial^{-}v|$ ) and the EDE (again with $|\partial^{-}v|$ ),

$$ \int|\alpha^{(s)}_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu^{(s)}_{t}=\big|\mu^{(s)}{}^{\prime}|(t)^{2}=\big(|\partial^{-}v|(\mu^{(s)}_{t})\big)^{2}=s^{2}\,\kappa(\mu^{(s)}_{t})^{2}, $$

$$ \ell(\mu^{(s)}_{t})=v(\mu^{(s)}_{t})+\tfrac{1}{2}\,|\partial^{-}v|(\mu^{(s)}_{t})^{2}=v(\mu^{(s)}_{t})+\tfrac{1}{2}s^{2}\,\kappa(\mu^{(s)}_{t})^{2}, $$

and hence

$$ \int|\alpha^{(s)}_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu^{(s)}_{t}+\ell(\mu^{(s)}_{t})=v(\mu^{(s)}_{t})+\tfrac{3}{2}\,s^{2}\,\kappa(\mu^{(s)}_{t})^{2}. $$

Therefore, for $s_{\max}>s_{\min}$ we have strictly larger instantaneous kinetic and running cost:

$$ \int|\alpha^{(\max)}_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu^{(\max)}_{t}+\ell(\mu^{(\max)}_{t})-\Big(\int|\alpha^{(\min)}_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu^{(\min)}_{t}+\ell(\mu^{(\min)}_{t})\Big)=\tfrac{3}{2}\,(s_{\max}^{2}-s_{\min}^{2})\,\kappa(\mu_{t})^{2}\;>\;0, $$

at least for small $t$ while $\kappa(\mu_{t})$ stays the same. After multiplying with the discount factor $e^{-t}$ in time, and integrating over $t$ from $0$ to infinity, we conclude that

$$ J(\mu^{(\max)},\alpha^{(\max)})\;>\;J(\mu^{(\min)},\alpha^{(\min)}). $$

Conclusion. Both $\mu^{(\min)}$ and $\mu^{(\max)}$ are gradient flows (curves of maximal slope) for $v$ with respect to the relaxed slope $|\partial^{-}v|$ , because $v$ is only used in viscosity form and the kink allows multiple $s\in\partial h(0)$ . However, only the flow with the minimal selector $s_{\min}=a-1$ minimizes the control cost. The larger-selector flow $s_{\max}=a+1$ is a gradient flow but not a minimizer of the control formulation.

This shows that, at viscosity regularity (with relaxed slopes and without a calibrating chain rule), a gradient flow of $v$ need not be optimal for the control problem.

#### Lemma B.1.

There exist constants $C_{0},\,C_{1}$ such that, for all $\varepsilon\geq 0$ and $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(E)$ ,

$$ \ell_{\varepsilon}(\mu)\ \geq\ -\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\big(C_{0}+C_{1}\,m_{2}(\mu)\big). $$

#### Proof.

By the definition of $\ell_{\epsilon}$ (2.20),

$$ \displaystyle\ell_{\epsilon}(\mu) \displaystyle:=V(\mu)+\tfrac{1}{2}\!\int_{E}\!\|\nabla_{x}\partial_{\mu}V(\mu)\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu\;-\;\tfrac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\!\int_{E}\!\Delta_{x}\partial_{\mu}V(\mu)\,\mathrm{d}\mu \displaystyle\geq-\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{2}\int_{E}\Delta_{x}\partial_{\mu}V(\mu)\mathrm{d}\mu\geq-\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{2}C(1+m_{2}(\mu)). $$

∎

#### Lemma B.2.

The functional $\ell_{0}$ is ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ –lower semicontinuous on $\{\mu:\ m_{2}(\mu)\leq R\}$ for every $R>0$ .

This follows directly from the definition of $\ell_{0}$ and the regularity assumption on $L$ .

#### Lemma B.3 (Equi-coercivity).

Fix $T>0$ and $\mu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ . For $\varepsilon\geq 0$ define

$$ F_{\varepsilon}(\nu):=d_{T,\varepsilon}^{2}(\mu,\nu)+e^{-T}V(\nu). $$

Then for every $C\in\mathbb{R}$ there exist $\varepsilon_{*}(T)\in(0,1]$ and $\bar{C}$ such that, for all $\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{*}(T)]$ ,

$$ F_{\varepsilon}(\nu)\leq C\quad\Longrightarrow\quad m_{2}(\nu)\leq\bar{C}. $$

Consequently, the family $(F_{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}$ is equi-coercive on $({\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E),{\mathcal{W}}_{2})$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $C\in\mathbb{R}$ , $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ , and $\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ with $F_{\varepsilon}(\nu)\leq C$ . Pick $(\bm{\mu},\alpha)\in A_{T,\varepsilon}(\mu,\nu)$ such that

$$ \int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}+\ell_{\varepsilon}(\mu_{t})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq d_{T,\varepsilon}^{2}(\mu,\nu)+1\leq C+1. $$

Set $M(t):=m_{2}(\mu_{t})$ . By Ito’s formula,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}M(t)=2\int_{E}x\cdot\alpha_{t}(x)\,\mu_{t}(\mathrm{d}x)+\varepsilon^{2}d\leq 2\|x\|_{L^{2}(\mu_{t})}\|\alpha_{t}\|_{L^{2}(\mu_{t})}+\varepsilon^{2}d. $$

Hence, by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}M(t)\leq M(t)+\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}+\varepsilon^{2}d. $$

From Grönwall’s inequality,

$$ \sup_{t\in[0,T]}M(t)\leq e^{T}M(0)+e^{T}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t+\varepsilon^{2}de^{T}. $$

From the near-optimality inequality and the lower bound (B.1),

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle\leq C+1-\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\ell_{\varepsilon}(\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle\leq C+1+\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\Big(C_{0}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\mathrm{d}t+C_{1}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}M(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\Big) \displaystyle\leq C+1+\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\Big(C_{0}+C_{1}\sup_{t\in[0,T]}M(t)\Big). $$

Using $e^{-t}\geq e^{-T}$ on $[0,T]$ , we have

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t\leq e^{T}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t\leq 2e^{T}(C+1)+\varepsilon^{2}e^{T}\Big(C_{0}+C_{1}\sup_{t\in[0,T]}M(t)\Big). $$

Inserting (B.3) into (B.2),

$$ \sup_{t\in[0,T]}M(t)\leq e^{T}M(0)+2e^{2T}(C+1)+\varepsilon^{2}e^{2T}C_{0}+\varepsilon^{2}e^{2T}C_{1}\sup_{t\in[0,T]}M(t)+\varepsilon^{2}de^{T}. $$

Now choose $\varepsilon_{*}(T)\in(0,1]$ such that $\varepsilon_{*}^{2}e^{2T}C_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2}$ . Then, for all $\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{*}(T)]$ ,

$$ \sup_{t\in[0,T]}M(t)\leq 2\Big(e^{T}m_{2}(\mu)+2e^{2T}(C+1)+e^{2T}C_{0}+de^{T}\Big)=:\bar{C}. $$

In particular $m_{2}(\nu)=M(T)\leq\bar{C}$ , which is the desired uniform moment bound. Finally, uniform second-moment bounds imply ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ -precompactness of sublevel sets, hence equi-coercivity. ∎

Now we present the proof of Theorem 3.3.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.3.

By Lemma B.3, the family $(F_{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}$ is equi-coercive in $({\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E),{\mathcal{W}}_{2})$ . It remains to prove the $\Gamma$ – $\liminf$ and $\Gamma$ – $\limsup$ inequalities.

Step 1 ( $\Gamma$ – $\liminf$ inequality). Let $\nu_{\varepsilon}\to\nu$ in ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ . If $\liminf_{\varepsilon\to 0}F_{\varepsilon}(\nu_{\varepsilon})=+\infty$ there is nothing to prove, so assume it is finite. Extract a sequence $\varepsilon_{n}\downarrow 0$ such that

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}F_{\varepsilon_{n}}(\nu_{\varepsilon_{n}})=\liminf_{\varepsilon\to 0}F_{\varepsilon}(\nu_{\varepsilon})<\infty. $$

For each $n$ , choose $(\bm{\mu}^{n},\alpha^{n})\in A_{T,\varepsilon_{n}}(\mu,\nu_{\varepsilon_{n}})$ such that

$$ \int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}^{n}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}^{n}+\ell_{\varepsilon_{n}}(\mu_{t}^{n})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq d_{T,\varepsilon_{n}}^{2}(\mu,\nu_{\varepsilon_{n}})+\frac{1}{n}. $$

By the uniform bound on $F_{\varepsilon_{n}}(\nu_{\varepsilon_{n}})$ and Lemma B.3, the curves $(\bm{\mu}^{n})_{n\geq 1}$ have uniformly bounded second moments and are equi-continuous in ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ . Hence, up to a subsequence,

$$ \bm{\mu}^{n}\to\bm{\mu}\quad\text{in }C([0,T];({\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E),{\mathcal{W}}_{2})),\qquad\mu_{0}=\mu,\ \mu_{T}=\nu. $$

Define the space–time flux measures $\mathbf{m}^{n}:=\mu_{t}^{n}\alpha_{t}^{n}\,\mathrm{d}t$ on $(0,T)\times E$ . The kinetic part in (B.4) yields a uniform bound on $\alpha^{n}$ in $L^{2}((0,T)\times E;\mu_{t}^{n}\mathrm{d}t)$ , hence $\{\mathbf{m}^{n}\}_{n\geq 1}$ is bounded in the dual of $C_{c}((0,T)\times E;\mathbb{R}^{m})$ . Thus, up to a subsequence, $\mathbf{m}^{n}\rightharpoonup\mathbf{m}$ weakly as vector measures.

Passing to the limit in the weak formulation of the Fokker–Planck equations

$$ \partial_{t}\mu_{t}^{n}+\nabla\!\cdot(\mu_{t}^{n}\alpha_{t}^{n})=\frac{\varepsilon_{n}^{2}}{2}\Delta\mu_{t}^{n}, $$

we obtain, since $\varepsilon_{n}^{2}\to 0$ ,

$$ \partial_{t}\mu_{t}+\nabla\!\cdot\mathbf{m}_{t}=0\quad\text{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}((0,T)\times E). $$

Moreover, $\mathbf{m}\ll\mu_{t}\mathrm{d}t$ , so there exists $\alpha\in L^{2}(\mu_{t}\mathrm{d}t)$ such that $\mathbf{m}_{t}=\mu_{t}\alpha_{t}$ ; hence $(\bm{\mu},\alpha)\in A_{T,0}(\mu,\nu)$ .

By convexity and standard lower semicontinuity,

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}^{n}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}^{n}\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

For the $\Gamma$ – $\liminf$ we only need

$$ \liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\ell_{\varepsilon_{n}}(\mu_{t}^{n})\,\mathrm{d}t\ \geq\ \int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\ell_{0}(\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t, $$

which follows from (B.5), the fact that $\ell_{\varepsilon}\to\ell_{0}$ pointwise, $\ell_{0}$ is lower-semicontinuous from Lemma B.2, and $(\ell_{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon\geq 0}$ are uniformly bounded from below on moment balls by Lemma B.1, allowing an application of Fatou’s lemma after extracting a further subsequence if needed.

Combining (B.4)–(B.8) gives

$$ \displaystyle d_{T,0}^{2}(\mu,\nu) \displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}+\ell_{0}(\mu_{t})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}^{n}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}^{n}+\ell_{\varepsilon_{n}}(\mu_{t}^{n})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}d_{T,\varepsilon_{n}}^{2}(\mu,\nu_{\varepsilon_{n}}). $$

Finally, since $V$ is ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ –l.s.c. and $\nu_{\varepsilon_{n}}\to\nu$ ,

$$ e^{-T}V(\nu)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}e^{-T}V(\nu_{\varepsilon_{n}}). $$

Therefore,

$$ F_{0}(\nu)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}F_{\varepsilon_{n}}(\nu_{\varepsilon_{n}})=\liminf_{\varepsilon\to 0}F_{\varepsilon}(\nu_{\varepsilon}), $$

which proves the $\Gamma$ – $\liminf$ inequality.

Step 2 ( $\Gamma$ – $\limsup$ inequality). Fix $\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E)$ and $\eta>0$ . Choose $(\bm{\mu},\alpha)\in A_{T,0}(\mu,\nu)$ such that

$$ \int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}+\ell_{0}(\mu_{t})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq d_{T,0}^{2}(\mu,\nu)+\eta. $$

We construct admissible pairs for $\varepsilon>0$ with terminal marginals $\nu_{\varepsilon}\to\nu$ .

Let $P_{s}$ denote the heat semigroup on $E$ . For $\varepsilon>0$ , define

$$ \mu_{t}^{\varepsilon}:=P_{\varepsilon^{2}t}\mu_{t},\qquad\mathbf{m}_{t}^{\varepsilon}:=P_{\varepsilon^{2}t}(\mu_{t}\alpha_{t}),\qquad\nu_{\varepsilon}:=\mu_{T}^{\varepsilon}=P_{\varepsilon^{2}T}\nu. $$

Then $\nu_{\varepsilon}\to\nu$ in ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$ . A standard commutation identity yields

$$ \partial_{t}\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon}+\nabla\!\cdot\mathbf{m}_{t}^{\varepsilon}=\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\Delta\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon}\quad\text{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}((0,T)\times E),\qquad\mu_{0}^{\varepsilon}=\mu,\ \mu_{T}^{\varepsilon}=\nu_{\varepsilon}, $$

so $(\bm{\mu}^{\varepsilon},\alpha^{\varepsilon})\in A_{T,\varepsilon}(\mu,\nu_{\varepsilon})$ , where $\mathbf{m}_{t}^{\varepsilon}=\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon}\alpha_{t}^{\varepsilon}$ .

By Jensen’s inequality, for a.e. $t$ ,

$$ \int_{E}|\alpha_{t}^{\varepsilon}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon}\leq\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}. $$

Hence, using (B.10) and the pointwise convergence $\ell_{\varepsilon}\to\ell_{0}$ on moment balls, together with $\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon}\to\mu_{t}$ in ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ uniformly in $t\in[0,T]$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle d_{T,\varepsilon}^{2}(\mu,\nu_{\varepsilon}) \displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}^{\varepsilon}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon}+\ell_{\varepsilon}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}+\ell_{\varepsilon}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle\xrightarrow[\varepsilon\to 0]{}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-t}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\int_{E}|\alpha_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}+\ell_{0}(\mu_{t})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq d_{T,0}^{2}(\mu,\nu)+\eta, $$

where the last inequality is (B.9). Moreover, $V(\nu_{\varepsilon})\to V(\nu)$ . Therefore,

$$ \limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}F_{\varepsilon}(\nu_{\varepsilon})\leq d_{T,0}^{2}(\mu,\nu)+\eta+e^{-T}V(\nu). $$

Letting $\eta\downarrow 0$ proves the $\Gamma$ – $\limsup$ inequality.

Step 3 (Convergence of minimizers). By Lemma B.3, $(F_{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon\geq 0}$ is equi-coercive, and by Steps 1–2 we have that $F_{\varepsilon}\ \Gamma$ –converges to $F_{0}$ in $({\mathcal{P}}_{2}(E),{\mathcal{W}}_{2})$ . The fundamental theorem of $\Gamma$ –convergence then yields: (i) $\min F_{\varepsilon}\to\min F_{0}$ , and (ii) any sequence of minimizers $\nu_{\varepsilon,T}\in\arg\min F_{\varepsilon}$ is precompact in ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ , and every ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ –limit point is a minimizer of $F_{0}$ . This proves the claim on convergence of minimizers (along subsequences). ∎

$$ \mathbb{E}\|g(\mu,\Theta)\|^{2}\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\|g(\mu_{n},\Theta_{n})\|^{2}. $$

Since $\Theta\sim\mu,\Theta_{n}\sim\mu_{n}$ , we conclude that

$$ G(\mu)^{2}\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}G(\mu_{n})^{2}. $$

∎

#### Proof of Corollary 4.5.

Let $\nu_{n}\to\nu$ in ${\mathcal{W}}_{2}$ . If $\liminf_{n}\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu_{n})=+\infty$ , there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, pass to a subsequence (not relabeled) such that

$$ \sup_{n}\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu_{n})<\infty. $$

For each $n$ , pick $\eta^{n}\in{\mathcal{A}}_{T,0}(\mu,\nu_{n})$ such that

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}|\eta^{n}{}^{\prime}|^{2}(t)+\tfrac{1}{2}G^{2}(\eta^{n}_{t})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu_{n})+\frac{1}{n}\leq\sup_{n}\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu_{n})+1. $$

In particular, the curves $(\eta^{n})_{n\geq 1}$ are equicontinuous since

$$ {\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\eta^{n}_{t},\eta^{n}_{s})\leq\int_{s}^{t}|\eta^{n}{}^{\prime}|(r)\,\mathrm{d}r\leq|t-s|^{1/2}\Big(\int_{0}^{T}|\eta^{n}{}^{\prime}|^{2}(r)\mathrm{d}r\Big)^{1/2},\quad\forall\,n\geq 1. $$

Moreover, since $\eta^{n}_{0}=\mu$ , we have

$$ {\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\mu,\eta^{n}_{t})\leq\int_{0}^{t}|\eta^{n}{}^{\prime}|(r)\,\mathrm{d}r\leq\sqrt{T}\Big(\int_{0}^{T}|\eta^{n}{}^{\prime}|^{2}(r)\,\mathrm{d}r\Big)^{1/2}\leq\sqrt{T}(\sup_{n}\mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu_{n})+1). $$

Hence $\{\eta^{n}_{t}:n\in\mathbb{N},\ t\in[0,T]\}$ is tight with uniformly bounded second moments, thus it is relatively compact in $({\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\Theta),{\mathcal{W}}_{2})$ . By Arzelà–Ascoli, there exist a subsequence (not relabeled) and a limit curve $\eta\in{\mathcal{A}}_{T,0}(\mu,\nu)$ , such that

$$ \sup_{t\in[0,T]}{\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\eta^{n}_{t},\eta_{t})\to 0. $$

From Lemma 4.4,

$$ G^{2}(\eta_{t})\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}G^{2}(\eta^{n}_{t})\qquad\text{for all }\,t\in[0,T], $$

and by Fatou’s lemma,

$$ \int_{0}^{T}G^{2}(\eta_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_{0}^{T}G^{2}(\eta^{n}_{t})\mathrm{d}t. $$

Combined with the fact that

$$ \int_{0}^{T}|\eta^{\prime}|^{2}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_{0}^{T}|\eta^{n}{}^{\prime}|^{2}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t, $$

this gives

$$ \mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu)\leq\int_{0}^{T}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}|\eta^{\prime}|^{2}(t)+\tfrac{1}{2}G^{2}(\eta_{t})\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\ \mathcal{E}_{G}^{T}(\mu,\nu_{n}). $$

∎

#### Proof of Lemma 4.15.

Let $\nu_{T}$ be the minimizer of $\Phi_{T}$ . Taking the constant curve $\bm{\eta}\equiv\mu$ , we obtain

$$ \Phi_{T}(\nu_{T})=L(\nu_{T})+\frac{1}{2T}{\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\mu,\nu_{T})^{2}\ \leq\ L(\mu)+\frac{1}{2T}{\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\mu,\mu)^{2}\ \leq\ L(\mu), $$

hence

$$ {\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\mu,\nu_{T})^{2}\leq 2T\,L(\mu), $$

and

$$ m_{2}(\nu_{T})\ \leq\ 2m_{2}(\mu)+2{\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\mu,\nu_{T})^{2}\ \leq\ 2m_{2}(\mu)\ +\ 4T\,L(\mu). $$

∎

## Abstract

This paper develops a policy gradient method for entropy-regularized mean-field control in the discounted infinite-horizon setting. We consider randomized feedback policies and a coupled representative-particle/population system, in which the representative state evolves jointly with a population law governed by a McKean–Vlasov equation. The resulting value function is therefore defined on the product space $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ .

A key distinction from existing policy gradient methods for mean-field control is that, after computing the value function under a fixed policy, our approach does not require solving an additional equation to obtain the policy gradient. Instead, we derive an explicit policy gradient formula directly in terms of the value function. The formulation is based on an instantaneous advantage function, which quantifies the gain of taking a given action relative to the current randomized policy. We establish a Gâteaux policy-gradient formula, which gives the first-order variation of the objective along arbitrary policy perturbations, and then derive the corresponding ascent direction under finite-dimensional policy parametrization.

The resulting formula leads to a model-based actor–critic scheme. The critic is obtained by solving the associated linear stationary Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation for the value function, using cylindrical functions to represent dependence on the population law. The actor is then updated according to the derived policy-gradient formula. We further analyze the well-posedness of the PDE in a polynomial-growth function class. Finally, we illustrate the proposed method through numerical experiments on an LQR model and a crowd-motion problem.

## 1. Introduction

Many control problems involve a large population of identical agents whose dynamics interact weakly, and only through the empirical distribution of the population. Such models arise naturally in applications including opinion formation [75, 40], biological swarming and flocking [34, 31], crowd dynamics [30], and financial systemic risk [26]. See also [24, 25, 17] for general background. When the number of agents $N$ is large, directly optimizing the full interacting $N$ -particle system becomes prohibitively difficult, both computationally and analytically. The mean-field viewpoint then replaces the full microscopic system by a limiting problem in which a representative agent interacts with the distribution of the population. This limit is closely related to the theory of interacting particle systems, propagation of chaos, and McKean–Vlasov (MKV) stochastic differential equations, where under suitable assumptions, the empirical measure of the $N$ -particle system converges to a measure-valued limit, and the state of a representative particle is then described by a stochastic differential equation whose coefficients depend on its own law; see, for instance, [24, 49].

From this large-population perspective, two different limiting formulations emerge. If one starts from a central control problem for the full population, or equivalently takes the mean-field limit of a socially optimal large-agent control problem, one is led to mean-field control (MFC), which is also known as McKean–Vlasov optimal control. If instead each agent optimizes an individual objective against the population and one then passes to the limit, one obtains a mean-field game (MFG), whose solution concept is Nash equilibrium. In this sense, MFC and MFG should be viewed as two distinct asymptotic regimes of large-population systems of exchangeable interacting agents. The key difference lies in whether the optimization is collective or strategic, and in the order in which optimization and passage to the limit are performed; see [22, 49, 50, 29, 17]. The present paper is concerned exclusively with the control formulation, namely MFC.

A distinctive feature of the present framework is the formulation of the controlled dynamics through a decoupled system: a MKV equation governing the evolution of the population law, coupled with an independent stochastic differential equation for a representative agent [20, 8]. In this formulation, the population flow $(\mu_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ is generated by the MKV equation and is deterministic, while the representative agent evolves according to its own SDE driven by an independent Brownian motion. A key advantage of this decoupled structure is that it allows the value function to be defined not only at the level of the population distribution, as is standard in the Wasserstein-space formulation [57], but also for any given initial position of the representative agent. The value function therefore takes as arguments both an initial state $s\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for the representative agent and an initial population law $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , a joint dependence that plays a central role in the derivation of the policy gradient and in the design of the actor-critic algorithm.

We work in the infinite-horizon discounted setting with entropy regularization and randomized feedback policies. This choice is natural for several reasons. First, entropy regularization promotes exploration and smooths the optimization over policies, a feature that is central in continuous-time reinforcement learning and remains analytically useful even when the controlled dynamics are known [76, 45, 46]. Second, the temperature parameter $\lambda>0$ connects the regularized problem to the classical deterministic formulation and yields a family of problems with better structural properties. Third, in the linear-quadratic setting, entropy regularization leads to explicit Gaussian optimal policies, which provide a tractable benchmark for the general theory.

The goal of this paper is to develop a model-based actor–critic method for mean-field control problems. Actor–critic methods are a standard class of algorithms in reinforcement learning, combining a critic, which evaluates the current policy, with an actor, which updates the policy [70, Chapter 13]. In our setting, for a fixed randomized feedback policy, the critic evaluates its performance through a HJB equation. The actor then improves the policy within a parametrized class, using a policy gradient formula for the performance functional, which is derived from a policy gradient theorem. We work in the model-based setting, that is, the dynamics are known. This allows us to focus on the analytic structure of the problem and provides a foundation for future data-driven extensions in [12].

A key difficulty is the structure of the policy gradient. In classical single-agent control, the gradient of the performance functional with respect to the policy parameters depends only on the state process and the corresponding advantage function. In the mean-field setting, by contrast, the performance functional depends on the policy through both the representative dynamics and the population flow induced by the same policy. As a result, the policy gradient theorem provided in this work decomposes into two structurally distinct contributions: a representative term, capturing the direct effect of the policy through the state dynamics, and a population term, capturing the indirect effect through the dependence of the value function on the population law. This decomposition has no counterpart in the standard single-agent theory and is one of the main contributions of the present paper.

#### Contributions.

- (1) Policy gradient theorem. We derive a rigorous policy gradient theorem for the coupled representative agent-population system in the infinite-horizon setting. The resulting formula separates the representative and population contributions to the gradient of the performance functional, expressed in terms of two advantage functions: the representative advantage function, which extends the classical single-agent structure, and the population advantage function, which is specific to the mean-field framework and involves the derivative of the value function on probability measure space. We also establish a parametric version of this formula for families of randomized policies, providing a rigorous basis for gradient-based policy improvement.

- (2) Policy evaluation and infinite-horizon mean-field LQR. We analyze the linear stationary Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation on $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ arising in the policy evaluation step and establish classical well-posedness results. We also study the infinite-horizon entropy-regularized mean-field LQR problem, deriving an explicit characterization of the optimal value function and the associated optimal Gaussian policy. This LQR analysis provides both an explicit benchmark for the general theory and a natural reference setting for the numerical experiments.

- (3) Actor-critic algorithm and numerical experiments. Based on the theoretical analysis, we introduce a finite-dimensional actor-critic algorithm combining a Galerkin approximation of the stationary HJB equation for policy evaluation with the policy gradient formula for policy improvement. Basis functions are constructed using cylindrical functions of the population law, for which the Lions derivatives entering the HJB operator can be evaluated in closed form. Numerical experiments on the mean-field systemic risk model and on a nonlinear two-dimensional crowd-aversion problem corroborate the theoretical results and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed method.

Related work.

Mean-field limits, propagation of chaos, and McKean–Vlasov control. The mean-field description of large populations of exchangeable interacting particles is classically tied to propagation of chaos and McKean–Vlasov (MKV) dynamics; see, for instance, [72, 16, 32, 24]. In the uncontrolled setting, the connection between MKV SDEs and associated PDEs was developed in [20]. In the controlled setting, rigorous limit theory linking finite-agent control problems with MKV control was established in [49] and further developed in [35]. The distinction between the cooperative mean-field control limit and the strategic mean-field game limit was clarified in [22]; see also [50, 29, 17, 25] for general background.

The theoretical foundations of MKV optimal control are well developed, particularly in finite time horizon. The stochastic Pontryagin maximum principle was derived in [23]; see also [18, 3, 19] for dynamics depending on moments of the law. The dynamic programming approach, leading to HJB equations on the Wasserstein space, was initiated in [57, 51]. Feynman–Kac representations for HJB equations on Wasserstein spaces were obtained in [8, 33]. Viscosity-solution results for MKV control were first studied in [39] for a problem from classical mechanics, and were later developed through the Lions lifting in [57, 58]. Related viscosity theories for equations on the Wasserstein space include the Eikonal equation [64, 65], comparison results for second-order PDEs [10, 9], and a fully second-order HJB theory [7]. We also refer to [21] for viscosity solutions in the setting of controlled MKV jump-diffusions. Infinite-horizon problems on Wasserstein spaces have been studied, for instance, in [43], although most of the above theory is formulated in finite time horizon.

Our analysis is complementary to this literature. Motivated by policy iteration (see [41, 70]), we focus on the linear stationary HJB equation associated with a fixed randomized policy. While most of the above works study HJB equations on $\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , our coupled system leads to a linear stationary HJB on $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , for which we establish existence and uniqueness of classical solutions.

Numerical methods for mean-field control and policy gradient. A broad range of numerical methods has been developed for mean-field control problems with known dynamics. PDE-based and augmented-Lagrangian methods have been proposed for mean-field type control problems with congestion effects [2, 1], while MKV control problems have also been approached through numerical schemes for the associated forward-backward stochastic differential equations [33]. We refer to [52] for a comprehensive survey on FBSDE for MKV, and dynamic programming based methods, including particle methods, and PDE-based discretizations. Related particle approximations for second-order PDEs on the Wasserstein space have been studied in [11]. In high-dimensional regimes, these methods are complemented by a growing literature based on deep learning and neural-network parametrizations; see, for instance, [62, 28, 63].

A related approximation paradigm, in the context of actor-critic, is linear value-function approximation, which is classical in reinforcement learning and is widely used to make policy evaluation and policy iteration computationally feasible in large or continuous state spaces; see, for instance, [71, 48, 4, 80]. In the mean-field-control setting, [15] develops learning algorithms with linear function approximation for finite-state, finite-action MFC problems and proves quantitative performance bounds. In the linear-quadratic setting, convergence and error analyses of policy-gradient methods have been studied in both discrete and continuous time [27, 77, 38]. The present paper is complementary to these works. Methods developed for discrete-time MDPs or mean-field MDPs do not transfer directly to the continuous-time diffusion setting. Indeed, the conventional state-action value function collapses to the value function as the sampling interval tends to zero, so that its action dependence survives only at the infinitesimal level through an instantaneous advantage rate; see [74, 47]. This motivates formulations of actor-critic methods that are intrinsic to the continuous-time dynamics.

We would like to mention two lines of work that is most related to this paper (also see Remarks 4.3, 4.7 and 4.10 for more detailed discussion). [37] derived a policy gradient formula for MFC in finite horizon by differentiating the HJB characterization of the value function with respect to the policy parameter, and more recently, they generalized this algorithm to moment neural network approximations [56]. Our work is closest in spirit to the above two works. Differentiating the HJB provides a natural route for parametric actor–critic methods, but it also requires solving an additional sensitivity equation, or equivalently an additional critic-type problem, to compute the ascent direction. In contrast, our approach derives an explicit policy-gradient formula directly in terms of the value function. This avoids the need for a separate sensitivity equation and leads to a simpler actor update. In addition, our formulation is first developed at the level of randomized feedback policies themselves. We characterize the Gâteaux policy gradient, namely the first-order variation of the objective along arbitrary admissible policy perturbations, before specializing it to finite-dimensional policy parametrizations. This gives a parameterization-free description of policy improvement and then yields an explicit ascent direction for parametrized policies. Finally, the policy gradient formulation is expressed through two instantaneous advantage functions, one for the representative-agent dynamics and one for the population-law dynamics. These advantages are defined from the value function and the infinitesimal generators, and do not require derivatives of the drift or diffusion with respect to the policy parameters. This form is closer to the classical policy-gradient structure in reinforcement learning, where the policy gradient is expressed in terms of an advantage function.

On the other hand, [79] also derives a related instantaneous advantage q-function for mean-field control. Their formulation is population-based, whereas ours is built on the coupled representative-agent/population system. More importantly, the advantage function plays a different role. [79] uses the instantaneous advantage to construct the integrated $q$ -functions for all test policies in a neighbourhood of the target policy. Then the martingale property of the integrated q-functions is used to solve the MFC. This integrated $q$ -function approach has been further developed in [78] for MFG and MFC problems, including jump-diffusion dynamics. More recent works extend this continuous-time $q$ -learning framework to MFC with controlled common noise [60, 61]. In that setting, the conditional population law is stochastic and the policy-improvement step becomes more implicit, leading to fixed-point characterizations of the optimal policy. In contrast with these papers, we use the pointwise-in-action $q$ -function directly to derive the policy-gradient formula, yielding an explicit actor update once $V^{\pi}$ and its derivatives are available. Thus, our actor–critic pipeline does not require an auxiliary integrated $q$ -function or testing over a neighborhood of policies.

Mean-field linear-quadratic control. The linear-quadratic structure has played a central role in mean-field control theory. In the finite-horizon setting, Riccati-based characterizations for mean-field stochastic linear-quadratic control were developed in [81], while the infinite-horizon problem with deterministic coefficients was studied in [42]. Subsequent works investigated the structural solvability of mean-field linear-quadratic problems, including closed-loop solvability [53], open-loop solvability [68], and weak closed-loop solvability [66]. Extensions to conditional McKean–Vlasov dynamics with random coefficients and common noise were obtained in [59, 6]. [37] analyze the entropy regularized finite-time mean-field LQR. More recently, long-time asymptotic properties, including turnpike behavior, have been studied in [13, 14].
