We complement this literature by analyzing an entropy-regularized infinite-horizon mean-field LQR problem with stationary randomized policies, for which the optimal Gaussian policy and the optimal value function are characterized explicitly through a coupled algebraic Riccati system.

## 2. Problem Formulation

Let $d,n,m\in\mathbb{N}$ . The state space is $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the action space is a Borel set $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}$ , and the population state is described by a measure in $\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , the set of Borel probability measures on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with finite second moment. We equip $\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ with the $2$ -Wasserstein distance

$$ \mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu,\varrho):=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu,\varrho)}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}|x-y|^{2}\,\gamma(dx,dy)\right)^{1/2}. $$

We consider an infinite-horizon discounted mean-field optimal control problem. Starting from an initial condition $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , where $s$ denotes the state of a representative agent and $\mu$ the distribution of the population, a social planner seeks to optimize the collective performance of the system over time. The objective is to maximize the expected discounted reward generated by the controlled mean-field dynamics. This leads to the optimal value function over an admissible set $\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$

$$ \displaystyle V^{*}(s,\mu)\,:=\,\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}}V^{\pi}(s,\mu),\qquad(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). $$

Here $V^{\pi}(s,\mu)$ denotes the value associated with a policy $\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ when the system starts from $(s,\mu)$ . Whenever there exists a policy $\pi^{*}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ such that $V^{*}(s,\mu)=V^{\pi^{*}}(s,\mu)$ for all $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , we call $\pi^{*}$ an optimal policy.

More precisely, for a given policy $\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ , the corresponding value is defined by

$$ \displaystyle V^{\pi}(s,\mu)\,:=\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\,r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t},\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\;\bigg|\;s_{0}=s,\ \mu_{0}=\mu\right], $$

where $\beta>0$ is the discount factor, $r_{\lambda}^{\pi}$ is the running reward, and $(s_{t},\mu_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ denotes the controlled representative-population state process. In classical mean-field control, one often works with deterministic feedback controls. In the present work, by contrast, we allow for randomized feedback policies. This choice is natural in reinforcement learning, where exploration plays a central role and is naturally encoded through Markov kernels. Accordingly, we take $\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ to be the class of Markov kernels

$$ \pi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\longrightarrow\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}),\qquad(x,\mu)\longmapsto\pi(\cdot|x,\mu), $$

such that $\pi(\cdot|x,\mu)\ll\nu$ for every $(x,\mu)$ , with jointly measurable density $p_{\pi}(\cdot|x,\mu)$ , where $\nu$ denotes a $\sigma$ -finite reference measure on $(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{A}))$ . The running reward in (2) is the entropy-regularized averaged reward

$$ \displaystyle r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(x,\mu) \displaystyle:=r^{\pi}(x,\mu)+\lambda\,\mathcal{H}\bigl(\pi(\cdot|x,\mu)\bigr) \displaystyle:=\int_{\mathcal{A}}r(x,\mu,a)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a|x,\mu)-\lambda\int_{\mathcal{A}}\log p_{\pi}(a|x,\mu)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a|x,\mu), $$

where $\lambda>0$ is the temperature parameter. Entropy regularization is standard in continuous-time reinforcement learning and promotes exploration; see, for instance, [76, 45, 46, 47, 79, 37].

We now introduce the controlled dynamics associated with a policy $\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ . Let $b:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\sigma:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ be measurable coefficients. The averaged drift and diffusion matrix induced by $\pi$ are defined by

$$ \displaystyle b^{\pi}(x,\mu):=\int_{\mathcal{A}}b(x,\mu,a)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a|x,\mu),\qquad\Sigma^{\pi}(x,\mu):=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\sigma(x,\mu,a)\sigma(x,\mu,a)^{\top}\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a|x,\mu), $$

and we write $\sigma^{\pi}(x,\mu):=\bigl(\Sigma^{\pi}(x,\mu)\bigr)^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ for the symmetric positive semidefinite square root of $\Sigma^{\pi}$ . The representative state process then solves

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}s_{t}=b^{\pi}(s_{t},\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma^{\pi}(s_{t},\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}B_{t},\qquad s_{0}=s, $$

while the population distribution $\mu_{t}$ is generated by the McKean-Vlasov equation

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}\tilde{s}_{t}=b^{\pi}(\tilde{s}_{t},\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma^{\pi}(\tilde{s}_{t},\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{B}_{t},\qquad\tilde{s}_{0}\sim\mu,\qquad\mu_{t}=\Law(\tilde{s}_{t}), $$

where $B$ and $\tilde{B}$ are independent $d$ -dimensional Brownian motions. The pair $(s_{t},\mu_{t})$ appearing in (2) is therefore obtained by coupling a representative agent with the population law generated by (5).

Formally, for each initial condition $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and each horizon $T>0$ , we work on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ endowed with a filtration $\mathbb{F}=(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{0\leq t\leq T}$ such that $\mathcal{F}_{0}$ contains all $\mathbb{P}$ -null sets of $\mathcal{F}$ , the filtration is right-continuous, and $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{F},\mathbb{P})$ supports two independent $d$ -dimensional $\mathbb{F}$ -Brownian motions $B$ and $\tilde{B}$ , together with an $\mathcal{F}_{0}$ -measurable random variable $\tilde{s}_{0}$ satisfying $\Law(\tilde{s}_{0})=\mu$ and independent of $(B,\tilde{B})$ . The representative component starts from the deterministic value $s$ . Under Assumption 3.1 (below), the population equation admits a unique strong $\mathbb{F}$ -adapted solution $\tilde{s}$ , and we then define $\mu_{t}:=\Law(\tilde{s}_{t})$ ; in particular, $(\mu_{t})_{0\leq t\leq T}$ is a deterministic flow in $\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ ; see [29, Chapter 4]. Once this flow is fixed, due to Assumption 3.1, the representative dynamics is an $\mathbb{F}$ -adapted stochastic differential equation, and therefore it also admits a unique strong solution.

#### Remark 2.1 (On randomized and aggregated formulations).

The state–law formulation adopted here, namely a representative state coupled with a population law flow on $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , is consistent with the general McKean–Vlasov framework of [20] in the uncontrolled case and [8] in the control setting.

Given a stochastic policy $\pi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}),$ the most direct non-averaged formulation is to sample actions continuously in time according to the current state and population law, namely

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}s_{t}=b(s_{t},\mu_{t},a_{t}^{s})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma(s_{t},\mu_{t},a_{t}^{s})\,\mathrm{d}B_{t},\quad a_{t}^{s}\sim\pi(\cdot|s_{t},\mu_{t}), \displaystyle\mathrm{d}\tilde{s}_{t}=b(\tilde{s}_{t},\mu_{t},a_{t}^{\mu})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma(\tilde{s}_{t},\mu_{t},a_{t}^{\mu})\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{B}_{t},\quad a_{t}^{\mu}\sim\pi(\cdot|\tilde{s}_{t},\mu_{t}),\quad\mu_{t}=\Law(\tilde{s}_{t}) $$

Formally, one may realize the sampling through a measurable map $\Phi_{\pi}(x,\mu,u)$ such that $\Phi_{\pi}(x,\mu,U)\sim\pi(\cdot|x,\mu)$ for $U\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1]$ , and then set $a_{t}^{s}=\Phi_{\pi}(s_{t},\mu_{t},U_{t}^{s})$ , $a_{t}^{\mu}=\Phi_{\pi}(\tilde{s}_{t},\mu_{t},U_{t}^{\mu})$ . The difficulty is that, on the usual product space, a continuum of independent samples in time need not be jointly measurable in $(t,\omega)$ , so the coefficients may fail to be progressively measurable; see [73, Remark 2.1]. A rigorous pathwise construction is nevertheless possible on a suitable enriched product space, for instance a rich Fubini extension in the sense of [69]; this is precisely the route taken in [37] for (6)–(7).

A different non-averaged interpretation is to sample the action only on a time grid and then keep it constant between intervention times. This produces an SDE with piecewise constant random controls on the usual probability space. Related piecewise constant randomizations also appear in [8] within the randomized McKean–Vlasov control problem, while in the continuous-time reinforcement learning literature such sampled dynamics are studied in [73, 44]. In general, discretely sampled dynamics do not coincide with the aggregated dynamics; rather, they converge to them as the mesh size tends to zero; see [44, Theorems 4.1–4.2].

By contrast, the aggregated formulation (4)–(5) is the appropriate law-level representation of the continuously randomized model (6)-(7). More precisely, whenever (6)-(7) is constructed on an enriched space and is well posed, the law of its state process solves the same McKean–Vlasov martingale problem as the aggregated system (4)–(5). Hence, under weak uniqueness, both formulations induce the same law and therefore the same value functional; see [79, Lemma A.1], [36, 49] and [37, Proof of Prop. 2.1].

#### Organization of the paper.

The rest of the paper is devoted to approximating the optimal policy of (1) through an actor–critic iteration. Given a parametrized randomized policy $\pi_{\omega}$ , each iteration consists of two steps:

- (1) Policy evaluation. For the current policy $\pi_{\omega}$ , the critic computes or approximates the value function $V^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)$ by solving the associated linear stationary HJB equation.

- (2) Policy improvement. The actor updates the policy parameters using a policy gradient formula for the performance functional $J(\omega)=\mathbb{E}[V^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)]$ , for instance through the gradient ascent step $\omega\leftarrow\omega+\alpha\nabla_{\omega}J(\omega)$ .

In Section 3, we study the policy-evaluation step and show that, for a fixed admissible policy, the value function is the unique classical solution of the associated stationary Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation. In Section 4, we derive the policy gradient theorem and its parametric version for the coupled representative agent–population system. In Section 5, we describe how the actor–critic method can be implemented in practice in the model-based setting. Section 6 analyzes the entropy-regularized infinite-horizon mean-field linear-quadratic regulator, which provides an explicit benchmark for the general theory. Finally, Section 7 presents numerical examples illustrating our method.

## 3. The Stationary HJB Equation

The central object of study in this section is the value function $V^{\pi}$ defined in (2). Our goal is to characterize it as the unique classical solution of a stationary Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation.

### 3.1. The infinitesimal generator and stationary HJB equation

The dynamics of the pair $(s_{t},\mu_{t})$ under policy $\pi$ are governed by (4)-(5). To differentiate a function $F:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to\mathbb{R}$ with respect to the measure argument $\mu$ , we rely on the notion of Lions derivative, introduced by Lions in his lectures at the Collège de France [54] and further developed in [24, 29]. Applying the Itô-Lions formula to a smooth function $F:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to\mathbb{R}$ and taking expectations, one identifies the infinitesimal generator of $(s_{t},\mu_{t})$ as the operator

$$ \displaystyle(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}F)(s,\mu) \displaystyle:=b^{\pi}(s,\mu)\cdot\nabla_{s}F(s,\mu)+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\Sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu):\nabla^{2}_{ss}F(s,\mu) \displaystyle+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\Bigl[b^{\pi}(\xi,\mu)\cdot\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\Sigma^{\pi}(\xi,\mu):D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)\Bigr]\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\xi), $$

where $\xi\mapsto\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)$ denotes the Lions derivative of $F$ with respect to $\mu$ , evaluated at $(s,\mu,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . We also denote by $D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)$ the Jacobian matrix of $\xi\mapsto\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)$ with respect to $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . For a comprehensive treatment we refer to [24, Chapter 5] and [29, Chapter 1]. Also $A:B:=\mathrm{Tr}(A^{\top}B)$ is the Frobenius inner product, $\nabla_{s}F$ and $\nabla^{2}_{ss}F$ are the gradient and Hessian of $F$ with respect to $s\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ .

The generator (8) has two parts: the first line is the classical Itô generator for $s_{t}$ driven by $b^{\pi}$ and $\Sigma^{\pi}$ , that is (4), while the integral term captures the variation of $F$ as the measure $\mu_{t}=\mathcal{L}(\tilde{s}_{t})$ evolves under the McKean-Vlasov equation (5).

In order to simplify the exposition we introduce the following class of functions.

#### Definition 3.1 ( $\mathcal{C}^{2,2}$ functions with polynomial growth).

Let $k\in\mathbb{N}$ . A map $F:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to\mathbb{R}^{k}$ belongs to $\mathcal{C}^{2,2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ if, for every $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , the map $s\mapsto F(s,\mu)$ is twice continuously differentiable on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , and, for every $s\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the map $\mu\mapsto F(s,\mu)$ is Lions differentiable on $\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ . Moreover, the maps $(s,\mu,\xi)\mapsto\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)$ and $(s,\mu,\xi)\mapsto D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)$ are jointly continuous.

We say that $F\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ if $F\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ and there exists a constant $C_{F}>0$ such that, for all $(s,\mu,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|F(s,\mu)| \displaystyle\leq C_{F}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), \displaystyle\|\nabla_{s}F(s,\mu)\|+|\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)| \displaystyle\leq C_{F}\bigl(1+|s|+|\xi|+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), \displaystyle\|D^{2}_{ss}F(s,\mu)\|+\|D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)\| \displaystyle\leq C_{F}\bigl(1+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), $$

where $m_{p}(\mu)$ denotes the $p-$ th moment of $\mu$ .

To establish $\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}$ regularity of $V^{\pi}$ and the existence of a solution of the HJB equation in the classical sense, we additionally require the following smoothness on the policy-aggregated coefficients.

(A1) $\mathcal{C}^{2,2}$ -regularity of averaged coefficients. Let $\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ be fixed. We assume that, for every component $h\in\{b_{i}^{\pi},\sigma_{i,j}^{\pi}:i,j=1,\dots,d\}$ , the derivatives $\nabla_{s}h(s,\mu)$ , $D^{2}_{ss}h(s,\mu)$ , $\partial_{\mu}h(s,\mu)(\xi)$ , and $D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}h(s,\mu)(\xi)$ exist for all $(s,\mu,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , are bounded by a constant $K_{\pi}$ , and are locally Lipschitz continuous in $(s,\mu,\xi)$ . Also assume that $r_{\lambda}^{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})).$

#### Remark 3.2.

Using Section 3.1 we can assume for simplicity that $K_{\pi}>0$ is big enough such that for all $s\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|b^{\pi}(s,\mu)|+\|\sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)\|\leq K_{\pi}\bigl(1+|s|+\sqrt{m_{2}(\mu)}\bigr). $$

Also, since the bounded derivatives in Section 3.1 ensure the existence of $L_{\pi}>0$ such that for all $s,s^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\mu,\mu^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|b^{\pi}(s,\mu)-b^{\pi}(s^{\prime},\mu^{\prime})|+\|\sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)-\sigma^{\pi}(s^{\prime},\mu^{\prime})\|\leq L_{\pi}\bigl(|s-s^{\prime}|+\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu,\mu^{\prime})\bigr). $$

Moreover, since $\Sigma^{\pi}=\sigma^{\pi}(\sigma^{\pi})^{\top}$ , it follows from Section 3.1 and the product rule that $\Sigma^{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ , and there exists $C_{\pi}>0$ such that, for all $(s,\mu,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\Sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)\|\leq C_{\pi}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), \displaystyle\|\nabla_{s}\Sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)\|+|\partial_{\mu}\Sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)|+\|D^{2}_{ss}\Sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)\|+\|D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}\Sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)\| \displaystyle\leq C_{\pi}\bigl(1+|s|+\sqrt{m_{2}(\mu)}\bigr). $$

We can now state the main result of this section, which characterizes the infinite-horizon value function as the unique classical solution of the stationary Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation.

#### Theorem 3.3 (Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation).

Let $\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ be a fixed admissible policy and suppose Assumption 3.1 holds. Then there exists a constant $\bar{\beta}_{\pi}>0$ , depending only on the structural constants in Assumption 3.1, such that the following holds. If $\beta>\bar{\beta}_{\pi}$ , then the value function $V^{\pi}$ defined in (2) is well defined and belongs to $\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ . Moreover, $V^{\pi}$ is a classical solution of

$$ \displaystyle(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}-\beta)V^{\pi}(s,\mu)+r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s,\mu)=0,\qquad(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), $$

where $\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}$ is given by (8). Finally, $V^{\pi}$ is the unique classical solution of (11) in the class $\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ . Moreover, assume in addition for all $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$

$$ \displaystyle 2\,s\cdot b^{\pi}(s,\mu)+\|\sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)\|_{F}^{2}\leq C_{0}-\kappa|s|^{2}+C_{\mathrm{diss}}\,m_{2}(\mu) $$

holds. Then the value function $V^{\pi}$ is well defined for every $\beta>0$ and there exists $C_{r}>0$ such that $|r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s,\mu)|\leq C_{r}(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu))$ . Furthermore, if $C_{0}=0$ then $V^{\pi}$ is also well defined for $\beta=0$ .

The proof of Theorem 3.3 is provided in Section A.1. Several remarks on the above theorem follows.

First, the constant $\bar{\beta}_{\pi}$ in Theorem 3.3 is defined by $\bar{\beta}_{\pi}=\max\{\beta_{0}(2),\beta_{\mathrm{var}}(2)\}$ , where $\beta_{0}(2)$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{var}}(2)$ are given explicitly in Remarks A.2 and A.5, and depend only on $d$ and $K_{\pi}$ .

Second, once the policy $\pi$ is fixed, the stationary HJB equation becomes linear. The proof of Proposition 6.4 then relies on two preliminary lemmas. The first one provides explicit exponential-in-time $L^{p}$ bounds for the state processes, while the second one gives exponential-in-time bounds for the derivatives with respect to the state and measure variables. These estimates are the key input in the infinite-horizon argument, since they quantify precisely how the growth in time interacts with the discount factor. Starting from these identities, the proof combines the finite-horizon result of [38] with a passage to the limit as $T\to\infty$ . The previous lemmas ensure that this limit can be performed both at the level of the value function and in the equation itself, which yields the classical solution of the stationary HJB equation together with uniqueness in the polynomial-growth class. The argument is also closely related in spirit to the McKean-Vlasov PDE framework of [20], although the latter deals with finite-horizon problems, whereas here we consider an infinite-horizon discounted setting.

## 4. Policy Gradient

This section develops the policy improvement step for the mean-field control problem introduced in Section 2. The policy evaluation step has already been addressed in Section 3: given a feedback randomized policy $\pi$ , the value function $V^{\pi}$ is well defined and can be characterized as the unique classical solution of a stationary HJB equation. The goal of the present section is to derive an explicit formula for the gradient of the performance functional with respect to a parametric family of policies.

A distinctive feature of the mean-field setting is that the performance functional depends on two initial data: the initial law $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ generating the population flow, and the initial distribution $\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ of the representative agent. Throughout this section, $\mu$ is fixed and the performance of a policy $\pi$ is measured by

$$ J_{\mu,\mu_{0}}(\pi)\;:=\;\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)\,\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}s). $$

For a parametric family $\{\pi_{\omega}\}_{\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}$ we write

$$ J(\omega)\;:=\;J_{\mu,\mu_{0}}(\pi_{\omega})\;=\;\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)\,\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}s). $$

The main difficulty is that $J(\omega)$ depends on $\omega$ both through the representative dynamics and through the induced mean-field flow. In what follows we will provide a policy gradient theorem and a result for the parametrized case.

#### Remark 4.1.

For any $s_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the Dirac measure $\delta_{s_{0}}$ belongs to $\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ . Hence, by choosing $\mu_{0}=\delta_{s_{0}}$ , the results of this section apply to the pointwise performance functional $J_{\mu,s_{0}}(\pi):=V^{\pi}(s_{0},\mu)$ as well.

### 4.1. Policy gradient theorem

Let $\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ and let $\varphi$ be a measurable signed kernel $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{A})$ satisfying

$$ \varphi(\cdot\mid s,\mu)\ll\pi(\cdot\mid s,\mu),\qquad\int_{\mathcal{A}}\varphi(\mathrm{d}a\mid s,\mu)=0,\qquad(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), $$

with bounded Radon-Nikodym derivative $\psi:=\mathrm{d}\varphi/\mathrm{d}\pi\in L^{\infty}$ . The zero-mass condition in (14) ensures that $\pi^{\varepsilon}$ remains a probability kernel for small $\varepsilon$ . For $|\varepsilon|$ small, define the perturbed kernel

$$ \pi^{\varepsilon}(\mathrm{d}a\mid s,\mu):=\pi(\mathrm{d}a\mid s,\mu)+\varepsilon\,\varphi(\mathrm{d}a\mid s,\mu)=\bigl(1+\varepsilon\psi(s,\mu,a)\bigr)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a\mid s,\mu), $$

and assume $\pi^{\varepsilon}$ is an admissible feedback randomized policy for all sufficiently small $|\varepsilon|$ .

Before introducing the policy gradient theorem, we introduce the following advantage functions.

#### Definition 4.2 (Advantage functions).

Let $\pi$ be a feedback randomized policy with value function $V^{\pi}$ . For $(s,\mu,a)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\times\mathcal{A}$ , define the representative advantage function

$$ q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{rep}}(s,\mu,a)\;:=\;r(s,\mu,a)-\lambda\log p_{\pi}(a\mid s,\mu)+b(s,\mu,a)\cdot\nabla_{s}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\Sigma(s,\mu,a):D^{2}_{ss}V^{\pi}(s,\mu), $$

and for $(\xi,a)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{A}$ , define the population advantage function

$$ q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{pop}}(s,\mu,\xi,a)\;:=\;b(\xi,\mu,a)\cdot\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\Sigma(\xi,\mu,a):D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi). $$

#### Remark 4.3 (Interpretation of the advantage functions).

In standard reinforcement learning, the advantage function can be written through the Bellman evaluation identity as

$$ A^{\pi}(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[V^{\pi}(S^{\prime})\mid S=s,\mathfrak{a}=a\right]-V^{\pi}(s). $$

Thus, it compares the effect of taking the action $a$ with the value generated by the policy. In the single-agent continuous-time setting, the same structure is expressed through the infinitesimal generator, so that the corresponding action-dependent term is given by the running reward plus the generator applied to the value function, minus the discount term.

The present mean-field setting preserves this structure. The representative advantage function $q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{rep}}$ is the natural extension of the single-agent continuous-time term: it contains the entropy-regularized instantaneous reward together with the contribution of the generator acting on the state variable [47, 5, 74, 82]. The population advantage function $q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{pop}}$ is specific to the mean-field framework and describes the additional contribution coming from the dependence of $V^{\pi}$ on the population law through its Lions derivatives. In this way, the classical advantage structure is decomposed into a representative part and a population part.

Finally, let us note that [79] introduces two q-functions in the McKean–Vlasov control setting, an integrated q-function and an essential q-function. The integrated q-function is a central object in the proposed learning procedure. Since its weak martingale characterization is formulated with respect to all test policies in a neighbourhood of the target policy, its practical implementation relies on averaging the corresponding loss over nearby test policies. The essential q-function plays the role of a pointwise-in-action quantity for policy improvement, and in this respect our kernels $q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{rep}}$ and $q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{pop}}$ are closer in spirit to that object, although our formulation is for the coupled representative-agent / population system rather than for the population-only formulation. The main difference is that, in our actor–critic pipeline, the policy gradient theorem requires only the pointwise-in-action kernels $q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{rep}}$ and $q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{pop}}$ , which are obtained directly from $V^{\pi}$ and its derivatives. Therefore, no auxiliary integrated q-function is needed, nor does our approach require testing over a neighbourhood of the target policy.

#### Definition 4.4 (Discounted occupancy measure).

Let $\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ be a fixed policy, and let $(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})_{t\geq 0}$ be the state-population process associated with (4)-(5) starting from $s_{0}^{\pi}=s\sim\mu_{0},$ and $\mu_{0}^{\pi}=\mu$ . The discounted occupancy measure $\rho_{\mu,\mu_{0}}^{\pi}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ is defined by

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{\mu,\mu_{0}}^{\pi}(B):=\beta\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\in B\}}\,\mathrm{d}t\right],\qquad B\in\mathcal{B}\bigl(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\bigr). $$

#### Remark 4.5 (Equivalent representations of $\rho_{\mu,\mu_{0}}^{\pi}$ ).

For $t\geq 0$ , let $P_{t}^{\pi}(s_{0},\mu;\cdot):=\Law(s_{t}^{\pi}\mid s_{0},\mu)$ . Then, by Tonelli’s theorem, $\rho_{\mu,\mu_{0}}^{\pi}$ admits the representation

$$ \rho_{\mu,\mu_{0}}^{\pi}(B)=\beta\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathbf{1}_{B}(x,\mu_{t}^{\pi})\,P_{t}^{\pi}(s_{0},\mu;\mathrm{d}x)\,\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}s_{0})\right)\mathrm{d}t,\qquad B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})). $$

Moreover, denoting by $\delta_{\mu_{t}^{\pi}}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ the Dirac measure at $\mu_{t}^{\pi}$ , the previous identity can be written equivalently, in measure form, as

$$ \rho_{\mu,\mu_{0}}^{\pi}(\mathrm{d}x,\mathrm{d}\nu)=\beta\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}P_{t}^{\pi}(s_{0},\mu;\mathrm{d}x)\,\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}s_{0})\right)\delta_{\mu_{t}^{\pi}}(\mathrm{d}\nu)\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

#### Theorem 4.6 (Gâteaux policy gradient).

Fix a baseline policy $\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ . Let $\varphi$ be a signed kernel satisfying (14), and let $\pi^{\varepsilon}$ be as in (15), admissible for all $|\varepsilon|\leq\varepsilon_{0}$ . Suppose Assumption 3.1 holds for both $\pi$ and $\pi^{\varepsilon}$ , with $|\varepsilon|\leq\varepsilon_{0}$ . Assume $\mu,\;\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and $\beta>2\bar{\beta}_{\pi}$ , where $\bar{\beta}_{\pi}$ from Theorem 3.3. Then the map $\varepsilon\mapsto J(\varepsilon):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s,\mu)\,\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}s)$ is differentiable at $\varepsilon=0$ , with

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}J(\varepsilon)\bigg|_{\varepsilon=0}=\frac{1}{\beta}\mathbb{E}_{(s,\mu)\sim\rho_{\mu,\mu_{0}}^{\pi}}\!\left[\int_{\mathcal{A}}q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{rep}}(s,\mu,a)\,\varphi(\mathrm{d}a\mid s,\mu)+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\int_{\mathcal{A}}q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{pop}}(s,\mu,\xi,a)\,\varphi(\mathrm{d}a\mid\xi,\mu)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\xi)\right]. $$

The proof of Theorem 4.6 is provided in Section A.2.

#### Remark 4.7.

The preceding theorem, together with Theorem 4.9, is a key contribution of this paper and distinguishes our approach from existing policy-gradient methods and related $q$ -function-based algorithms. Compared with [37], we provide a parameterization-free formulation of the policy gradient, which describes the first-order variation of the objective under arbitrary admissible perturbations of the policy. Compared with [79], we use the pointwise $q$ -functions to derive the policy-gradient formula directly, while their method requires computing the integrated q-functions for all test policies in a neighbourhood of the target policy.

### 4.2. Parametric policy gradient

The Gâteaux gradient formula (16) expresses the directional derivative of $J$ in terms of an arbitrary signed kernel $\varphi$ . In practice, policies are often parametrized by a finite dimensional vector $\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ , and one wishes to compute $\nabla_{\omega}J(\omega)$ directly. The parametric policy gradient theorem below reduces this computation to a weighted expectation of the advantage functions against the score function. To state the result precisely, we require the following two assumptions on the parametric family.

(A2) Parametric differentiability of averaged coefficients. For $\nu$ -almost every $a\in\mathcal{A}$ and every $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , the map $\omega\mapsto\log p_{\pi_{\omega}}(a\mid s,\mu)$ is continuously differentiable. Moreover, for every compact set $K\subset\mathbb{R}^{p}$ , there exists $C_{K}>0$ and a function $g_{K}(\cdot,s,\mu)\in L^{1}(\mathcal{A},\nu)$ such that for all $\omega\in K$ and all $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , the maps $\omega\mapsto p_{\pi_{\omega}}(\cdot\mid s,\mu)$ , $\omega\mapsto b^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)$ , $\omega\mapsto\Sigma^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)$ , and $\omega\mapsto r_{\lambda}^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)$ are continuously differentiable, satisfying

$$ \displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\bigl\|\nabla_{\omega}p_{\pi_{\omega}}(a\mid s,\mu)\bigr\|\leq g_{K}(a,s,\mu)\qquad\text{for $\nu$-a.e. }a\in\mathcal{A}.\\
&\|\nabla_{\omega}b^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)\|\leq C_{K}\bigl(1+|s|+\sqrt{m_{2}(\mu)}\bigr),\\
\|\nabla_{\omega}r_{\lambda}^{\pi_{\omega}}&(s,\mu)\|+\|\nabla_{\omega}\Sigma^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)\|\leq C_{K}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr).\end{aligned} $$

(A3) Uniform regularity of the parametric family. Assumption 3.1 holds for every $\pi_{\omega}$ , with Lipschitz constant $L_{\pi}$ and regularity constant $K_{\pi}$ independent of $\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ .

#### Remark 4.8 (On the Assumptions 3.1-4.2).

The Gaussian policy $\pi_{\omega}(\cdot\mid s,\mu):=\mathcal{N}(f_{\omega}(s,\mu),\Sigma_{0})$ , with $\Sigma_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ positive definite, satisfies Assumptions 3.1-4.2 whenever $f_{\omega}$ is Lipschitz with linear growth in $(s,\mu)$ , belongs to $\mathcal{C}^{2,2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ with all spatial and Lions derivatives of at most polynomial growth in $(s,\mu,\xi)$ , and $\omega\mapsto f_{\omega}(s,\mu)$ is continuously differentiable with at most polynomial growth in $(s,\mu)$ ; all uniformly in $\omega$ on compact sets. In particular, this holds when $f_{\omega}$ is linear in $s$ and $m_{1}(\mu)$ , or when $f_{\omega}$ is a cylindrical neural network [55, Section 2.2] with $\mathcal{C}^{2}$ activation function of at most linear growth, such as $\tanh$ or $\mathrm{GELU}$ .

#### Theorem 4.9 (Parametric policy gradient).

Let $\{\pi_{\omega}\}_{\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}$ be a family of feedback randomized policies satisfying Assumptions 3.1-4.2. Fix $\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ and set $\pi:=\pi_{\omega}$ . Assume $\mu,\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and $\beta>\widetilde{\beta}_{\pi}:=\max(\bar{\beta}_{\pi},\,2\beta_{0}(2))$ . Then the map $\omega\mapsto J(\omega)$ , defined in (13), is differentiable at $\omega$ , and

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{\omega}J(\omega) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\beta}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(s,\mu)\sim\rho_{\mu,\mu_{0}}^{\pi}\\
a\sim\pi(\cdot|s,\mu)\end{subarray}}\!\Bigl[q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{rep}}(s,\mu,a)\,\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi}(a|s,\mu)\Bigr]\!+\frac{1}{\beta}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(s,\mu)\sim\rho_{\mu,\mu_{0}}^{\pi}\\
\xi\sim\mu\\
a\sim\pi(\cdot|\xi,\mu)\end{subarray}}\!\Bigl[q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{pop}}(s,\mu,\xi,a)\,\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi}(a|\xi,\mu)\Bigr]. $$

Equivalently, this can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{\omega}J(\omega) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\beta}\mathbb{E}_{(s,\mu)\sim\rho_{\mu,\mu_{0}}^{\pi}}\!\left[\int_{\mathcal{A}}q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{rep}}(s,\mu,a)\,\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi}(a\mid s,\mu)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a\mid s,\mu)\right] \displaystyle+\frac{1}{\beta}\mathbb{E}_{(s,\mu)\sim\rho_{\mu,\mu_{0}}^{\pi}}\!\left[\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\!\int_{\mathcal{A}}q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{pop}}(s,\mu,\xi,a)\,\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi}(a\mid\xi,\mu)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a\mid\xi,\mu)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\xi)\right]. $$

The proof of Theorem 4.9 is given in Section A.2.

#### Remark 4.10.

The identity (18) keeps the classical policy-gradient form of advantage times score, but now with two terms. The first expectation involves $q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{rep}}$ and corresponds to the representative-agent contribution, whereas the second involves $q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{pop}}$ and captures the population contribution.

From a computational viewpoint, once $V^{\pi}$ has been evaluated or approximated, the quantities entering (18) are obtained directly from $V^{\pi}$ , $b^{\pi}$ , $\Sigma^{\pi}$ , and the score function $\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi}(a\mid s,\mu)$ . The expectations with respect to $\rho_{\mu,\mu_{0}}^{\pi}$ can then be approximated from trajectories of the controlled dynamics under the current policy $\pi_{\omega}$ , together with samples of actions drawn from $\pi_{\omega}(\cdot\mid s,\mu)$ . This is precisely the mechanism underlying the actor–critic algorithm described in Section 5.

The formula (18) should be contrasted with the policy-gradient representation in [37]. In [37], the gradient is obtained by differentiating the HJB characterization of the value function with respect to the policy parameter. As a result, the gradient itself is characterized as the solution of another linear HJB equation, whose source term is constructed from the value function under the current policy. Thus, computing the ascent direction requires solving an additional policy-evaluation-type problem. By contrast, (18) gives an explicit gradient formula once $V^{\pi}$ and its derivatives are available. This makes the actor step more direct.

Moreover, the differentiated HJB equation in [37] contains an additional term $H_{\omega}[J]$ , which involves the derivatives $\nabla_{\omega}b^{\pi_{\omega}}$ and $\nabla_{\omega}\Sigma^{\pi_{\omega}}$ . As emphasized in [37, Remark 3.3], when the underlying dynamics are unknown, this term is explicitly computable only in special settings, such as separable models. In contrast, our gradient formula is expressed directly through the pointwise-in-action kernels derived from $V^{\pi}$ and its derivatives. This form avoids differentiating the aggregated drift and diffusion with respect to the policy parameters, and is therefore better suited for the model-free extensions developed in the follow-up paper [12].

Finally, we note that Theorem 3.1 of [37] is equivalent to our parametric policy-gradient formula (18). When our initial distribution $\mu_{0}$ of the representative state is taken to be a Dirac measure $\mu_{0}=\delta_{s}$ , our pointwise form of (18) agrees with their gradient $G(s,\mu)$ . For a general initial distribution $\mu_{0}$ , averaging their pointwise gradient $\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mu_{0}}[G(s,\mu)]$ gives exactly our gradient $\nabla_{\omega}J$ defined in (18).

## 5. Actor-Critic Algorithm

We now use the previous results to formulate an actor–critic algorithm. For a fixed policy $\pi_{\omega}$ , the critic provides a finite-dimensional approximation of the value function $V^{\pi_{\omega}}$ solving (11), while the actor updates $\omega$ through the policy gradient formula derived in Section 4.

For the critic, we use a linear finite-dimensional ansatz on $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , with cylindrical basis functions to encode the dependence on the population law. This choice is consistent with classical linear value-function approximation in reinforcement learning for large state spaces [71, 48, 4, 80], as well as with related approximation methods in mean-field control [15].

Once such a finite-dimensional critic has been obtained, either by the Galerkin procedure below or by any other method, the policy gradient theorem can be applied directly. This yields an actor update that retains both the representative-agent and the population-law contributions of the coupled mean-field problem.

### 5.1. Policy evaluation via Galerkin approximation

Before introducing the Galerkin approximation, we emphasize that our actor-critic algorithm is not tied to a particular numerical method for solving the linear HJB equation. In principle, the critic can be computed using other approximation schemes, such as nonlinear function approximation with deep neural networks [56], or estimated through martingale-based characterizations of the value function [79]. The Galerkin method presented here should therefore be viewed as one possible critic approximation scheme, corresponding to linear function approximation. We focus on the Galerkin approach for two reasons. First, it gives a transparent and stable way to approximate the value function through projection onto a finite-dimensional function space. Second, this linear-projection structure is well suited for our subsequent extension to the model-free reinforcement-learning setting [12], where the dynamics are unknown and the critic must be estimated from data. In that setting, nonlinear function approximation for Bellman-type equations can suffer from the double-sampling issue, which may introduce instability in policy evaluation. By contrast, the Galerkin formulation leads to a more tractable projected critic equation and provides a useful starting point for developing stable model-free algorithms.

Let $\{\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n}\}$ be smooth functions on $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and define the trial space $\mathbb{V}_{n}:=\mathrm{span}\{\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n}\}.$ We approximate the value function by

$$ \displaystyle V_{\theta}(s,\mu):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{i}\,\phi_{i}(s,\mu)=\theta^{\top}\Phi(s,\mu),\qquad\Phi:=(\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n})^{\top}, $$

where $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the vector of critic coefficients. Although the basis functions are defined on $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , the approximation is finite-dimensional because only finitely many of them are used. In practice, the dependence on $\mu$ will be chosen through cylindrical functions, as explained in Subsection 5.2.

For a fixed policy $\pi_{\omega}$ , we impose the HJB residual associated with $V_{\theta}$ to be orthogonal to the trial space with respect to the reference measure $\mathfrak{m}$ . Thus, we seek $\theta^{*}(\omega)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that for every $j=1,\dots,n$ ,

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\Bigl((\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi_{\omega}}V_{\theta^{*}(\omega)})(s,\mu)-\beta V_{\theta^{*}(\omega)}(s,\mu)+r_{\lambda}^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)\Bigr)\phi_{j}(s,\mu)\,\mathfrak{m}(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}\mu)=0, $$

where $\mathfrak{m}$ is a fixed Borel probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ . Since the equation is linear in $V$ , (21) is equivalent to the linear system

$$ A(\omega)\,\theta^{*}(\omega)=b(\omega), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle A_{ji}(\omega) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\phi_{j}(s,\mu)\,\Bigl(\beta\,\phi_{i}(s,\mu)-(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi_{\omega}}\phi_{i})(s,\mu)\Bigr)\,\mathfrak{m}(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}\mu), \displaystyle b_{j}(\omega) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}r_{\lambda}^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)\,\phi_{j}(s,\mu)\,\mathfrak{m}(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}\mu). $$

Consequently, whenever $A$ is invertible, the solution of (22) is given by $\theta^{*}(\omega)=(A(\omega))^{-1}b(\omega)$ . In any case, independently of the particular approximation used for $A(\omega)$ and $b(\omega)$ , the corresponding critic is obtained as the Galerkin approximation

$$ \displaystyle V_{n}^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu):=V_{\theta^{*}(\omega)}(s,\mu). $$

### 5.2. Cylindrical basis functions and moment features

A central issue in the mean-field setting is the representation of the measure variable. A convenient class of functions is given by cylindrical functions, for which the Lions derivatives can be computed explicitly. This makes them particularly attractive for Galerkin approximations of the HJB equation.

Let $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and fix feature functions $\varphi_{1},\dots,\varphi_{k}\in C_{b}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ . We define the associated moment map

$$ m(\mu):=\bigl(m_{1}(\mu),\dots,m_{k}(\mu)\bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{k},\qquad m_{i}(\mu):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\varphi_{i}(\xi)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\xi),\quad i=1,\dots,k. $$

A function $F:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to\mathbb{R}$ is called cylindrical with respect to the feature family $\{\varphi_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}$ if there exists a smooth map $\Psi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{k}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that

$$ F(s,\mu)=\Psi\bigl(s,m(\mu)\bigr). $$

Thus, the dependence on $\mu$ is reduced to finitely many moments or, more generally, finitely many linear observables of $\mu$ .

This construction is useful for the policy-evaluation step for two reasons. First, it leads to a finite-dimensional parametrization of the measure argument. Second, the derivatives entering the HJB operator become explicit. Indeed, if $F(s,\mu)=\Psi(s,m(\mu))$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\begin{aligned} \nabla_{s}F(s,\mu)=\nabla_{s}\Psi\bigl(s,m(\mu)\bigr),&\qquad D^{2}_{ss}F(s,\mu)=D^{2}_{ss}\Psi\bigl(s,m(\mu)\bigr),\\
\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\partial_{m_{i}}\Psi\bigl(s,m(\mu)\bigr)\,\nabla\varphi_{i}(\xi),&\qquad D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\partial_{m_{i}}\Psi\bigl(s,m(\mu)\bigr)\,D^{2}_{\xi\xi}\varphi_{i}(\xi).\end{aligned} $$

Therefore, once the feature functions $\varphi_{i}$ are fixed, the operator $\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi_{\omega}}F$ can be evaluated explicitly for cylindrical functions. This motivates choosing, in the Galerkin approximation (21), basis functions of the form $\phi_{j}(s,\mu)=\psi_{j}\bigl(s,m(\mu)\bigr)$ , $j=1,\dots,n$ , with $\psi_{j}$ smooth on $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{k}$ . In this setting, the problem is naturally expressed in terms of the reduced variables $(s,m(\mu))\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{k}$ , and the reference measure may therefore be chosen as a Borel probability measure $\overline{\mathfrak{m}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{k}$ , built from $N>0$ observations $\{(s_{\tau},m_{\tau})\}_{\tau=1}^{N}$ , with $m_{\tau}=m(\mu_{\tau})$ , sampled on the time grid $t_{\tau}=(\tau-1)\Delta t$ along the trajectories of (4)–(5). A natural choice is to take $\overline{\mathfrak{m}}$ as the empirical discounted occupancy measure on the reduced space, namely

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\mathfrak{m}}=\beta\sum_{\tau=1}^{N}e^{-\beta t_{\tau}}\Delta t\,\delta_{(s_{\tau},m(\mu_{\tau}))},\qquad\text{or}\qquad\overline{\mathfrak{m}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\tau=1}^{N}\delta_{(s_{\tau},m(\mu_{\tau}))}, $$

the latter corresponding to the empirical undiscounted measure on the finite observation window. In Section 7.1, we also implemented the undiscounted measure. Our numerical results indicate that the algorithm is robust with respect to the choice of measure $\overline{\mathfrak{m}}$ .

In practice, one may average over $L>0$ independent trajectories in order to reduce the variance of the empirical estimator. This is naturally reflected in the definition of $\overline{\mathfrak{m}}$ by averaging the empirical measure across trajectories. Consequently, if $\{(s_{\eta},m_{\eta})\}_{\eta=1}^{N_{D}}$ , with $N_{D}=N\cdot L$ , denotes the collection of $N$ observations obtained from these $L$ trajectories, then one empirical approximation of (23), based on the undiscounted measure, is given by

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{A}_{ji}(\omega) \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{N_{D}}\sum_{\eta=1}^{N_{D}}\psi_{j}(s_{\eta},m_{\eta})\,\Bigl(\beta\,\psi_{i}(s_{\eta},m_{\eta})-(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi_{\omega}}\phi_{i})(s_{\eta},m_{\eta})\Bigr), \displaystyle\widehat{b}_{j}(\omega) \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{N_{D}}\sum_{\eta=1}^{N_{D}}r_{\lambda}^{\pi_{\omega}}(s_{\eta},m_{\eta})\,\psi_{j}(s_{\eta},m_{\eta}), $$

for $i,j=1,\dots,n$ . From a modeling viewpoint, the choice of the features $\varphi_{1},\dots,\varphi_{k}$ should reflect the expected structure of the value function. In linear-quadratic problems, moment-based features are especially natural, because the value function depends on $\mu$ through a small number of low-order moments; see Proposition 6.4. For more general problems, one may enrich the family of features by adding nonlinear observables of the population distribution.

### 5.3. Policy gradient

Let $\pi_{\omega}$ be a parametrized policy, with parameter $\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ , and let $V_{n}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ be either the critic obtained from (24), or, more generally, any finite-dimensional approximation of $V^{\pi_{\omega}}$ for which the derivatives entering the policy gradient formula are well defined and can be evaluated. The policy gradient theorem from Section 4 provides an exact gradient formula in terms of a representative contribution and a population contribution. For implementation, we keep exactly the same structure, but replace the exact value function $V^{\pi_{\omega}}$ by its approximation $V_{n}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ .

Accordingly, we define $q_{\mathrm{rep},n}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ and $q_{\mathrm{pop},n}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ as in Definition 4.2, with $V^{\pi}$ replaced by $V_{n}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ . The resulting approximate policy-gradient direction is

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{\omega}J_{n}^{\pi_{\omega}} \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\beta}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\Biggl(\int_{\mathcal{A}}q_{\mathrm{rep},n}^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu,a)\,\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi_{\omega}}(a\mid s,\mu)\,\pi_{\omega}(\mathrm{d}a\mid s,\mu) \displaystyle+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\!\int_{\mathcal{A}}q_{\mathrm{pop},n}^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu,\xi,a)\,\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi_{\omega}}(a\mid\xi,\mu)\,\pi_{\omega}(\mathrm{d}a\mid\xi,\mu)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\xi)\Biggr)\rho^{\pi_{\omega}}(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}\mu). $$

When the critic is expanded in cylindrical basis functions, $q_{\mathrm{rep},n}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ and $q_{\mathrm{pop},n}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ can be evaluated explicitly. Indeed, in that case the derivatives of $V_{n}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ are given directly by the formulas in (25). For numerical purposes, (27) may be approximated from a finite collection of observations $\{(s_{\eta},\mu_{\eta})\}_{\eta=1}^{N_{D}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ together with nonnegative weights $\{w_{\eta}\}_{\eta=1}^{N_{D}}$ . This yields the empirical approximation

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{\nabla_{\omega}J_{n}^{\pi_{\omega}}} \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{\eta=1}^{N_{D}}w_{\eta}\Biggl(\int_{\mathcal{A}}q_{\mathrm{rep},n}^{\pi_{\omega}}(s_{\eta},\mu_{\eta},a)\,\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi_{\omega}}(a\mid s_{\eta},\mu_{\eta})\,\pi_{\omega}(\mathrm{d}a\mid s_{\eta},\mu_{\eta}) \displaystyle+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\!\int_{\mathcal{A}}q_{\mathrm{pop},n}^{\pi_{\omega}}(s_{\eta},\mu_{\eta},\xi,a)\,\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi_{\omega}}(a\mid\xi,\mu_{\eta})\,\pi_{\omega}(\mathrm{d}a\mid\xi,\mu_{\eta})\,\mu_{\eta}(\mathrm{d}\xi)\Biggr). $$

Several remarks on numerically computing the above gradient are in order. First, the integral can be approximated by empirical mean through sampling actions $a_{j}$ from the current policy and sampling states $s_{i}$ from the current $\mu_{\eta}(\xi)$ . Second, regarding the weight $w_{\eta}$ , when the measure in (27) is chosen as the discounted occupancy measure $\rho^{\pi_{\omega}}$ , we consider $L$ independent trajectories $\{(s_{\tau}^{\ell},\mu_{\tau}^{\ell})\}_{\tau=0}^{N-1}$ , $\ell=1,\dots,L$ , of the controlled process $(s_{t}^{\pi_{\omega}},\mu_{t}^{\pi_{\omega}})$ sampled on the time grid $t_{\tau}=\tau\Delta t$ , and identify the observations in (28) with these data, so that $N_{D}=LN$ and $w_{\tau}^{\ell}=\frac{1}{L}e^{-\beta t_{\tau}}\Delta t$ . However, numerically we found that simply setting $w_{\eta}=\frac{1}{N_{D}}$ also provides a good approximation of the ascent direction. Finally, regardless of the specific approximation used for $\nabla_{\omega}J_{n}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ , the parameter update is of the form

$$ \omega^{(k+1)}=\omega^{(k)}+\alpha_{k}\,\widehat{\nabla_{\omega}J_{n}^{\pi_{\omega}}}, $$

where $\alpha_{k}>0$ is the stepsize.

The discussion above leads to Algorithm 1.

*Algorithm 1 Computational policy iteration for the coupled system*

```
1: Choose a parametrized policy family $\{\pi_{\omega}\}_{\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}$ .
2: Choose a finite-dimensional trial space $\mathbb{V}_{n}=\mathrm{span}\{\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n}\}$ , preferably with cylindrical basis functions in the measure variable.
3: Initialize the actor parameter $\omega^{(0)}$ .
4: for $k=0,1,\dots,K-1$ do
5: Policy evaluation: solve the linear Galerkin system (22) and define

$$ V_{n}^{\pi_{\omega^{(k)}}}(s,\mu):=(\theta^{(k)})^{\top}\Phi(s,\mu). $$
6: Policy improvement: construct the approximate advantage functions $q_{\mathrm{rep},n}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ and $q_{\mathrm{pop},n}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ using $V_{n}^{\pi_{\omega^{(k)}}}$ .
7: Estimate the gradient direction $\widehat{J}_{n}(\omega^{(k)})$ from (28).
8: Update the actor by

$$ \omega^{(k+1)}=\omega^{(k)}+\alpha_{k}\,\widehat{\nabla_{\omega}J_{n}^{\pi_{\omega}}}. $$
9: end for
10: Return the final policy $\pi_{\omega^{(K)}}$ and the associated critic $V_{n}^{\pi_{\omega^{(K)}}}$ .
```

## 6. Infinite-Time Mean-Field Linear Quadratic Regulator

In this section we analyze the infinite-horizon mean-field linear-quadratic regulator with stationary randomized feedback policies and entropy regularization. Our aim is to derive an explicit characterization of the optimal policy and of the associated value function in terms of a stationary algebraic Riccati system. Besides its intrinsic interest as a solvable class of mean-field control problems, this model is also relevant as a benchmark for entropy-regularized reinforcement learning, where randomized policies and Shannon regularization naturally arise in connection with exploration.

### 6.1. Problem setting

Let $d,m\in\mathbb{N}$ and set $\mathcal{A}=\mathbb{R}^{m}$ . For notational simplicity we take a one-dimensional Brownian motion; the extension to a multi-dimensional Brownian motion is immediate by interpreting $\|\cdot\|_{F}$ and $\sigma\sigma^{\top}$ accordingly. Fix $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and consider the representative and population dynamics introduced in (4)-(5), where $\tilde{s}_{0}\sim\mu$ and $s_{0}=s$ , with coefficients

$$ b(x,\mu,a)=Ax+\bar{A}\,\bar{\mu}+Ba,\qquad\sigma(x,\mu,a)=\gamma+Dx+\bar{D}\,\bar{\mu}+Fa,\qquad\bar{\mu}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}x\,\mu(\mathrm{d}x), $$

for fixed matrices $A,\bar{A},D,\bar{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ , $B,F\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}$ , and $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . Let $Q,\bar{Q}\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{d}$ , $N\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m}$ , $I\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ , and $M\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $H\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ . We consider the running reward

$$ r(x,\mu,a)=-\Bigl(x^{\top}Qx+\bar{\mu}^{\top}\bar{Q}\,\bar{\mu}+a^{\top}Na+2a^{\top}Ix+2M^{\top}x+2H^{\top}a\Bigr), $$

and, for $\lambda>0$ , the entropy-regularized reward $r_{\lambda}$ introduced in (3). For $\beta>0$ we define

$$ V^{\pi}(s,\mu):=\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\,r_{\lambda}(s_{t},\mu_{t},a_{t}^{s})\,\mathrm{d}t\right],\qquad V^{*}(s,\mu):=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}}V^{\pi}(s,\mu), $$

where $\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ denotes the class of all stationary randomized feedback policies $\pi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{m})$ such that $\pi(\cdot\mid x,\mu)$ admits a density $p_{\pi}(x,\mu,\cdot)$ with respect to Lebesgue measure, $V^{\pi}(s,\mu)<\infty$ for every $(s,\mu)$ , and, for every initial condition $(s,\mu)$ , $\lim_{t\to\infty}e^{-\beta t}\bigl(\mathbb{E}|s_{t}|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu_{t})\bigr)=0.$

#### Remark 6.1.

A sufficient, but not necessary, condition to ensure that $\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ is that $b^{\pi}$ , $\sigma^{\pi}$ , and $r_{\lambda}^{\pi}$ satisfy Assumption 3.1, and that the dissipativity estimate (12) holds. Thus, $\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ by Theorem 3.3. In the LQ setting, Assumption 3.1 is ensured by assuming that $m_{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}$ with bounded derivatives, that $q_{\pi}$ and $\mathcal{H}\bigl(\pi(\cdot\mid x,\mu)\bigr)$ belong to $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{poly}}^{2,2}$ , and that $m_{\pi}$ has at most linear growth in $(x,\sqrt{m_{2}(\mu)})$ , where

$$ m_{\pi}(x,\mu):=\int_{\mathcal{A}}a\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a\mid x,\mu),\qquad q_{\pi}(x,\mu):=\int_{\mathcal{A}}a^{\top}Na\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a\mid x,\mu), $$

and $\mathcal{H}\bigl(\pi(\cdot\mid x,\mu)\bigr)$ is defined in (3). A sufficient condition for (12) is that $2\,x^{\top}Ax+\|Dx\|_{F}^{2}\leq c_{0}-\alpha|x|^{2}$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},$ for some $c_{0}\geq 0$ and some $\alpha>0$ such that the remaining terms involving $\bar{A},\bar{D},B,F$ and $m_{\pi}$ can be absorbed by Young’s inequality.

#### Definition 6.2 (Stabilizability, detectability, and mean-square stabilizability).

The pair $(A,B)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}$ is stabilizable if there exists $\Theta\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ such that $A+B\Theta$ is Hurwitz. The pair $(A,H)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\times\mathbb{R}^{q\times d}$ is detectable if there exists $L\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times q}$ such that $A-LH$ is Hurwitz.

(A4) Discounted LQ conditions. Let $A_{\beta}:=A-\frac{\beta}{2}I_{d},$ and $\tilde{A}_{\beta}:=A+\bar{A}-\frac{\beta}{2}I_{d}.$ We assume that the following conditions hold:

- (H1) $N\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m}$ and

$$ Q-I^{\top}N^{-1}I\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d},\qquad Q+\bar{Q}-I^{\top}N^{-1}I\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d}. $$

- (H2) The pair $(\tilde{A}_{\beta},B)$ is stabilizable, and there exist $\Theta\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ and $P_{0}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d}$ such that

$$ (A_{\beta}+B\Theta)^{\top}P_{0}+P_{0}(A_{\beta}+B\Theta)+(D+F\Theta)^{\top}P_{0}(D+F\Theta)\preceq-I_{d}. $$

#### Remark 6.3.

Assumption (H1) implies in particular that the pairs $(A_{\beta},(Q-I^{\top}N^{-1}I)^{1/2})$ and $(\tilde{A}_{\beta},(Q+\bar{Q}-I^{\top}N^{-1}I)^{1/2})$ are detectable. On the other hand, when $D=F=0$ , condition (H2) is equivalent to assuming that both pairs $(A_{\beta},B)$ and $(\tilde{A}_{\beta},B)$ are stabilizable.

Let us consider the quadratic function

$$ V(s,\mu)=-\Bigl((s-\bar{\mu})^{\top}K(s-\bar{\mu})+\bar{\mu}^{\top}\Lambda\,\bar{\mu}+2Y^{\top}s+R\Bigr), $$

where $K,\Lambda\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{d}$ , $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , and $R\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy the algebraic system

$$ \displaystyle\beta K \displaystyle=Q+KA+A^{\top}K+D^{\top}KD-U^{\top}S^{-1}U, \displaystyle\beta\Lambda \displaystyle=Q+\bar{Q}+\Lambda(A+\bar{A})+(A+\bar{A})^{\top}\Lambda+(D+\bar{D})^{\top}K(D+\bar{D})-W^{\top}S^{-1}W, \displaystyle\beta Y \displaystyle=M+A^{\top}Y+D^{\top}K\gamma-U^{\top}S^{-1}O, \displaystyle\beta R \displaystyle=\gamma^{\top}K\gamma-O^{\top}S^{-1}O-\frac{\lambda}{2}\Bigl(m\log(\pi_{0}\lambda)-\log\det S\Bigr), $$

where

$$ S:=N+F^{\top}KF,\qquad O:=H+B^{\top}Y+F^{\top}K\gamma, $$

and

$$ U:=I+B^{\top}K+F^{\top}KD,\qquad W:=I+B^{\top}\Lambda+F^{\top}K(D+\bar{D}). $$

Here $\pi_{0}$ denotes the mathematical constant.

#### Proposition 6.4.

Assume Section 6.1 and let $(K,\Lambda,Y,R)$ be a solution of (32)-(35). Let $V$ be given by (31), and let $\pi^{*}$ be defined as

$$ \pi^{*}(\cdot\mid s,\mu)=\mathcal{N}\!\left(-S^{-1}\bigl(Us+(W-U)\bar{\mu}+O\bigr),\;\frac{\lambda}{2}S^{-1}\right). $$

Then

$$ V^{*}(s,\mu)=V^{\pi^{*}}(s,\mu)=V(s,\mu)\qquad\text{for all }(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), $$

and $\pi^{*}$ is the unique optimal stationary feedback policy in $\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ .

The proof of Proposition 6.4 is provided in Section A.3.

## 7. Numerical Examples

### 7.1. Example 1: Mean-field systemic risk model

Mean-field models of systemic risk describe a large population of interacting agents whose individual states are attracted to the current population average, while each agent can act through a control representing, for instance, borrowing or lending to the system; See [26, 24]. In our stationary discounted setting introduced in Section 6, this leads to a one-dimensional linear-quadratic specification in which the state is penalized through its deviation from the population mean and the control is penalized quadratically.

#### 7.1.1. Problem setup

We consider the one-dimensional mean-field LQR dynamics in the particular systemic risk configuration, namely

$$ \mathrm{d}s_{t}=\bigl(A(s_{t}-\bar{\mu}_{t})+Ba_{t}\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t+\gamma\,\mathrm{d}B_{t},\qquad a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\,|\,s_{t},\mu_{t}),\qquad\bar{\mu}_{t}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}}x\,\mu_{t}(\mathrm{d}x), $$

where $\mu_{t}=\Law(\tilde{s}_{t})$ is the population law generated by the mean-field environment (5). This corresponds to the general framework of Section 6 with $d=m=1,$ $\bar{A}=-A$ , $D=\bar{D}=F=0,$ and $I=M=H=0.$ We take the running reward

$$ r(x,\mu,a)=-\Bigl(Q(x-\bar{\mu})^{2}+\bar{Q}\,\bar{\mu}^{2}+Na^{2}\Bigr), $$

with $Q,\bar{Q}\geq 0$ and $N>0$ . Our goal is to maximize the expected long-run regularized reward

$$ \displaystyle V^{*}(s,\mu)\,:=\,\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}}\left\{V^{\pi}(s,\mu):=\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\,r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t},\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\;\bigg|\;s_{0}=s,\ \mu_{0}=\mu\right]\right\}, $$

for every $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , where the entropy-regularized $r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s,\mu)$ is as in (3) with $r(s,\mu,a)$ defined in (39). Following Proposition 6.4, the optimal policy is given by

$$ \pi^{*}(\cdot\mid s,\mu)=\mathcal{N}\!\left(-N^{-1}B^{\top}\bigl(K(s-\bar{\mu})+\Lambda\,\bar{\mu}\bigr),\frac{\lambda}{2}N^{-1}\right). $$

The corresponding optimal value function is

$$ V^{*}(s,\mu)=V^{\pi^{*}}(s,\mu)=-\Bigl((s-\bar{\mu})^{\top}K(s-\bar{\mu})+\bar{\mu}^{\top}\Lambda\,\bar{\mu}+R\Bigr), $$

where $K,\Lambda\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{d}$ and $R\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy the reduced algebraic system

$$ \displaystyle\begin{cases}\beta K&=Q+KA+A^{\top}K-KBN^{-1}B^{\top}K,\\
\beta\Lambda&=Q+\bar{Q}-\Lambda BN^{-1}B^{\top}\Lambda,\\
\beta R&=\gamma^{\top}K\gamma-\frac{\lambda}{2}\Bigl(m\log(\pi_{0}\lambda)-\log\det N\Bigr).\end{cases} $$

#### 7.1.2. Policy parametrization and value approximation

Following the theoretical optimal policy (41), we consider the family of Gaussian policies parametrized as

$$ \pi_{\omega}(\cdot\mid s,\mu)=\mathcal{N}\bigl(\omega_{1}(s-\bar{\mu})+\omega_{2}\bar{\mu},\,\lambda\bigr), $$

where $\omega=(\omega_{1},\omega_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ . On the other hand, following (42), the value function can be approximated by the quadratic cylindrical ansatz

$$ V_{\theta}(s,\mu)=\theta_{3}\,(s-\bar{\mu})^{2}+\theta_{2}\,\bar{\mu}^{2}+\theta_{1},\qquad\theta=(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, $$

that is, following the notation of (20), we are taking $\phi_{1}(s,\mu)=1$ , $\phi_{2}(s,\mu)=\bar{\mu}^{2}$ , and $\phi_{3}(s,\mu)=(s-\bar{\mu})^{2}$ .

#### 7.1.3. Implementation and numerical results

We implement the model-based actor–critic procedure described in Section 5 for the scalar mean-field LQR example. The actor is parametrized by the Gaussian policy (43), and the critic is sought in the quadratic space generated by (44). Throughout the experiment we use

$$ A=-1,\qquad B=1,\qquad Q=1,\qquad\bar{Q}=1,\qquad N=\tfrac{1}{2},\qquad\beta=1,\qquad\gamma=0.5,\qquad\lambda=0.2. $$

The population is initialized with mean $\bar{\mu}_{0}=1$ , and the initial representative state is sampled from $\mu_{0}=\mathcal{N}(1,1)$ . Since the population dynamics are closed at the level of the mean $\bar{\mu}_{t}$ , no auxiliary particle approximation of the population law is needed in this example. The representative state is sampled from the exact closed-loop Gaussian transition, while $\bar{\mu}_{t}$ is propagated through the corresponding deterministic mean equation. The discounted integrals are approximated on $[0,T]$ , with $T=8$ and $\Delta t=0.05$ . We use $100$ Monte Carlo trajectories per actor step, a constant learning rate $\alpha=5\times 10^{-2}$ , and run $1000$ policy-improvement iterations.

For a fixed actor parameter $\omega=(\omega_{1},\omega_{2})$ , the aggregated coefficients are

$$ b^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)=A(s-\bar{\mu})+B\bigl(\omega_{1}(s-\bar{\mu})+\omega_{2}\bar{\mu}\bigr),\qquad\Sigma^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)=\gamma^{2}. $$

Thus, the Galerkin critic is computed by solving the linear system (22), with $A(\omega)$ and $b(\omega)$ defined in (23), after replacing the general generator $\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ by the present LQR generator. For the basis

$$ \phi_{1}(s,\mu)=1,\qquad\phi_{2}(s,\mu)=\bar{\mu}^{2},\qquad\phi_{3}(s,\mu)=(s-\bar{\mu})^{2}, $$

one obtains

$$ \mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi_{\omega}}\phi_{1}=0,\qquad\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi_{\omega}}\phi_{2}=2B\omega_{2}\,\bar{\mu}^{2},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi_{\omega}}\phi_{3}=2(A+B\omega_{1})(s-\bar{\mu})^{2}+\gamma^{2}. $$

At each actor step, the identities above are inserted into the Galerkin system (22), with $A(\omega)$ and $b(\omega)$ defined in (23), to compute the critic coefficients $\theta^{(k)}$ and then update the actor through the policy-gradient direction in (28). From a computational viewpoint, in this benchmark the critic space has dimension three, so policy evaluation reduces to solving a $3\times 3$ linear system. Moreover, the Gaussian structure of the policy allows the conditional expectation over the action variable in the actor update to be evaluated analytically. The remaining numerical cost comes from the empirical approximation of the discounted occupancy measure along simulated trajectories. Since the closed-loop dynamics are linear and Gaussian for each fixed actor parameter, these trajectories are sampled from the exact transition law, while the population mean is propagated through its deterministic closed equation.

The closed-form Riccati solution provides a benchmark for the optimal feedback and the optimal value function. Figure 1 compares the final learned policy mean and its induced value function with the Riccati benchmark for several fixed values of the population mean $\bar{\mu}$ . Figure 2 reports the evolution of the critic and actor coefficients during training. The convergence of both sets of coefficients toward the Riccati values confirms that the HJB–Galerkin actor–critic iteration recovers the quadratic structure of the optimal solution in this benchmark example.

We also implement the undiscounted empirical measure $\overline{\mathfrak{m}}$ in (26), which can be viewed as a biased empirical approximation of the discounted occupancy measure in (27), since it assigns uniform rather than discounted weights along the finite time window. The corresponding results, shown in Figure 3 with stepsize $\alpha=1\times 10^{-1}$ , illustrate the same qualitative behavior as in the discounted case.

### 7.2. Example 2: Crowd-aversion transport

The second example illustrates the actor–critic method in a nonlinear mean-field setting for which no closed-form Riccati benchmark is available. The objective is to transport a representative agent toward a prescribed target while penalizing trajectories that pass through regions of high crowd density. The crowd is described by a population law $\mu_{t}$ , which is approximated numerically by an empirical measure generated by a finite particle system.

#### 7.2.1. Problem setup

We consider the controlled diffusion on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$

$$ \mathrm{d}s_{t}=a_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma\,\mathrm{d}B_{t},\qquad a_{t}\sim\pi_{\omega}(\cdot\mid s_{t},\mu_{t}), $$

where $a_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ is the control, $\sigma>0$ is a constant volatility, and $\mu_{t}$ denotes the population distribution observed by the representative agent. The reward is defined by

$$ r(s,\mu,a)=-\left(\frac{1}{2}\|a\|^{2}+\frac{\kappa}{2}\|s-s_{\mathrm{tar}}\|^{2}+\gamma\,(K_{\eta}*\mu)(s)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|s\|^{2}\right), $$

where $s_{\mathrm{tar}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ is the target location, $\kappa>0$ controls the strength of the attraction to the target, $\gamma>0$ controls the crowd-aversion penalty, and $\rho\geq 0$ is a confinement parameter. The crowd-density term is computed through the Gaussian kernel convolution

$$ (K_{\eta}*\mu)(s):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\exp\left(-\frac{\|s-s^{\prime}\|^{2}}{2\eta^{2}}\right)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}), $$

with bandwidth $\eta>0$ . The goal is to maximize the corresponding infinite-horizon entropy-regularized objective (2) with reward given by (45).

#### Remark 7.1.

The four terms in (45) have distinct roles. The first one penalizes large controls, the second one attracts the representative agent toward $s_{\mathrm{tar}}$ , the third one penalizes positions located in high-density regions of the crowd, and the last one adds a mild confinement on the unbounded domain.

#### 7.2.2. Policy parametrization and value approximation

We use a Gaussian policy on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with fixed exploration variance,

$$ \pi_{\omega}(\cdot\mid s,\mu)=\mathcal{N}\bigl(m_{\omega}(s,\mu),\sigma_{a}^{2}I_{2}\bigr), $$

where the mean is parametrized as $m_{\omega}(s,\mu)=Wf(s,\mu)$ , with $\omega\equiv W\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times d_{f}}$ . In order to generate trajectories without an Euler–Maruyama approximation, we use an affine feature map depending on the state and on the empirical population mean,

$$ f(s,\mu)=\bigl(1,\,s_{1},\,s_{2},\,s_{1}-s_{\mathrm{tar},1},\,s_{2}-s_{\mathrm{tar},2},\,\bar{\mu}_{1},\,\bar{\mu}_{2}\bigr),\qquad\bar{\mu}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}x\,\mu(\mathrm{d}x). $$

With this choice, the finite-particle approximation of the aggregated representative–population system is an affine linear diffusion. Hence, at each actor–critic iteration, the training trajectories are sampled from the exact Gaussian transition of this affine system, computed through the corresponding matrix exponential.

The critic is constructed as in the Galerkin policy-evaluation procedure of Section 5.1. To represent the dependence on the population law, we use kernel-embedding features

$$ u_{j}(\mu):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\exp\left(-\frac{\|x-c_{j}\|^{2}}{2h^{2}}\right)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}x),\qquad j=1,\dots,M_{\mu}, $$

where $\{c_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M_{\mu}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}$ are fixed centers and $h>0$ is the bandwidth. For the state variable we use Gaussian radial basis functions $\psi_{m}(s)=\exp(-\|s-z_{m}\|^{2}/(2s_{x}^{2}))$ , $m=1,\dots,M_{s}$ . The critic basis is then given by

$$ \phi_{m,0}(s,\mu)=\psi_{m}(s),\qquad\phi_{m,j}(s,\mu)=\psi_{m}(s)\,u_{j}(\mu),\qquad m=1,\dots,M_{s},\quad j=1,\dots,M_{\mu}. $$

Thus, with $n=M_{s}(M_{\mu}+1)$ , the value function is approximated in $\mathbb{V}_{n}=\mathrm{span}\{\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n}\}$ by $V_{n}^{\pi_{\omega}}(s,\mu)=\theta^{\top}\Phi(s,\mu)$ .

#### 7.2.3. Implementation and numerical results

The implementation follows the actor–critic algorithm of Section 5. For each actor parameter $W$ , the critic is obtained by solving the Galerkin system (22), with $A(W)$ and $b(W)$ defined as in (23), after replacing the abstract generator $\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ by the known generator of the crowd-aversion dynamics. The resulting critic $V_{n}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ is then inserted into the empirical policy-gradient formula (28) to update the actor.

The numerical parameters are

$$ \sigma=0.2,\qquad\beta=0.1,\qquad\kappa=1000,\qquad\gamma=10,\qquad\eta=0.8,\qquad\rho=0.1. $$

The entropy parameter is $\lambda=2$ , the exploration standard deviation is $\sigma_{a}=0.25$ , and the target is $s_{\mathrm{tar}}=(2,0)$ . In the reported experiment, both the initial population law and the initial representative law are centered near $(-2,0)$ , with Gaussian perturbations of standard deviation $0.02$ . The implementation also allows these two initial laws to be chosen independently.

The population law is approximated by an empirical measure

$$ \widehat{\mu}_{t}^{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{X_{t}^{i}}. $$

Accordingly, the crowd-density term is evaluated as

$$ (K_{\eta}*\widehat{\mu}_{t}^{N})(s_{t})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\exp\left(-\frac{\|s_{t}-X_{t}^{i}\|^{2}}{2\eta^{2}}\right). $$

From an implementation viewpoint, the main additional cost in this crowd-aversion example comes from the particle approximation of the population law. Since $\widehat{\mu}_{t}^{N}$ is represented by the empirical measure in (46), several realizations of the coupled representative–population dynamics must be generated to assemble the Galerkin system and evaluate the policy-gradient direction. Nevertheless, the implementation exploits the affine structure of the actor with respect to the state and the empirical population mean, which allows us to sample the coupled system from its exact Gaussian transition.

At each actor–critic iteration we generate $L=24$ independent simulations, each with $N=64$ particles representing the crowd. The discounted objective is truncated at $T=5$ and evaluated on the time grid $\Delta t=0.05$ . We run $500$ actor updates with constant stepsize $\alpha=5\times 10^{-4}$ . The actor matrix is initialized at zero, its entries are clipped for stability, and the Galerkin system is solved with ridge parameter $10^{-2}$ . The RBF centers for both the state and measure features are placed on a $5\times 5$ Cartesian grid on $[-8,4]^{2}$ . State and particle locations are clipped only when evaluating the RBF features; the simulated dynamics themselves are not clipped.

Unlike the LQR example, this nonlinear crowd-aversion problem does not admit a closed-form optimal policy or value function. We therefore assess the method through diagnostics that measure stability and qualitative performance. Figure 4 reports the estimated regularized reward and the norms of the actor, critic, and policy-gradient direction along training. Figure 6 shows the trajectories generated by the final learned policy. The reward curve provides a numerical indication of policy improvement, while the parameter and gradient norms monitor the stability of the actor–critic iteration. The trajectory plot illustrates whether the learned policy transports the representative agent from the initial region near $(-2,0)$ toward the target while accounting for the crowd-aversion term. Finally, Figure 5 illustrate the convergence when the undiscounted measure $\bar{\mathrm{m}}$ , defined in (26), is considered. Note that its qualitative behavior is similar to the discounted case shown in Figure 4.
