## Appendix A Proofs of the Main Results

### A.1. Proofs for Section 3

We first establish well-posedness of the system together with moment estimates that are explicit in time. Estimates of this type are standard in the literature; see, for instance, [8, 20]. However, for the infinite-horizon argument we need bounds with an explicit exponential dependence on $t$ , so that they can be combined with the discount factor $e^{-\beta t}$ when passing to the limit as $T\to\infty$ . A generic finite-horizon bound of the form $C_{T}$ , with no explicit control of its dependence on $T$ , would not be sufficient for this purpose. We therefore state and prove the corresponding estimates for general $p$ -moments.

#### Lemma A.1 (Well-posedness and exponential moment growth).

Suppose Assumption 3.1 holds. Fix an even integer $p\geq 2$ . Then, for every $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , the system (4)-(5) admits a unique strong solution on $[0,\infty)$ . Moreover, there exist constants $C_{p}\geq 1$ and $\beta_{0}(p)>0$ , depending only on $p$ and the structural constants in Assumption 3.1, such that for all $t\geq 0$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}\!\left[|s_{t}|^{p}\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[|\tilde{s}_{t}|^{p}\right]\leq C_{p}\,e^{\beta_{0}(p)\,t}\bigl(1+|s|^{p}+m_{p}(\mu)\bigr). $$

In particular, for $p=4$ , for each $T>0$ there exists $C_{T}>0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\left[|s_{t}|^{4}\right]+\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\left[|\tilde{s}_{t}|^{4}\right]\Bigr)\leq C_{p}e^{\beta_{0}(p)T}\bigl(1+|s|^{4}+m_{4}(\mu)\bigr), $$

and $\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}m_{2}(\mu_{t})\leq C_{T}(1+m_{4}(\mu)^{1/2})$ .

#### Proof.

Step 1 (Existence and uniqueness). Under Assumption 3.1, the McKean-Vlasov SDE (5) has globally Lipschitz and linearly growing coefficients $b^{\pi}$ and $\sigma^{\pi}$ ; see Remark 3.2. Hence, by the standard well-posedness theory for McKean-Vlasov SDEs, (5) admits a unique strong solution $\tilde{s}$ for every initial law $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ . The population flow $\mu_{t}:=\mathcal{L}(\tilde{s}_{t})$ is therefore well defined. Conditioning on the deterministic flow $(\mu_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ , the representative equation (4) is an SDE with progressively measurable coefficients, globally Lipschitz in $s$ and with linear growth, so it also admits a unique strong solution.

Step 2 ( $p$ -moment bound for $\tilde{s}_{t}$ ). Let $f(x)=|x|^{p}$ . Since $p\geq 2$ is even, $f\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and

$$ \nabla f(x)=p|x|^{p-2}x,\qquad D^{2}f(x)=p(p-2)|x|^{p-4}xx^{\top}+p|x|^{p-2}I_{d}. $$

For $n\geq 1$ , define the stopping time $\tau_{n}:=\inf\{t\geq 0:\,|\tilde{s}_{t}|>n\}.$ Applying Itô’s formula to $f(\tilde{s}_{t})$ on $[0,t\wedge\tau_{n}]$ gives

$$ \displaystyle|\tilde{s}_{t\wedge\tau_{n}}|^{p}=|\tilde{s}_{0}|^{p}+\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau_{n}}\Bigl[\nabla f(\tilde{s}_{u})\cdot b^{\pi}(\tilde{s}_{u},\mu_{u})+\tfrac{1}{2}D^{2}f(\tilde{s}_{u}):\Sigma^{\pi}(\tilde{s}_{u},\mu_{u})\Bigr]\mathrm{d}u+M_{t\wedge\tau_{n}}, $$

where $M_{t}$ is a local martingale, hence $\mathbb{E}[M_{t\wedge\tau_{n}}]=0$ . Using (9), Cauchy-Schwarz, and Young’s inequality, there exists a constant $C_{p}>0$ , depending only on $p$ and $K_{\pi}$ , such that for all $(x,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla f(x)\cdot b^{\pi}(x,\mu)|\leq C_{p}\bigl(1+|x|^{p}+m_{2}(\mu)^{p/2}\bigr),\quad D^{2}f(x):\Sigma^{\pi}(x,\mu)\leq C_{p}\bigl(1+|x|^{p}+m_{2}(\mu)^{p/2}\bigr). $$

Taking expectations in (49) yields

$$ \mathbb{E}\!\left[|\tilde{s}_{t\wedge\tau_{n}}|^{p}\right]\leq m_{p}(\mu)+C_{p}\int_{0}^{t}\Bigl(1+\mathbb{E}\!\left[|\tilde{s}_{u\wedge\tau_{n}}|^{p}\right]+m_{2}(\mu_{u})^{p/2}\Bigr)\,\mathrm{d}u. $$

Set $y_{n}(t):=\mathbb{E}\!\left[|\tilde{s}_{t\wedge\tau_{n}}|^{p}\right]$ , $y(t):=\mathbb{E}\!\left[|\tilde{s}_{t}|^{p}\right],$ and $z(t):=\sup_{n\geq 1}y_{n}(t).$ Since $\mu_{u}=\mathcal{L}(\tilde{s}_{u})$ , Hölder’s inequality gives

$$ m_{2}(\mu_{u})^{p/2}=\Bigl(\mathbb{E}[|\tilde{s}_{u}|^{2}]\Bigr)^{p/2}\leq\mathbb{E}[|\tilde{s}_{u}|^{p}]=y(u). $$

Therefore, for every $n\geq 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle y_{n}(t)\leq m_{p}(\mu)+C_{p}\int_{0}^{t}\bigl(1+y_{n}(u)+y(u)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}u. $$

Now, for each fixed $u\geq 0$ , Fatou’s lemma implies $y(u)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lim_{n\to\infty}|\tilde{s}_{u\wedge\tau_{n}}|^{p}\right]\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}y_{n}(u)\leq z(u).$ Hence (51) implies

$$ y_{n}(t)\leq m_{p}(\mu)+C_{p}\int_{0}^{t}\bigl(1+2z(u)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}u,\qquad n\geq 1. $$

Taking the supremum over $n$ gives

$$ z(t)\leq m_{p}(\mu)+C_{p}\int_{0}^{t}\bigl(1+2z(u)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}u. $$

By Grönwall’s inequality, $z(t)\leq\bigl(m_{p}(\mu)+1\bigr)e^{2C_{p}t}$ for $t\geq 0$ . Since $y(t)\leq z(t)$ , we conclude that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[|\tilde{s}_{t}|^{p}\right]\leq\bigl(m_{p}(\mu)+1\bigr)e^{\beta_{0}t},\qquad\beta_{0}:=2C_{p}. $$

Step 3 ( $p$ -moment bound for $s_{t}$ ). Define $\sigma_{n}:=\inf\{t\geq 0:\,|s_{t}|>n\},$ and $v_{n}(t):=\mathbb{E}\!\left[|s_{t\wedge\sigma_{n}}|^{p}\right].$ Repeating the same localized Itô argument for (4), and using (52) to control $m_{2}(\mu_{t})^{p/2}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle v_{n}(t)\leq|s|^{p}+C_{p}\int_{0}^{t}\bigl(1+v_{n}(u)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}u+C_{p}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[|\tilde{s}_{u}|^{p}\right]\,\mathrm{d}u. $$

Using (52), it follows that

$$ v_{n}(t)\leq|s|^{p}+C_{p}\int_{0}^{t}\bigl(1+v_{n}(u)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}u+C_{p}\bigl(m_{p}(\mu)+1\bigr)\int_{0}^{t}e^{\beta_{0}u}\,\mathrm{d}u. $$

Another application of Grönwall’s inequality yields

$$ v_{n}(t)\leq C_{p}e^{\beta_{0}t}\bigl(1+|s|^{p}+m_{p}(\mu)\bigr),\qquad t\geq 0, $$

after enlarging $C_{p}$ if necessary. Letting $n\to\infty$ and using Fatou’s lemma gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[|s_{t}|^{p}\right]\leq C_{p}e^{\beta_{0}t}\bigl(1+|s|^{p}+m_{p}(\mu)\bigr). $$

Step 4 (Conclusion). Combining (52) and (53), and enlarging the constant if necessary, we obtain (47). For $p=4$ , the same argument gives the finite-horizon estimate (48). Finally, for $t\in[0,T]$ ,

$$ m_{2}(\mu_{t})=\mathbb{E}[|\tilde{s}_{t}|^{2}]\leq\Bigl(\mathbb{E}[|\tilde{s}_{t}|^{4}]\Bigr)^{1/2}\leq C_{T}\bigl(1+m_{4}(\mu)^{1/2}\bigr), $$

which completes the proof. ∎

#### Remark A.2 (Explicit value of $\beta_{0}(2)$ ).

Taking $p=2$ in Lemma A.1 and applying Young’s inequality to (50), using $(u+v+w)^{2}\leq 3(u^{2}+v^{2}+w^{2})$ and the bound (9), one obtains

$$ 2s\cdot b^{\pi}(s,\mu)\leq K_{\pi}+4K_{\pi}|s|^{2}+K_{\pi}\,m_{2}(\mu),\qquad\|\sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)\|^{2}\leq 3K_{\pi}^{2}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), $$

from which (51) with $p=2$ becomes

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}[|\tilde{s}_{t}|^{2}]\leq(K_{\pi}+3K_{\pi}^{2})+(5K_{\pi}+6K_{\pi}^{2})\,\mathbb{E}[|\tilde{s}_{t}|^{2}]. $$

Therefore $\beta_{0}:=\beta_{0}(2)=5K_{\pi}+6K_{\pi}^{2}$ .

#### Remark A.3 (A dissipative case).

Assume that there exist constants $\kappa>C_{\mathrm{diss}}>0$ and $C_{0}\geq 0$ such that, for all $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , (12) holds. Applying Itô’s formula to $|\tilde{s}_{t}|^{2}$ , one obtains

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}m_{2}(\mu_{t})\leq C_{0}-(\kappa-C_{\mathrm{diss}})\,m_{2}(\mu_{t}), $$

hence

$$ m_{2}(\mu_{t})\leq e^{-(\kappa-C_{\mathrm{diss}})t}m_{2}(\mu)+\frac{C_{0}}{\kappa-C_{\mathrm{diss}}}\bigl(1-e^{-(\kappa-C_{\mathrm{diss}})t}\bigr),\qquad t\geq 0. $$

In particular, $m_{2}(\mu_{t})$ is uniformly bounded on $[0,\infty)$ . Applying Itô’s formula to $|s_{t}|^{2}$ and using the previous bound, we deduce that there exists $C>0$ independent of $t$ such that

$$ \sup_{t\geq 0}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}[|s_{t}|^{2}]\leq C\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr). $$

We next establish differentiability properties of the decoupled flow with respect to the state and measure variables. While such properties are standard in the McKean-Vlasov literature, for our purposes we also need explicit exponential-in-time bounds for the corresponding derivatives. As noted before Lemma A.1, these explicit bounds are essential for the infinite-horizon analysis.

#### Lemma A.4 (Exponential bounds for the derivatives of the decoupled flow).

Suppose Assumption 3.1 holds. Fix an even integer $p\geq 2$ . For $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , let $(\mu_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ be the measure flow generated by (5). For each $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , let $X_{t}^{x,\mu}$ denote the unique strong solution of

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t}^{x,\mu}=b^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}B_{t},\qquad X_{0}^{x,\mu}=x. $$

Then, for every $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the derivatives $\nabla_{x}X_{t}^{x,\mu}$ , $D_{xx}^{2}X_{t}^{x,\mu}$ , $\partial_{\mu}X_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)$ , and $D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}X_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)$ exist. Moreover, there exists a constant $C_{p,d}>0$ , depending only on $p$ and $d$ , such that with $\beta_{\mathrm{var}}(p):=C_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2},$ one has, for all $t\geq 0$ , $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , and $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\nabla_{x}X_{t}^{x,\mu}\|^{p}+\|D^{2}_{xx}X_{t}^{x,\mu}\|^{p}+\|\partial_{\mu}X_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}+\|D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}X_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\right]\leq C_{p,d}(1+K_{\pi}^{p})e^{\beta_{\mathrm{var}}(p)t}. $$

#### Proof.

Under Assumption 3.1, the coefficients $b^{\pi}$ and $\sigma^{\pi}$ are twice differentiable with respect to the state variable and Lions differentiable with respect to the measure argument, with bounded derivatives up to second order. Therefore, the differentiability results of [20, Theorem 3.1 and Proposition 4.1] apply, and the derivatives $\nabla_{x}X_{t}^{x,\mu}$ , $D^{2}_{xx}X_{t}^{x,\mu}$ , $\partial_{\mu}X_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)$ , and $D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}X_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)$ are well defined. It remains to prove the estimate (54). For simplicity, write

$$ J_{t}^{x,\mu}:=\nabla_{x}X_{t}^{x,\mu},\qquad H_{t}^{x,\mu}:=D^{2}_{xx}X_{t}^{x,\mu},\qquad U_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi):=\partial_{\mu}X_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi),\qquad V_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi):=D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}X_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi). $$

We denote by $\sigma^{\pi}_{\ell}$ the $\ell$ -th column of $\sigma^{\pi}$ , $\ell=1,\dots,d$ . Since only upper bounds are relevant, we may enlarge $K_{\pi}$ once and for all and assume $K_{\pi}\geq 1$ .

Step 1 (Bounds for the first spatial derivative). Differentiating the decoupled SDE with respect to $x$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}J_{t}^{x,\mu}=\nabla_{s}b^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})J_{t}^{x,\mu}\,\mathrm{d}t+\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\nabla_{s}\sigma_{\ell}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})J_{t}^{x,\mu}\,\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{\ell},\qquad J_{0}^{x,\mu}=I_{d}. $$

Since each entry of $\nabla_{s}b^{\pi}$ and $\nabla_{s}\sigma^{\pi}_{\ell}$ is bounded by $K_{\pi}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla_{s}b^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})\|\leq\sqrt{d}\,K_{\pi},\qquad\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\|\nabla_{s}\sigma_{\ell}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})\|^{2}\leq d^{2}K_{\pi}^{2}. $$

Applying Itô’s formula to $\|J_{t}^{x,\mu}\|^{p}$ , integrating over $[0,t]$ , and taking expectations, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|J_{t}^{x,\mu}\|^{p}\right] \displaystyle=\|I_{d}\|^{p}+p\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|J_{r}^{x,\mu}\|^{p-2}\left\langle J_{r}^{x,\mu},\nabla_{s}b^{\pi}(X_{r}^{x,\mu},\mu_{r})J_{r}^{x,\mu}\right\rangle\right]\mathrm{d}r \displaystyle\quad+\frac{p}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|J_{r}^{x,\mu}\|^{p-2}\|\nabla_{s}\sigma_{\ell}^{\pi}(X_{r}^{x,\mu},\mu_{r})J_{r}^{x,\mu}\|^{2}\right]\mathrm{d}r \displaystyle\quad+\frac{p(p-2)}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|J_{r}^{x,\mu}\|^{p-4}\left\langle J_{r}^{x,\mu},\nabla_{s}\sigma_{\ell}^{\pi}(X_{r}^{x,\mu},\mu_{r})J_{r}^{x,\mu}\right\rangle^{2}\right]\mathrm{d}r. $$

Using (56), and $\langle z,Az\rangle\leq\|A\|\,\|z\|^{2}$ , and recalling $K_{\pi}\geq 1$ , we infer that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|J_{t}^{x,\mu}\|^{p}\right]\leq d^{p/2}+a_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|J_{r}^{x,\mu}\|^{p}\right]\mathrm{d}r. $$

Grönwall’s inequality gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|J_{t}^{x,\mu}\|^{p}\right]\leq d^{p/2}e^{a_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2}t}. $$

Step 2 (Bounds for the second spatial derivative). Differentiating (55) once more with respect to $x$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}H_{t}^{x,\mu} \displaystyle=\Bigl[\nabla_{s}b^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})H_{t}^{x,\mu}+D^{2}_{ss}b^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})[J_{t}^{x,\mu},J_{t}^{x,\mu}]\Bigr]\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle\quad+\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\Bigl[\nabla_{s}\sigma_{\ell}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})H_{t}^{x,\mu}+D^{2}_{ss}\sigma_{\ell}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})[J_{t}^{x,\mu},J_{t}^{x,\mu}]\Bigr]\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{\ell},\qquad H_{0}^{x,\mu}=0. $$

By Assumption 3.1,

$$ \displaystyle\|D^{2}_{ss}b^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})[J_{t}^{x,\mu},J_{t}^{x,\mu}]\|+\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\|D^{2}_{ss}\sigma_{\ell}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})[J_{t}^{x,\mu},J_{t}^{x,\mu}]\|\leq(d+1)K_{\pi}\|J_{t}^{x,\mu}\|^{2}. $$

Applying Itô’s formula to $\|H_{t}^{x,\mu}\|^{p}$ in (58), integrating over $[0,t]$ , taking expectations, and using (56), (56), (59), and Young’s inequality, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|H_{t}^{x,\mu}\|^{p}\right]\leq a_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|H_{r}^{x,\mu}\|^{p}\right]\mathrm{d}r+C_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{p}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|J_{r}^{x,\mu}\|^{2p}\right]\mathrm{d}r. $$

Using (57) with $2p$ in place of $p$ and then Grönwall’s inequality, we get

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|H_{t}^{x,\mu}\|^{p}\right]\leq C_{p,d}(1+K_{\pi}^{p})e^{C_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2}t}. $$

Step 3 (Bounds for the Lions derivative). Let $(\widetilde{\Omega},\widetilde{\mathcal{F}},\widetilde{\mathbb{P}})$ be an independent copy of the original probability space, and denote by $\widetilde{X}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}$ and $\widetilde{J}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}:=\nabla_{x}X_{t}^{x,\mu}\big|_{x=\xi},$ the corresponding independent copies of the decoupled flow and its first spatial derivative, started from $\xi$ . Then $U_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}U_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi) \displaystyle=\Bigl[\nabla_{s}b^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})U_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)+F_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\Bigr]\mathrm{d}t+\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\Bigl[\nabla_{s}\sigma_{\ell}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})U_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)+G_{t,\ell}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\Bigr]\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{\ell} $$

where $U_{0}^{x,\mu}(\xi)=0,$ and

$$ \displaystyle F_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi):=\widetilde{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\partial_{\mu}b^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})(\widetilde{X}_{t}^{\xi,\mu})\,\widetilde{J}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}\right],\qquad G_{t,\ell}^{x,\mu}(\xi):=\widetilde{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\partial_{\mu}\sigma_{\ell}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})(\widetilde{X}_{t}^{\xi,\mu})\,\widetilde{J}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}\right]. $$

Since $\partial_{\mu}b^{\pi}$ and $\partial_{\mu}\sigma^{\pi}_{\ell}$ are bounded by $K_{\pi}$ , Jensen’s inequality yields

$$ \|F_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\leq K_{\pi}^{p}\,\widetilde{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\|\widetilde{J}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}\|^{p}\right],\qquad\|G_{t,\ell}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\leq K_{\pi}^{p}\,\widetilde{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\|\widetilde{J}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}\|^{p}\right]. $$

Taking expectations and using (57) with $x=\xi$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|F_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\right]+\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|G_{t,\ell}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\right]\leq C_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{p}e^{C_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2}t}. $$

Applying Itô’s formula to $\|U_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}$ in (61), integrating over $[0,t]$ , taking expectations, and using (62), we infer

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|U_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\right]\leq a_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|U_{r}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\right]\mathrm{d}r+C_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{p}\int_{0}^{t}e^{C_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2}r}\,\mathrm{d}r. $$

Grönwall’s inequality gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|U_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\right]\leq C_{p,d}(1+K_{\pi}^{p})e^{C_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2}t}. $$

Step 4 (Bounds for $D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}X_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)$ ). Let $\widetilde{H}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}:=D^{2}_{xx}X_{t}^{x,\mu}\big|_{x=\xi}$ denote the independent copy of the second spatial derivative started from $\xi$ . Differentiating (61) with respect to $\xi$ yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}V_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi) \displaystyle=\Bigl[\nabla_{s}b^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})V_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)+\bar{F}_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\Bigr]\mathrm{d}t+\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\Bigl[\nabla_{s}\sigma_{\ell}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})V_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)+\bar{G}_{t,\ell}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\Bigr]\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{\ell}, $$

where $V_{0}^{x,\mu}(\xi)=0,$ and

$$ \displaystyle\bar{F}_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi) \displaystyle:=\widetilde{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}b^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})(\widetilde{X}_{t}^{\xi,\mu})[\widetilde{J}_{t}^{\xi,\mu},\widetilde{J}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}]+\partial_{\mu}b^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})(\widetilde{X}_{t}^{\xi,\mu})\widetilde{H}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}\right], \displaystyle\bar{G}_{t,\ell}^{x,\mu}(\xi) \displaystyle:=\widetilde{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}\sigma_{\ell}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})(\widetilde{X}_{t}^{\xi,\mu})[\widetilde{J}_{t}^{\xi,\mu},\widetilde{J}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}]+\partial_{\mu}\sigma_{\ell}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{x,\mu},\mu_{t})(\widetilde{X}_{t}^{\xi,\mu})\widetilde{H}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}\right]. $$

Since $D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}b^{\pi}$ , $D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}\sigma^{\pi}_{\ell}$ , $\partial_{\mu}b^{\pi}$ , and $\partial_{\mu}\sigma^{\pi}_{\ell}$ are all bounded by $K_{\pi}$ , Jensen’s inequality gives

$$ \|\bar{F}_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\leq C_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{p}\,\widetilde{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\|\widetilde{J}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}\|^{2p}+\|\widetilde{H}_{t}^{\xi,\mu}\|^{p}\right], $$

and similarly for $\bar{G}_{t,\ell}^{x,\mu}(\xi)$ . Taking expectations, and using (57) with $2p$ in place of $p$ together with (60), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\bar{F}_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\right]+\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\bar{G}_{t,\ell}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\right]\leq C_{p,d}(1+K_{\pi}^{p})e^{C_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2}t}. $$

Applying Itô’s formula to $\|V_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}$ in (64), integrating over $[0,t]$ , taking expectations, and using (65), we infer

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|V_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\right]\leq a_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|V_{r}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\right]\mathrm{d}r+C_{p,d}(1+K_{\pi}^{p})\int_{0}^{t}e^{C_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2}r}\,\mathrm{d}r. $$

Grönwall’s inequality yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|V_{t}^{x,\mu}(\xi)\|^{p}\right]\leq C_{p,d}(1+K_{\pi}^{p})e^{C_{p,d}K_{\pi}^{2}t}. $$

Combining (57), (60), (63), and (66), we obtain (54). ∎

#### Remark A.5 (Explicit value of $\beta_{\mathrm{var}}(2)$ ).

A careful analysis shows that the constant $C_{p,d}$ from Lemma A.4 is given by

$$ \displaystyle C_{p,d}:=2^{2p}(1+d^{p})\bigl(1+2p\sqrt{d}+\frac{2p(2p-1)}{2}d^{2}+(d+1)^{p}\bigr), $$

In particular, we have that $\beta_{\mathrm{var}}(2)=(32+32d+64\sqrt{d}+144d^{2}+32d^{3}+64d^{5/2}+112d^{4})K_{\pi}^{2}$ .

We can now prove Theorem 3.3.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.3.

We proceed in several steps.

Step 1 (Finite-horizon problem). For each $T>0$ , define

$$ \displaystyle V_{T}^{\pi}(t,s,\mu):=\mathbb{E}^{t,s,\mu,\pi}\!\left[\int_{t}^{T}e^{-\beta(\tau-t)}\,r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{\tau},\mu_{\tau})\,\mathrm{d}\tau\right],\qquad V_{T}^{\pi}(T,\cdot,\cdot)\equiv 0. $$

Under Assumption 3.1, the finite-horizon policy-evaluation problem with coefficients $b^{\pi}$ , $\sigma^{\pi}$ , running reward $r_{\lambda}^{\pi}$ , and terminal cost $g\equiv 0$ falls under the time-homogeneous version of [37, Assumption 2.1]. Therefore, by [37, Proposition 2.1], $V_{T}^{\pi}\in C^{1,2,2}\bigl([0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\bigr)$ and $V_{T}^{\pi}$ solves

$$ \partial_{t}V_{T}^{\pi}+\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}V_{T}^{\pi}-\beta V_{T}^{\pi}+r_{\lambda}^{\pi}=0,\qquad 0\leq t<T, $$

with terminal condition $V_{T}^{\pi}(T,\cdot,\cdot)=0$ .

Set

$$ \displaystyle U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu):=V_{T}^{\pi}(0,s,\mu)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}e^{-\beta t}\,r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{s,\mu},\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\right]. $$

Step 2 (Well-definedness of $V^{\pi}$ and convergence of $U_{T}^{\pi}$ ). Since $r_{\lambda}^{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ , Definition 3.1 yields

$$ \displaystyle|r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s,\mu)|\leq C_{r}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr) $$

for some constant $C_{r}>0$ . By Lemma A.1 with $p=2$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}[|s_{t}|^{2}]+\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}[|\tilde{s}_{t}|^{2}]\leq C_{2}e^{\beta_{0}(2)t}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr),\qquad t\geq 0. $$

Since $m_{2}(\mu_{t})=\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}[|\tilde{s}_{t}|^{2}]$ , it follows from (68) and (69) that

$$ \displaystyle e^{-\beta t}\,\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\left[|r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t},\mu_{t})|\right]\leq Ce^{-(\beta-\beta_{0}(2))t}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr). $$

Therefore, if $\beta>\bar{\beta}_{\pi}$ , then the right-hand side of (70) is integrable on $[0,\infty)$ , and the value function $V^{\pi}(s,\mu)$ is well defined. Moreover, dominated convergence yields

$$ \displaystyle U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{}V^{\pi}(s,\mu) $$

for every $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ . If $K_{R}:=\bigl\{(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}):|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\leq R\bigr\},$ then (70) also gives

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{(s,\mu)\in K_{R}}|V^{\pi}(s,\mu)-U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)|\leq C_{R}\int_{T}^{\infty}e^{-(\beta-\beta_{0}(2))t}\,\mathrm{d}t\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{}0. $$

Step 3 (Uniform finite-horizon bounds in $\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}$ ). We first record the corresponding moment bound for the decoupled flow $X_{t}^{x,\mu}$ . By the same Itô-Grönwall argument used in the proof of Lemma A.1, together with (9) and the estimate on $m_{2}(\mu_{t})$ coming from (69), there exists a constant $C>0$ , depending only on the structural constants in Assumption 3.1, such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[|X_{t}^{x,\mu}|^{2}\right]\leq Ce^{\beta_{0}(2)t}\bigl(1+|x|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr),\qquad t\geq 0. $$

We now estimate the derivatives of $U_{T}^{\pi}$ . Since $U_{T}^{\pi}$ is the finite-horizon value function, Step 2 of [37, Appendix A.1] provides explicit representation formulas for $\nabla_{s}U_{T}^{\pi}$ , $D^{2}_{ss}U_{T}^{\pi}$ , $\partial_{\mu}U_{T}^{\pi}$ , and $D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}U_{T}^{\pi}$ . These formulas show that each derivative is given by an integral over $[0,T]$ of $e^{-\beta t}$ times the expectation of a finite linear combination of terms involving derivatives of $r_{\lambda}^{\pi}$ evaluated at $(X_{t}^{s,\mu},\mu_{t})$ and $(X_{t}^{\xi,\mu},\mu_{t})$ , together with the corresponding derivatives of the flow. To avoid an unnecessarily long proof, we refer to [37, Appendix A.1, Step 2] for the explicit expressions. Therefore, by using Lemma A.4 with $p=2$ , and the fact that $r_{\lambda}^{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ we derive the estimates

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left|\nabla_{s}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{s,\mu},\mu_{t})\,\nabla_{x}X_{t}^{s,\mu}\right|\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left|\nabla_{s}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{s,\mu},\mu_{t})\,\partial_{\mu}X_{t}^{s,\mu}(\xi)\right|\right] \displaystyle\leq Ce^{\bar{\beta}_{\pi}t}\bigl(1+|s|+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left|\nabla_{s}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{s,\mu},\mu_{t})\,D^{2}_{xx}X_{t}^{s,\mu}\right|\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left|\nabla_{s}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{s,\mu},\mu_{t})\,D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}X_{t}^{s,\mu}(\xi)\right|\right] \displaystyle+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left|D^{2}_{ss}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{s,\mu},\mu_{t})[\nabla_{x}X_{t}^{s,\mu},\nabla_{x}X_{t}^{s,\mu}]\right|\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left|D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{s,\mu},\mu_{t})(X_{t}^{\xi,\mu})\,\nabla_{x}X_{t}^{\xi,\mu}\right|\right] \displaystyle\leq Ce^{\bar{\beta}_{\pi}t}\bigl(1+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left|\partial_{\mu}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{s,\mu},\mu_{t})(X_{t}^{\xi,\mu})\right|\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left|\partial_{\mu}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(X_{t}^{s,\mu},\mu_{t})(X_{t}^{\xi,\mu})\,D^{2}_{xx}X_{t}^{\xi,\mu}\right|\right]\leq Ce^{\beta_{0}(2)t}\bigl(1+|s|+|\xi|+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr). $$

Integrating (73)-(74) over $[0,T]$ , multiplying by $e^{-\beta t}$ , and using $\beta>\bar{\beta}_{\pi}$ , we conclude that there exists a constant $C>0$ , independent of $T$ , such that for all $(s,\mu,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)| \displaystyle\leq C\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), \displaystyle|\nabla_{s}U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)|+|\partial_{\mu}U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)| \displaystyle\leq C\bigl(1+|s|+|\xi|+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), \displaystyle\|D^{2}_{ss}U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)\|+\|D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)\| \displaystyle\leq C\bigl(1+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr). $$

Step 4 (Passage to the limit in the derivatives). Let

$$ K_{R}:=\bigl\{(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}):|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\leq R\bigr\},\qquad B_{R}:=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:|\xi|\leq R\}. $$

By (72), the family $(U_{T}^{\pi})_{T>0}$ is uniformly Cauchy on $K_{R}$ . Using the representation formulas from [37, Appendix A.1, Step 2] together with the estimations (73)-(74), we obtain, for every $D_{\alpha}\in\{1,\nabla_{s},\partial_{\mu},D_{ss}^{2},D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}\}$ , for all $T^{\prime}>T\geq 0$ , all $(s,\mu)\in K_{R}$ , and all $\xi\in B_{R}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|D_{\alpha}U_{T^{\prime}}^{\pi}(s,\mu)-D_{\alpha}U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)| \displaystyle\leq C_{R}\int_{T}^{T^{\prime}}e^{-(\beta-\bar{\beta}_{\pi})t}\,\mathrm{d}t, $$

Since $\beta>\bar{\beta}_{\pi}$ , the right-hand sides tend to zero as $T\to\infty$ . Hence, for each $D_{\alpha}$ , the families $\{D_{\alpha}U_{T}^{\pi}\}_{T\geq 0}$ are locally uniformly Cauchy and thus converge locally uniformly to continuous limits.

By (71), the limit of $U_{T}^{\pi}$ is precisely $V^{\pi}$ . The local uniform convergence of $U_{T}^{\pi}$ , $\nabla_{s}U_{T}^{\pi}$ , and $D^{2}_{ss}U_{T}^{\pi}$ implies that $V^{\pi}$ is twice continuously differentiable in $s$ , with

$$ \nabla_{s}V^{\pi}=\lim_{T\to\infty}\nabla_{s}U_{T}^{\pi},\qquad D^{2}_{ss}V^{\pi}=\lim_{T\to\infty}D^{2}_{ss}U_{T}^{\pi}. $$

For the measure derivative, let $\vartheta,\vartheta^{\prime}$ be square-integrable random variables with laws $\mu$ and $\mu^{\prime}$ , and set $\vartheta_{\lambda}:=\vartheta+\lambda(\vartheta^{\prime}-\vartheta)$ , $\mu_{\lambda}:=\Law(\vartheta_{\lambda})$ . Since each $U_{T}^{\pi}$ is Lions differentiable, the mean-value formula on $\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ gives

$$ \displaystyle U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu^{\prime})-U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)=\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\partial_{\mu}U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu_{\lambda})(\vartheta_{\lambda})\cdot(\vartheta^{\prime}-\vartheta)\right]\mathrm{d}\lambda. $$

Passing to the limit $T\to\infty$ in (78), using the local uniform convergence of $U_{T}^{\pi}$ and $\partial_{\mu}U_{T}^{\pi}$ together with dominated convergence, we obtain that $V^{\pi}$ is Lions differentiable and

$$ \partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}=\lim_{T\to\infty}\partial_{\mu}U_{T}^{\pi}. $$

Applying the same argument to $\partial_{\mu}U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)$ as a function of $\xi$ , and using the local uniform convergence of $D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)$ , we conclude that $D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}$ exists and is jointly continuous. Therefore, $V^{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})).$ Letting $T\to\infty$ in (75), (76), and (77), we obtain that $V^{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})).$

Step 5 (The stationary HJB equation). Evaluating (67) at $t=0$ yields

$$ \displaystyle\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}-\beta\bigr)U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)+r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s,\mu)=-\partial_{t}V_{T}^{\pi}(0,s,\mu). $$

Since the problem is time-homogeneous, $V_{T}^{\pi}(t,s,\mu)=U_{T-t}^{\pi}(s,\mu),$ and therefore

$$ \displaystyle-\partial_{t}V_{T}^{\pi}(0,s,\mu)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}T}U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{-\beta T}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(X_{T}^{s,\mu},\mu_{T})\right]. $$

Thus, by (70),

$$ \displaystyle\left|\partial_{t}V_{T}^{\pi}(0,s,\mu)\right|\leq\left|\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{-\beta T}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(X_{T}^{s,\mu},\mu_{T})\right]\right|\leq Ce^{-(\beta-\beta_{0}(2))T}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr)\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{}0. $$

It remains to pass to the limit in $\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}-\beta\bigr)U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)$ . The terms involving $\nabla_{s}U_{T}^{\pi}$ and $D^{2}_{ss}U_{T}^{\pi}$ converge pointwise by Step 4. For the Lions terms, using (9), (10), (76), and (77), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle|b^{\pi}(\xi,\mu)\cdot\partial_{\mu}U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)| \displaystyle\leq C_{s,\mu}(1+|\xi|^{2}), \displaystyle|\Sigma^{\pi}(\xi,\mu):D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)| \displaystyle\leq C_{s,\mu}(1+|\xi|^{2}), $$

with constants independent of $T$ . Since $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , the dominating function is $\mu$ -integrable, and dominated convergence yields

$$ \displaystyle\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}-\beta\bigr)U_{T}^{\pi}(s,\mu)\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{}\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}-\beta\bigr)V^{\pi}(s,\mu). $$

Combining (79), (80), and (81), and letting $T\to\infty$ , we obtain

$$ (\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}-\beta)V^{\pi}(s,\mu)+r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s,\mu)=0. $$

Thus $V^{\pi}$ is a classical solution of (11).

Step 6 (Uniqueness). Let $U\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ be another classical solution of (11). Fix $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and define the stopping times $\tau_{n}:=\inf\{t\geq 0:|s_{t}|+|\tilde{s}_{t}|\geq n\},$ with $n\in\mathbb{N}.$ Applying the Itô-Lions formula to $e^{-\beta(t\wedge\tau_{n})}U(s_{t\wedge\tau_{n}},\mu_{t\wedge\tau_{n}})$ on $[0,T]$ , taking expectations, and using (11), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle U(s,\mu) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\left[e^{-\beta(T\wedge\tau_{n})}U(s_{T\wedge\tau_{n}},\mu_{T\wedge\tau_{n}})\right]+\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\left[\int_{0}^{T\wedge\tau_{n}}e^{-\beta t}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t},\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\right]. $$

Since $U\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ , together with (69), we have

$$ e^{-\beta T}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\left[|U(s_{T},\mu_{T})|\right]\leq Ce^{-(\beta-\beta_{0}(2))T}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), $$

which tends to zero as $T\to\infty$ . Letting first $n\to\infty$ in (82), and then $T\to\infty$ , and using dominated convergence together with (70), we conclude that

$$ U(s,\mu)=\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t},\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\right]=V^{\pi}(s,\mu). $$

Hence $U=V^{\pi}$ , and the classical solution of (11) is unique in the class $\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ . ∎

### A.2. Proofs for Section 4

We turn to the main policy gradient theorem. A technical ingredient is needed: a stability estimate that controls the first-order response of the controlled system to a policy perturbation.

#### Lemma A.6 (Stability with respect to policy perturbations).

Suppose Section 3.1 holds. Let $\pi$ be a fixed feedback policy and $\varphi$ a signed kernel satisfying (14) with $M_{\psi}:=\|\psi\|_{\infty}<\infty$ . For $|\varepsilon|$ small enough that $\pi^{\varepsilon}$ is admissible, let $(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})$ and $(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})$ be the solutions of (4)-(5) under $\pi^{\varepsilon}$ and $\pi$ respectively, with the same initial condition $s_{0}\sim\mu_{0}$ , $\mu_{0}^{\varepsilon}=\mu_{0}^{\pi}=\mu$ , and the same driving Brownian motions. Then there exist constants $C>0$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{stab}}>0$ , depending only on $L_{\pi}$ , $M_{\psi}$ , and $\beta_{0}(2)$ , such that for every $t\geq 0$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}\bigl[|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}-s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}\bigr]+\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\leq C\,\varepsilon^{2}\,e^{\beta_{\mathrm{stab}}\,t}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr). $$

In particular, $\mathbb{E}[|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}-s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}]+\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\to 0$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$ , for each fixed $t\geq 0$ .

#### Proof.

Set $\delta s_{t}:=s_{t}^{\varepsilon}-s_{t}^{\pi}$ and $\delta\tilde{s}_{t}:=\tilde{s}_{t}^{\varepsilon}-\tilde{s}_{t}^{\pi}$ . Since both pairs of processes are driven by the same Brownian motions $B$ and $\tilde{B}$ , the differences satisfy

$$ \mathrm{d}(\delta s_{t})=\bigl(b^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})-b^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t+\bigl(\sigma^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})-\sigma^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}B_{t}, $$

and analogously for $\delta\tilde{s}_{t}$ .

Step 1: Decomposition of the coefficient differences. By linearity of the averaged coefficients in the control measure:

$$ b^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s^{\varepsilon},\mu^{\varepsilon})-b^{\pi}(s^{\pi},\mu^{\pi})=\varepsilon\,b^{\varphi}(s^{\varepsilon},\mu^{\varepsilon})+\bigl[b^{\pi}(s^{\varepsilon},\mu^{\varepsilon})-b^{\pi}(s^{\pi},\mu^{\pi})\bigr], $$

where $b^{\varphi}(s,\mu):=\int_{\mathcal{A}}b(s,\mu,a)\,\varphi(\mathrm{d}a|s,\mu)$ . By the linear growth of $b$ in Section 3.1 and the zero-mass condition (14),

$$ |b^{\varphi}(s,\mu)|\leq C_{b}\bigl(1+|s|+\sqrt{m_{2}(\mu)}\bigr), $$

and by the Lipschitz condition of Section 3.1, the second term of (84) is bounded by $L_{\pi}(|\delta s|+\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu^{\varepsilon},\mu^{\pi}))$ .

For the diffusion coefficient, write

$$ \sigma^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s^{\varepsilon},\mu^{\varepsilon})-\sigma^{\pi}(s^{\pi},\mu^{\pi})=\bigl[\sigma^{\pi}(s^{\varepsilon},\mu^{\varepsilon})-\sigma^{\pi}(s^{\pi},\mu^{\pi})\bigr]+\bigl[\sigma^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s^{\varepsilon},\mu^{\varepsilon})-\sigma^{\pi}(s^{\varepsilon},\mu^{\varepsilon})\bigr]. $$

The first bracket is bounded by $L_{\pi}(|\delta s|+\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu^{\varepsilon},\mu^{\pi}))$ by Section 3.1. For the second bracket, since $\pi^{\varepsilon}=(1+\varepsilon\psi)\pi$ with $|\varepsilon|M_{\psi}<1$ , we have for every $(s,\mu)$ and every $z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ :

$$ z^{\top}\Sigma^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s,\mu)z=\int_{\mathcal{A}}z^{\top}\Sigma(s,\mu,a)z\,\bigl(1+\varepsilon\psi(s,\mu,a)\bigr)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a\mid s,\mu), $$

from which

$$ (1-M_{\psi}|\varepsilon|)\,\Sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)\leq\Sigma^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s,\mu)\leq(1+M_{\psi}|\varepsilon|)\,\Sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu). $$

Since the map $A\mapsto A^{1/2}$ is operator-monotone on the cone of symmetric positive semidefinite matrices (a consequence of the Löwner-Heinz inequality, which holds for any semidefinite matrix), taking square roots in (86) gives

$$ \sqrt{1-M_{\psi}|\varepsilon|}\,\sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)\leq\sigma^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s,\mu)\leq\sqrt{1+M_{\psi}|\varepsilon|}\,\sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu). $$

Using the elementary inequalities $1-\sqrt{1-x}\leq x$ and $\sqrt{1+x}-1\leq x$ for $x\in[0,1)$ , we conclude that

$$ \|\sigma^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s,\mu)-\sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)\|\leq M_{\psi}|\varepsilon|\,\|\sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)\|. $$

By the linear growth of $\sigma^{\pi}$ from Section 3.1:

$$ \|\sigma^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s,\mu)-\sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu)\|^{2}\leq C\,\varepsilon^{2}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr). $$

Note that (87) holds without any ellipticity assumption on $\Sigma^{\pi}$ ; the sandwich argument requires only that $\Sigma^{\pi}$ be positive semidefinite, which holds automatically. Combining both brackets in (85), we have

$$ \bigl\|\sigma^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s^{\varepsilon},\mu^{\varepsilon})-\sigma^{\pi}(s^{\pi},\mu^{\pi})\bigr\|^{2}\leq C\Bigl(|\delta s|^{2}+\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(\mu^{\varepsilon},\mu^{\pi})+\varepsilon^{2}\bigl(1+|s^{\varepsilon}|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu^{\varepsilon})\bigr)\Bigr). $$

Step 2: Itô formula, Grönwall, and exponential bound. Applying Itô’s formula to $|\delta s_{t}|^{2}$ , taking expectations (the stochastic integral is a true martingale by the moment estimates of Lemma A.1), and using Young’s inequality together with (84)-(88), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}\bigl[|\delta s_{t}|^{2}\bigr]\leq C_{1}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[|\delta s_{t}|^{2}\bigr]+C_{1}\,\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\pi})+C_{1}\,\varepsilon^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[1+|s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr], $$

where $C_{1}>0$ depends only on $L_{\pi}$ and $M_{\psi}$ . An identical estimate holds for $\delta\tilde{s}_{t}$ . Since $\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\leq\mathbb{E}[|\delta\tilde{s}_{t}|^{2}]$ , setting $\Phi_{t}:=\mathbb{E}[|\delta s_{t}|^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[|\delta\tilde{s}_{t}|^{2}]$ and summing the two estimates gives

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Phi_{t}\leq C_{2}\,\Phi_{t}+C_{2}\,\varepsilon^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[1+|s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}+|\tilde{s}_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr], $$

where $C_{2}$ depends only on $C_{1}$ . By Lemma A.1 with $p=2$ , the factor on the right-hand side satisfies

$$ \mathbb{E}\bigl[1+|s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}+|\tilde{s}_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]\leq Ce^{\beta_{0}(2)t}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr). $$

Since $\Phi_{0}=0$ , Grönwall’s inequality applied to (89) gives

$$ \Phi_{t}\leq C_{2}\varepsilon^{2}(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu))\int_{0}^{t}e^{C_{2}(t-r)}\,C\,e^{\beta_{0}(2)r}\,\mathrm{d}r\leq C^{\prime}\varepsilon^{2}e^{\max(C_{2},\,\beta_{0}(2))\,t}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), $$

where the last step uses $e^{C_{2}(t-r)}e^{\beta_{0}(2)r}\leq e^{\max(C_{2},\beta_{0}(2))t}$ for $r\in[0,t]$ . Setting $\beta_{\mathrm{stab}}:=\max(C_{2},\,\beta_{0}(2))$ and recalling $\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\leq\mathbb{E}[|\delta\tilde{s}_{t}|^{2}]\leq\Phi_{t}$ gives (83). ∎

We are now in a position to prove Theorem 4.6.

#### Proof of Theorem 4.6.

Since $\beta>\widetilde{\beta}_{\pi}\geq\bar{\beta}_{\pi}$ , Theorem 3.3 applies to both $\pi$ and $\pi^{\varepsilon}$ , giving $V^{\pi},V^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}$ with polynomial-growth constant bounded by $C/(\beta-\bar{\beta}_{\pi})$ uniformly in $|\varepsilon|\leq\varepsilon_{0}$ .

We fix $s\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and write $(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})_{t\geq 0}$ and $(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})_{t\geq 0}$ for the representative process and population flow under $\pi$ and $\pi^{\varepsilon}$ respectively, both starting from $(s,\mu)$ . Both value functions admit the stochastic representations

$$ \displaystyle V^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s,\mu) \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t,\qquad V^{\pi}(s,\mu)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t, $$

both convergent since $\beta>\beta_{0}(2)$ . We split the difference quotient as

$$ \frac{V^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s,\mu)-V^{\pi}(s,\mu)}{\varepsilon}=A(\varepsilon;s)+B(\varepsilon;s), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle A(\varepsilon;s) \displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\frac{\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]-\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]}{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{d}t, \displaystyle B(\varepsilon;s) \displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\frac{\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]-\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]}{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Intuitively, $A(\varepsilon;s)$ captures the sensitivity of the reward functional to the change in policy. In contrast, $B(\varepsilon;s)$ captures the effect of the change in dynamics.

Step 1: We compute the limit of $A(\varepsilon;s)$ . We first identify the derivative of $\varepsilon\mapsto r_{\lambda}^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(x,\nu)$ at $\varepsilon=0$ . Writing $p_{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(a|x,\nu)=(1+\varepsilon\psi(x,\nu,a))\,p_{\pi}(a|x,\nu)$ , the reward part differentiates as

$$ \frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\bigg|_{\varepsilon=0}\int_{\mathcal{A}}r(x,\nu,a)\,\pi^{\varepsilon}(\mathrm{d}a|x,\nu)=\int_{\mathcal{A}}r(x,\nu,a)\,\varphi(\mathrm{d}a|x,\nu). $$

For the entropy part, the identity $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}f}(f\log f)=\log f+1$ applied to $f=p_{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(a|x,\nu)$ gives

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}\bigg|_{\varepsilon=0}\left[-\lambda\int_{\mathcal{A}}p_{\pi^{\varepsilon}}\log p_{\pi^{\varepsilon}}\,\nu(\mathrm{d}a)\right]=-\lambda\int_{\mathcal{A}}\bigl(\log p_{\pi}(a|x,\nu)+1\bigr)\,\varphi(\mathrm{d}a|x,\nu). $$

Since $\int_{\mathcal{A}}\varphi(da|x,\nu)=0$ by (14), the constant term vanishes. Combining both parts yields

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}\bigg|_{\varepsilon=0}r_{\lambda}^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(x,\nu)=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\bigl(r(x,\nu,a)-\lambda\log p_{\pi}(a|x,\nu)\bigr)\,\varphi(\mathrm{d}a|x,\nu)=:r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(x,\nu). $$

By the mean value theorem applied to the differentiable map $\varepsilon\mapsto r_{\lambda}^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(x,\nu)$ and Section 3.1 (with constants uniform in $|\varepsilon|\leq\varepsilon_{0}$ ), the ratio satisfies

$$ \left|\frac{r_{\lambda}^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(x,\nu)-r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(x,\nu)}{\varepsilon}\right|\leq M_{\psi}C_{r}\bigl(1+|x|^{2}+m_{2}(\nu)\bigr),\qquad|\varepsilon|\leq\varepsilon_{0}, $$

with $C_{r}>0$ independent of $\varepsilon$ . Taking expectations against the $\pi^{\varepsilon}$ -dynamics, using Lemma A.1 with $p=2$ , and noting that $m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})$ is deterministic since there is no common noise, we obtain

$$ e^{-\beta t}\left|\frac{\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}[r_{\lambda}^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})]-\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})]}{\varepsilon}\right|\leq M_{\psi}C_{r}\,e^{-(\beta-\beta_{0}(2))t}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), $$

which is integrable since $\beta>\beta_{0}(2)$ . We now split $A(\varepsilon;s)$ as $A(\varepsilon;s)=A_{1}(\varepsilon;s)+A_{2}(\varepsilon;s),$ where

$$ \displaystyle A_{1}(\varepsilon;s) \displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\left[\frac{r_{\lambda}^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})-r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})}{\varepsilon}-r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\right]\mathrm{d}t, \displaystyle A_{2}(\varepsilon;s) \displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

The integrand of $A_{1}$ converges pointwise to zero as $\varepsilon\to 0$ by (92), and is dominated by twice the right-hand side of (93), so dominated convergence gives $A_{1}(\varepsilon;s)\to 0$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$ .

For $A_{2}$ , fix $t\geq 0$ . Then, for each $\theta\in[0,1]$ , define $\tilde{s}_{t}^{\theta}:=(1-\theta)\tilde{s}_{t}^{\pi}+\theta\tilde{s}_{t}^{\varepsilon},$ and $\mu_{t}^{\theta}:=\Law(\tilde{s}_{t}^{\theta}).$ Since $r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\bigl|\mathbb{E}[ \displaystyle r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})]-\mathbb{E}[r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})]\bigr|\leq\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\bigl|r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})-r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr|\Bigr]+\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\bigl|r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})-r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr|\Bigr] \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\Bigl[|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}-s_{t}^{\pi}|\int_{0}^{1}\bigl|\nabla_{s}r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}\bigl(s_{t}^{\pi}+\theta(s_{t}^{\varepsilon}-s_{t}^{\pi}),\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon}\bigr)\bigr|\,\mathrm{d}\theta\Bigr]+\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\bigl|\partial_{\mu}r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\theta})(\tilde{s}_{t}^{\theta})\bigr|\,|\tilde{s}_{t}^{\varepsilon}-\tilde{s}_{t}^{\pi}|\Bigr]\,\mathrm{d}\theta \displaystyle\leq C\,\mathbb{E}\Bigl[|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}-s_{t}^{\pi}|\bigl(1+|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}|+|s_{t}^{\pi}|+m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})^{1/2}\bigr)\Bigr]+C\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\bigl(1+|s_{t}^{\pi}|+|\tilde{s}_{t}^{\theta}|+m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\theta})^{1/2}\bigr)|\tilde{s}_{t}^{\varepsilon}-\tilde{s}_{t}^{\pi}|\Bigr]\,\mathrm{d}\theta \displaystyle\leq C\,\mathbb{E}[|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}-s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}]^{1/2}\Bigl(1+\mathbb{E}[|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}|^{2}]^{1/2}+\mathbb{E}[|s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}]^{1/2}+m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})^{1/2}\Bigr) \displaystyle\qquad+C\int_{0}^{1}\Bigl(1+\mathbb{E}[|s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}]^{1/2}+2\,m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\theta})^{1/2}\Bigr)\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\,\mathrm{d}\theta \displaystyle\leq C\,\mathbb{E}[|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}-s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}]^{1/2}\Bigl(1+\mathbb{E}[|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}|^{2}]^{1/2}+\mathbb{E}[|s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}]^{1/2}+m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})^{1/2}\Bigr) \displaystyle\qquad+C\Bigl(1+\mathbb{E}[|s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}]^{1/2}+m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\pi})^{1/2}+m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})^{1/2}\Bigr)\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\pi}). $$

By Lemma A.6, for each fixed $t\geq 0$ the right-hand side tends to $0$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$ . Hence $\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]\to\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$ . The dominating function for dominated convergence over $t$ is the same as in (93) (with $r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}$ in place of the ratio), and combining both terms gives

$$ \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}A(\varepsilon;s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Step 2: We derive an exact formula for $B(\varepsilon;s)$ . We apply the Itô-Lions formula to $V^{\pi}$ along the $\pi^{\varepsilon}$ -dynamics. For $n\geq 1$ , let $\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon}:=\inf\{t\geq 0:|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}|\geq n\}$ . Applying the Itô-Lions formula to $t\mapsto e^{-\beta(t\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon})}V^{\pi}(s_{t\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon})$ and taking expectations (the stochastic integral has zero expectation since $|s_{u}^{\varepsilon}|\leq n$ on $[0,T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon}]$ ensures the integrand is bounded) yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\beta(T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon})}V^{\pi}(s_{T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]-V^{\pi}(s,\mu)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon}}e^{-\beta t}(\mathcal{L}^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}-\beta)V^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\,\mathrm{d}t\right]. $$

Since $\mathcal{L}^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}=\mathcal{L}^{\pi}+\varepsilon\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}$ by linearity of the generator in the averaged coefficients, and since $(\mathcal{L}^{\pi}-\beta)V^{\pi}=-r_{\lambda}^{\pi}$ by the HJB equation (11), this simplifies to

$$ \mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\beta(T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon})}V^{\pi}(s_{T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]-V^{\pi}(s,\mu)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon}}e^{-\beta t}\bigl(-r_{\lambda}^{\pi}+\varepsilon\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}V^{\pi}\bigr)(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\,\mathrm{d}t\right]. $$

As $n\to\infty$ , $\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon}\to\infty$ almost surely. Since $|V^{\pi}(x,\nu)|\leq C(1+|x|^{2}+m_{2}(\nu))$ and $\mathbb{E}[\sup_{t\leq T}|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}|^{2}]<\infty$ by (48), dominated convergence gives

$$ \mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\beta T}V^{\pi}(s_{T}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{T}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]-V^{\pi}(s,\mu)=\int_{0}^{T}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}\bigl[(-r_{\lambda}^{\pi}+\varepsilon\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}V^{\pi})(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Since $V^{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}$ and $\beta>\beta_{0}(2)$ , the boundary term satisfies

$$ e^{-\beta T}\mathbb{E}\bigl[|V^{\pi}(s_{T}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{T}^{\varepsilon})|\bigr]\leq Ce^{-(\beta-\beta_{0}(2))T}(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu))\to 0\qquad\text{as }T\to\infty. $$

For the right-hand side, since $m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})$ is deterministic and Lemma A.1 gives $\mathbb{E}[|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}|^{2}]\leq Ce^{\beta_{0}(2)t}(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu))$ and $m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\leq Ce^{\beta_{0}(2)t}(1+m_{2}(\mu))$ , the generator term satisfies

$$ e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}\bigl[|\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}V^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})|\bigr]\leq Ce^{-\beta t}\bigl(e^{\beta_{0}(2)t}(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu))+e^{2\beta_{0}(2)t}(1+m_{2}(\mu))^{2}\bigr), $$

which is integrable over $[0,\infty)$ since $\beta>2\beta_{0}(2)$ . Similarly for $r_{\lambda}^{\pi}$ . Letting $T\to\infty$ in (95) by dominated convergence gives

$$ V^{\pi}(s,\mu)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})-\varepsilon\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}V^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

From the definition of $B(\varepsilon;s)$ and the representations (97) and (90), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle B(\varepsilon;s) \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\frac{\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]-\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]}{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\frac{\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]-\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})-\varepsilon\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}V^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]}{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\bigl[\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}V^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t, $$

where in the second equality we used (97). This yields (98), valid for all $\varepsilon\neq 0$ . For each fixed $t\geq 0$ , the same argument applied to $A_{2}$ above (fundamental theorem of calculus in state, Lions mean value formula in measure) applies here to $\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}V^{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}$ , using the convergence $\mathbb{E}[|s_{t}^{\varepsilon}-s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}]+\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\to 0$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$ from Lemma A.6, to give

$$ \mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi^{\varepsilon}}\!\bigl[\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}V^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})\bigr]\to\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\bigl[\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}V^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]\qquad\text{as }\varepsilon\to 0. $$

Since the dominating function from (96) is integrable over $[0,\infty)$ , dominated convergence in (98) gives

$$ \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}B(\varepsilon;s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\bigl[\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}V^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Step 3: We identify the limit and conclude. Combining (91), (94), and (99) gives

$$ \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{V^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s,\mu)-V^{\pi}(s,\mu)}{\varepsilon}=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})+(\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}V^{\pi})(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Note that by definition of $\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}$ we deduce by Fubini’s theorem (justified by polynomial growth and Section 3.1), that

$$ \displaystyle r_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(s,\mu) \displaystyle+(\mathcal{L}^{\varphi}V^{\pi})(s,\mu) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\!\Bigl[r(s,\mu,a)-\lambda\log p_{\pi}(a|s,\mu)+b(s,\mu,a)\cdot\nabla_{s}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)+\tfrac{1}{2}\Sigma(s,\mu,a):D^{2}_{ss}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)\Bigr]\varphi(\mathrm{d}a|s,\mu) \displaystyle\quad+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\!\int_{\mathcal{A}}\!\Bigl[b(\xi,\mu,a)\cdot\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)+\tfrac{1}{2}\Sigma(\xi,\mu,a):D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)\Bigr]\varphi(\mathrm{d}a|\xi,\mu)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\xi). \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{A}}q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{rep}}(s,\mu,a)\,\varphi(\mathrm{d}a|s,\mu)+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\int_{\mathcal{A}}q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{pop}}(s,\mu,\xi,a)\,\varphi(\mathrm{d}a|\xi,\mu)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\xi) $$

It remains to integrate over $\mu_{0}$ . From (93) integrated over $[0,\infty)$ and (98) bounded via (96), for all $|\varepsilon|\leq\varepsilon_{0}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\left|\frac{V^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s,\mu)-V^{\pi}(s,\mu)}{\varepsilon}\right| \displaystyle\leq|A(\varepsilon;s)|+|B(\varepsilon;s)| \displaystyle\leq\frac{M_{\psi}C_{r}(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu))}{\beta-\beta_{0}(2)}+C\left[\frac{1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)}{\beta-\beta_{0}(2)}+\frac{(1+m_{2}(\mu))^{2}}{\beta-2\beta_{0}(2)}\right] \displaystyle\leq K_{\mu}(1+|s|^{2}), $$

where $K_{\mu}>0$ depends on the fixed measure $\mu$ and the structural constants but not on $s$ or $\varepsilon$ . The factor $(1+m_{2}(\mu))^{2}$ is absorbed into $K_{\mu}$ because $m_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon})$ is deterministic and was already used to bound the expectation; the remaining $s$ -dependence is thus at most quadratic. Since $\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , we have $\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K_{\mu}(1+|s|^{2})\,\mu_{0}(ds)=K_{\mu}(1+m_{2}(\mu_{0}))<\infty$ . Dominated convergence over $\mu_{0}(ds)$ then gives

$$ \frac{d}{d\varepsilon}J(\varepsilon)\bigg|_{\varepsilon=0}=\frac{1}{\beta}\left(\beta\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{V^{\pi^{\varepsilon}}(s,\mu)-V^{\pi}(s,\mu)}{\varepsilon}\,\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}s)\right), $$

and substituting the pointwise limit (100), and (101), and using Definition 4.4, gives (16). ∎

We now provide the proof Theorem 4.9.

#### Proof of Theorem 4.9.

Fix $v\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ . We show that $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}J(\omega+\varepsilon v)|_{\varepsilon=0}$ equals the right-hand side of (19) dotted with $v$ ; since $v$ is arbitrary, this identifies $\nabla_{\omega}J(\omega)$ .

Directional kernel. Define the signed kernel

$$ \varphi_{v}(\mathrm{d}a\mid s,\mu):=\bigl(\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi}(a\mid s,\mu)\cdot v\bigr)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a\mid s,\mu). $$

The zero-mass condition $\int_{\mathcal{A}}\varphi_{v}(da\mid s,\mu)=0$ holds since $\int_{\mathcal{A}}\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi_{\omega}}(a\mid s,\mu)\pi_{\omega}(da\mid s,\mu)=\nabla_{\omega}\int_{\mathcal{A}}p_{\pi_{\omega}}\nu(da)=0$ , which follows from Section 4.2 and differentiation under the integral sign. We write $(s_{t}^{\varepsilon v},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon v})_{t\geq 0}$ for the dynamics under $\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}$ starting from $(s,\mu)$ , and $(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})_{t\geq 0}$ for those under $\pi_{\omega}$ . By Section 4.2, Lemma A.6 applies and gives, for every $t\geq 0$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}\bigl[|s_{t}^{\varepsilon v}-s_{t}^{\pi}|^{2}\bigr]+\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon v},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\leq C\varepsilon^{2}e^{\beta_{\rm stab}\,t}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), $$

so both terms tend to zero as $\varepsilon\to 0$ for each fixed $t\geq 0$ . For each fixed $s\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , we split the difference quotient as

$$ \frac{V^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}(s,\mu)-V^{\pi}(s,\mu)}{\varepsilon}=A(\varepsilon;s)+B(\varepsilon;s), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle A(\varepsilon;s) \displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\frac{\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon v},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon v})\bigr]-\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon v},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon v})\bigr]}{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{d}t, \displaystyle B(\varepsilon;s) \displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\frac{\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon v},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon v})\bigr]-\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]}{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Step 1: We compute the limit of $A(\varepsilon;s)$ . By Section 4.2, the map $\varepsilon\mapsto r_{\lambda}^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}(x,\nu)$ is differentiable at $\varepsilon=0$ with derivative $\nabla_{\omega}r_{\lambda}^{\pi_{\omega}}(x,\nu)\cdot v$ . By the zero-mass property of $\varphi_{v}$ , this derivative equals $r_{\lambda}^{\varphi_{v}}(x,\nu)$ as defined in (92) (with $\varphi_{v}$ in place of $\varphi$ ). By the mean value theorem and the bound (17) on $\nabla_{\omega}r_{\lambda}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ , uniformly in $\omega$ on compact sets:

$$ \left|\frac{r_{\lambda}^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}(x,\nu)-r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(x,\nu)}{\varepsilon}\right|\leq C_{K}\|v\|\bigl(1+|x|^{2}+m_{2}(\nu)\bigr),\qquad|\varepsilon|\leq\varepsilon_{0}. $$

The rest of the argument for $A$ follows the same $A_{1}+A_{2}$ decomposition as in Step 1 of Theorem 4.6, using (104) in place of the previous uniform bound and (102) for the convergence of the dynamics. The dominating function is $C_{K}\|v\|e^{-(\beta-\beta_{0}(2))t}(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu))$ , integrable since $\beta>\beta_{0}(2)$ , giving

$$ \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}A(\varepsilon;s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\varphi_{v}}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Step 2: We derive a formula for $B(\varepsilon;s)$ and compute its limit.

We apply the Itô-Lions formula to $V^{\pi}$ along the $\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}$ -dynamics. For $n\geq 1$ , let $\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon v}:=\inf\{t\geq 0:|s_{t}^{\varepsilon v}|\geq n\}$ . Applying the formula to $t\mapsto e^{-\beta(t\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon v})}V^{\pi}(s_{t\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon v}}^{\varepsilon v},\mu_{t\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon v}}^{\varepsilon v})$ , taking expectations, decomposing $\mathcal{L}^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}=\mathcal{L}^{\pi}+(\mathcal{L}^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}-\mathcal{L}^{\pi})$ , and substituting the HJB equation $(\mathcal{L}^{\pi}-\beta)V^{\pi}=-r_{\lambda}^{\pi}$ from (11) gives

$$ \mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\beta(T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon v})}V^{\pi}(s_{T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon v}}^{\varepsilon v},\mu_{T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon v}}^{\varepsilon v})\bigr]-V^{\pi}(s,\mu)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{T\wedge\tau_{n}^{\varepsilon v}}e^{-\beta t}\bigl(-r_{\lambda}^{\pi}+(\mathcal{L}^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}-\mathcal{L}^{\pi})V^{\pi}\bigr)(s_{t}^{\varepsilon v},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon v})\,\mathrm{d}t\right]. $$

We now bound the generator difference term. By Section 4.2 and the mean value theorem, the ratios $\frac{b^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}-b^{\pi}}{\varepsilon}$ and $\frac{\Sigma^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}-\Sigma^{\pi}}{\varepsilon}$ are bounded by $C_{K}\|v\|(1+|x|+\sqrt{m_{2}(\nu)})$ and $C_{K}\|v\|(1+|x|^{2}+m_{2}(\nu))$ respectively, uniformly in $|\varepsilon|\leq\varepsilon_{0}$ . Using the polynomial bounds on the derivatives of $V^{\pi}$ from Definition 3.1 and the growth of $b^{\pi}$ , $\Sigma^{\pi}$ from Sections 3.1 and 4.2, each of the four terms in $(\mathcal{L}^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}-\mathcal{L}^{\pi})V^{\pi}$ is bounded in absolute value. The dominant contribution comes from the term involving $\frac{\Sigma^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}-\Sigma^{\pi}}{\varepsilon}:D^{2}_{ss}V^{\pi}$ , which satisfies

$$ \left|\frac{(\mathcal{L}^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}-\mathcal{L}^{\pi})V^{\pi}(x,\nu)}{\varepsilon}\right|\leq C_{K}\|v\|\bigl(1+|x|^{2}+m_{2}(\nu)^{2}\bigr),\qquad|\varepsilon|\leq\varepsilon_{0}. $$

The passages $n\to\infty$ and then $T\to\infty$ in (106), with the subsequent recovery of (90), follow by dominated convergence using the same arguments as in Step 2 of Theorem 4.6 (the growth bounds are the same with $C_{K}\|v\|$ in place of $M_{\psi}$ , and integrability holds since $\beta>2\beta_{0}(2)$ ). Subtracting the stochastic representation (90) and dividing by $\varepsilon\neq 0$ :

$$ B(\varepsilon;s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}\!\bigl[(\mathcal{L}^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}-\mathcal{L}^{\pi})V^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\varepsilon v},\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon v})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

We now pass $\varepsilon\to 0$ in (108). By Section 4.2, the ratios $\frac{b^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}-b^{\pi}}{\varepsilon}\to\nabla_{\omega}b^{\pi_{\omega}}\cdot v=b^{\varphi_{v}}$ and $\frac{\Sigma^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}-\Sigma^{\pi}}{\varepsilon}\to\nabla_{\omega}\Sigma^{\pi_{\omega}}\cdot v=\Sigma^{\varphi_{v}}$ pointwise as $\varepsilon\to 0$ . Applying these limits to each of the four terms of the generator, using the polynomial growth of $V^{\pi}$ and dominated convergence over $\xi$ in the integral terms (justified by the $\mathcal{P}_{2}$ condition on $\mu$ ), gives

$$ \frac{(\mathcal{L}^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}-\mathcal{L}^{\pi})V^{\pi}(x,\nu)}{\varepsilon}\xrightarrow[\varepsilon\to 0]{}(\mathcal{L}^{\varphi_{v}}V^{\pi})(x,\nu)\quad\text{for every }(x,\nu). $$

Combining (109) with (102) and the same continuity argument applied to the polynomial-growth function $\mathcal{L}^{\varphi_{v}}V^{\pi}$ , the integrand in (108) converges for each fixed $t\geq 0$ . The bound (107) provides a dominating function integrable over $[0,\infty)$ since $\beta>2\beta_{0}(2)$ , so dominated convergence gives

$$ \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}B(\varepsilon;s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\bigl[\mathcal{L}^{\varphi_{v}}V^{\pi}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Step 3: We identify the limit and integrate over $\mu_{0}$ .

Combining (103), (105), and (110):

$$ \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{V^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}(s,\mu)-V^{\pi}(s,\mu)}{\varepsilon}=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\bigl[r_{\lambda}^{\varphi_{v}}(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})+(\mathcal{L}^{\varphi_{v}}V^{\pi})(s_{t}^{\pi},\mu_{t}^{\pi})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

We expand $r_{\lambda}^{\varphi_{v}}+\mathcal{L}^{\varphi_{v}}V^{\pi}$ using the definitions of $r_{\lambda}^{\varphi_{v}}$ , $\mathcal{L}^{\varphi_{v}}$ , and $\varphi_{v}$ , and Fubini’s theorem (justified by Sections 3.1 and 4.2 and the polynomial growth of $V^{\pi}$ ), we deduce (101) with $\varphi$ replaced by $\varphi_{v}$ . Substituting $\varphi_{v}(da|x,\nu)=(\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi}(a|x,\nu)\cdot v)\,\pi(da|x,\nu)$ gives

$$ r_{\lambda}^{\varphi_{v}}(s,\mu)+(\mathcal{L}^{\varphi_{v}}V^{\pi})(s,\mu)=v\cdot\int_{\mathcal{A}}q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{rep}}\,\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi}\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a)+v\cdot\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\!\int_{\mathcal{A}}q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{pop}}\,\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi}\,\pi(\mathrm{d}a)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}\xi), $$

so (111) gives $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}V^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}(s,\mu)|_{\varepsilon=0}=v\cdot R(s)$ , where $R(s)$ denotes the right-hand side of (19) at $s$ .

It remains to integrate over $\mu_{0}$ . From (104) and (107), the difference quotient satisfies

$$ \left|\frac{V^{\pi_{\omega+\varepsilon v}}(s,\mu)-V^{\pi}(s,\mu)}{\varepsilon}\right|\leq K_{\mu}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}\bigr),\qquad|\varepsilon|\leq\varepsilon_{0}, $$

where $K_{\mu}>0$ absorbs the deterministic factors involving $m_{2}(\mu)$ but does not depend on $s$ or $\varepsilon$ . Since $\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , dominated convergence over $\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}s)$ gives $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}J(\omega+\varepsilon v)|_{\varepsilon=0}=v\cdot\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}R(s)\,\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}s)$ . Since $v\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ is arbitrary, $J$ is differentiable at $\omega$ , we deduce that $\nabla_{\omega}J(\omega)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}R(s)\,\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}s)$ , which is (19). ∎

### A.3. Proofs for Section 6

#### Lemma A.7 (Stationary Riccati system: existence, uniqueness, and stabilizing solution).

Assume Section 6.1. Then there exists a unique quadruple $(K,\Lambda,Y,R)\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d}\times\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}$ solving (32)-(35). Moreover, $S=N+F^{\top}KF\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m},$ and the matrices

$$ A_{\beta}-BS^{-1}U\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tilde{A}_{\beta}-BS^{-1}W $$

are Hurwitz. Furthermore, among all solutions of (32)-(35), this is the unique one for which the matrices in (112) are Hurwitz.

#### Proof.

We first rewrite (32)-(33) in shifted form:

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=Q+KA_{\beta}+A_{\beta}^{\top}K+D^{\top}KD-U^{\top}S^{-1}U, \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=Q+\bar{Q}+\Lambda\tilde{A}_{\beta}+\tilde{A}_{\beta}^{\top}\Lambda+(D+\bar{D})^{\top}K(D+\bar{D})-W^{\top}S^{-1}W. $$

Then, a direct application of [67, Theorem 3.4.1] yields a unique pair $(K,\Lambda)\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d}\times\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d}$ solving (113)-(114), such that $S=N+F^{\top}KF\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m}$ and the matrices $A_{\beta}-BS^{-1}U,$ and $\tilde{A}_{\beta}-BS^{-1}W$ are Hurwitz. Once $(K,\Lambda)$ is fixed, equation (34) is linear in $Y$ . Since $O=H+B^{\top}Y+F^{\top}K\gamma,$ we rewrite (34) as

$$ \Bigl((A-BS^{-1}U)^{\top}-\beta I_{d}\Bigr)Y+M+D^{\top}K\gamma-U^{\top}S^{-1}(H+F^{\top}K\gamma)=0. $$

Because $A_{\beta}-BS^{-1}U$ is Hurwitz, the matrix

$$ (A-BS^{-1}U)-\beta I_{d}=\bigl(A_{\beta}-BS^{-1}U\bigr)-\frac{\beta}{2}I_{d} $$

is also Hurwitz, hence invertible. Therefore the above linear equation admits a unique solution $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . Finally, once $(K,\Lambda,Y)$ is fixed, equation (35) is linear in $R$ , and since $\beta>0$ it admits the unique solution. ∎

#### Lemma A.8 (Discounted second-moment bound and transversality under $\pi^{*}$ ).

Assume Section 6.1, and let $\pi^{*}$ be given by (38). Let $(s_{t},\tilde{s}_{t},\mu_{t})$ be the corresponding solution of (4)-(5) under $\pi^{*}$ , with $s_{0}=s$ , $\tilde{s}_{0}\sim\mu$ , and $\mu_{t}=\Law(\tilde{s}_{t})$ . Set $\xi_{t}:=s_{t}-\bar{\mu}_{t},$ and $\tilde{\xi}_{t}:=\tilde{s}_{t}-\bar{\mu}_{t}.$ Then there exist constants $C\geq 1$ and $\kappa>0$ , independent of $t$ , such that for all $t\geq 0$ ,

$$ e^{-\beta t}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}|\xi_{t}|^{2}+\mathbb{E}|\tilde{\xi}_{t}|^{2}+|\bar{\mu}_{t}|^{2}\Bigr)\leq C\,e^{-2\kappa t}\Bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)+\lambda\Bigr). $$

In particular, $\lim_{t\to\infty}e^{-\beta t}\bigl(\mathbb{E}|s_{t}|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu_{t})\bigr)=0$ and therefore, the function $V$ from (31) satisfies that

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}e^{-\beta t}\,\mathbb{E}|V(s_{t},\mu_{t})|=0 $$

#### Proof.

Define the feedback coefficients $\Theta^{*}:=-S^{-1}U,$ $\bar{\Theta}^{*}:=-S^{-1}W,$ and $\theta^{*}:=-S^{-1}O$ , so that the mean of the Gaussian kernel $\pi^{*}$ is $\hat{a}(s,\mu)=\Theta^{*}(s-\bar{\mu})+\bar{\Theta}^{*}\,\bar{\mu}+\theta^{*}.$ Hence

$$ b^{\pi^{*}}(s,\mu)=(A+B\Theta^{*})(s-\bar{\mu})+(\tilde{A}+B\bar{\Theta}^{*})\bar{\mu}+B\theta^{*}, $$

where $\tilde{A}:=A+\bar{A}$ . Moreover, if we set $C^{*}:=D+F\Theta^{*},$ $\bar{C}^{*}:=D+\bar{D}+F\bar{\Theta}^{*},$ and $\sigma_{0}^{*}:=\gamma+F\theta^{*},$ then

$$ \Sigma^{\pi^{*}}(s,\mu)=\bigl(C^{*}(s-\bar{\mu})+\bar{C}^{*}\,\bar{\mu}+\sigma_{0}^{*}\bigr)\bigl(C^{*}(s-\bar{\mu})+\bar{C}^{*}\,\bar{\mu}+\sigma_{0}^{*}\bigr)^{\top}+\frac{\lambda}{2}FS^{-1}F^{\top}. $$

Taking expectation in the population dynamics yields

$$ \dot{\bar{\mu}}_{t}=(\tilde{A}+B\bar{\Theta}^{*})\bar{\mu}_{t}+B\theta^{*}. $$

By Lemma A.7, $\tilde{A}_{\beta}+B\bar{\Theta}^{*}=\tilde{A}_{\beta}-BS^{-1}W$ is Hurwitz. Therefore there exist constants $C_{m}\geq 1$ and $\kappa_{m}>0$ such that

$$ e^{-\beta t}|\bar{\mu}_{t}|^{2}\leq C_{m}e^{-2\kappa_{m}t}\bigl(1+|m_{0}|^{2}\bigr). $$

Next, we derive the Lyapunov inequality needed for the fluctuation $\xi_{t}=s_{t}-\bar{\mu}_{t}$ . Set $M^{*}:=A+B\Theta^{*}.$ After completing squares in (113), we have

$$ K(A_{\beta}+B\Theta^{*})+(A_{\beta}+B\Theta^{*})^{\top}K+(D+F\Theta^{*})^{\top}K(D+F\Theta^{*})=-\mathcal{Q}_{\Theta^{*}}, $$

where $\mathcal{Q}_{\Theta^{*}}:=Q+(\Theta^{*})^{\top}N\Theta^{*}+(\Theta^{*})^{\top}I+I^{\top}\Theta^{*}.$ Equivalently, since $A_{\beta}=A-\frac{\beta}{2}I_{d}$ ,

$$ (M^{*})^{\top}K+KM^{*}+(C^{*})^{\top}KC^{*}=\beta K-\mathcal{Q}_{\Theta^{*}}. $$

Moreover, by Section 6.1, $\mathcal{Q}_{\Theta^{*}}=Q-I^{\top}N^{-1}I+(\Theta^{*}+N^{-1}I)^{\top}N(\Theta^{*}+N^{-1}I)\succ 0.$ Since $K\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d}$ , the two positive definite quadratic forms $\mathcal{Q}_{\Theta^{*}}$ and $K$ are comparable. Hence there exists $\kappa_{\xi}>0$ such that $\mathcal{Q}_{\Theta^{*}}\succeq 2\kappa_{\xi}K.$ Therefore,

$$ (M^{*})^{\top}K+KM^{*}+(C^{*})^{\top}KC^{*}=\beta K-\mathcal{Q}_{\Theta^{*}}\preceq\beta K-2\kappa_{\xi}K=(\beta-2\kappa_{\xi})K. $$

Thus, with $G:=K$ , we obtain

$$ (A+B\Theta^{*})^{\top}G+G(A+B\Theta^{*})+(D+F\Theta^{*})^{\top}G(D+F\Theta^{*})\preceq(\beta-2\kappa_{\xi})G. $$

We now apply Itô’s formula to the quadratic function $x\mapsto x^{\top}Gx$ along the fluctuation processes $\xi_{t}$ and $\tilde{\xi}_{t}$ . Set $h_{t}:=\bar{C}^{*}\bar{\mu}_{t}+\sigma_{0}^{*}.$ For $\xi_{t}$ , the drift is $M^{*}\xi_{t}$ and the covariance matrix is $(C^{*}\xi_{t}+h_{t})(C^{*}\xi_{t}+h_{t})^{\top}+\frac{\lambda}{2}FS^{-1}F^{\top}.$ Hence,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}[\xi_{t}^{\top}G\xi_{t}] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\xi_{t}^{\top}\bigl((M^{*})^{\top}G+GM^{*}\bigr)\xi_{t}\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[(C^{*}\xi_{t}+h_{t})^{\top}G(C^{*}\xi_{t}+h_{t})\right]+\frac{\lambda}{2}\Tr(GFS^{-1}F^{\top}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\xi_{t}^{\top}\bigl((M^{*})^{\top}G+GM^{*}+(C^{*})^{\top}GC^{*}\bigr)\xi_{t}\right]+2\mathbb{E}\!\left[\xi_{t}^{\top}(C^{*})^{\top}Gh_{t}\right] \displaystyle+h_{t}^{\top}Gh_{t}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\Tr(GFS^{-1}F^{\top}). $$

Using (118), we get

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}[\xi_{t}^{\top}G\xi_{t}] \displaystyle\leq(\beta-2\kappa_{\xi})\mathbb{E}[\xi_{t}^{\top}G\xi_{t}]+2\mathbb{E}\!\left[\xi_{t}^{\top}(C^{*})^{\top}Gh_{t}\right]+h_{t}^{\top}Gh_{t}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\Tr(GFS^{-1}F^{\top}). $$

The cross term is controlled by Young’s inequality: for every $\varepsilon>0$ , $2\xi_{t}^{\top}(C^{*})^{\top}Gh_{t}\leq\varepsilon\,\xi_{t}^{\top}G\xi_{t}+C_{\varepsilon}|h_{t}|^{2}.$ Moreover, since $h_{t}=\bar{C}^{*}\bar{\mu}_{t}+\sigma_{0}^{*}$ , we have $|h_{t}|^{2}\leq C(1+|\bar{\mu}_{t}|^{2})$ , while $\frac{\lambda}{2}\Tr(GFS^{-1}F^{\top})\leq C\lambda.$ Therefore, possibly reducing $\kappa_{\xi}>0$ and keeping the same notation, we obtain

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}[\xi_{t}^{\top}G\xi_{t}]\leq(\beta-2\kappa_{\xi})\mathbb{E}[\xi_{t}^{\top}G\xi_{t}]+C\bigl(1+|\bar{\mu}_{t}|^{2}+\lambda\bigr). $$

The same computation applied to $\tilde{\xi}_{t}$ gives

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\xi}_{t}^{\top}G\tilde{\xi}_{t}]\leq(\beta-2\kappa_{\xi})\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\xi}_{t}^{\top}G\tilde{\xi}_{t}]+C\bigl(1+|\bar{\mu}_{t}|^{2}+\lambda\bigr), $$

for some constant $C>0$ independent of $t$ . Multiplying by $e^{-\beta t}$ gives

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Bigl(e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}[\xi_{t}^{\top}G\xi_{t}]\Bigr)\leq-2\kappa_{\xi}\,e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}[\xi_{t}^{\top}G\xi_{t}]+C\,e^{-\beta t}\bigl(1+|\bar{\mu}_{t}|^{2}+\lambda\bigr), $$

and the same inequality with $\tilde{\xi}_{t}$ in place of $\xi_{t}$ .

Using (117) and Grönwall’s inequality, we deduce that there exist constants $C\geq 1$ and $\kappa>0$ such that

$$ e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}|\xi_{t}|^{2}+e^{-\beta t}\mathbb{E}|\tilde{\xi}_{t}|^{2}+e^{-\beta t}|\bar{\mu}_{t}|^{2}\leq C\,e^{-2\kappa t}\Bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)+\lambda\Bigr),\qquad t\geq 0, $$

which is exactly (115). Finally, since

$$ \mathbb{E}|s_{t}|^{2}\leq 2\mathbb{E}|\xi_{t}|^{2}+2|\bar{\mu}_{t}|^{2},\qquad m_{2}(\mu_{t})=\mathbb{E}|\tilde{s}_{t}|^{2}=\mathbb{E}|\tilde{\xi}_{t}|^{2}+|\bar{\mu}_{t}|^{2}, $$

(115) implies that $\lim_{t\to\infty}e^{-\beta t}\bigl(\mathbb{E}|s_{t}|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu_{t})\bigr)=0$ . Because the quadratic candidate satisfies

$$ |V(s,\mu)|\leq C_{V}\bigl(1+|s|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), $$

for some constant $C_{V}>0$ , we conclude (116). ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 6.4.

Fix $(s,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and let $\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ . For $t\geq 0$ , define

$$ \mathcal{S}_{t}^{\pi}:=e^{-\beta t}V(s_{t},\mu_{t})+\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\beta r}\Bigl(r(s_{r},\mu_{r},a_{r}^{s})-\lambda\log p_{\pi}(s_{r},\mu_{r},a_{r}^{s})\Bigr)\,\mathrm{d}r. $$

For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , let $\tau_{n}:=\inf\{t\geq 0:\ |s_{t}|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu_{t})\geq n\}.$

Step 1: Derivatives of the candidate value function. Since $V$ in (31) depends on $\mu$ only through $\bar{\mu}$ , one has

$$ \nabla_{s}V(s,\mu)=-2K(s-\bar{\mu})-2Y,\qquad\nabla^{2}_{ss}V(s,\mu)=-2K, $$

and

$$ \partial_{\mu}V(s,\mu)(\xi)=2K(s-\bar{\mu})-2\Lambda\bar{\mu},\qquad D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}V(s,\mu)(\xi)=0. $$

Step 2: Localized verification identity. Applying Itô’s formula to $e^{-\beta(t\wedge\tau_{n})}V(s_{t\wedge\tau_{n}},\mu_{t\wedge\tau_{n}})$ , using (120)-(121), and taking expectations, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{S}_{t\wedge\tau_{n}}^{\pi}\right] \displaystyle=V(s,\mu)+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau_{n}}e^{-\beta r}\Bigl(-\beta V(s_{r},\mu_{r})+(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}V)(s_{r},\mu_{r})+r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{r},\mu_{r})\Bigr)\,\mathrm{d}r\right]. $$

Step 3: Static entropy minimization. For $\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ and for every probability density $p$ on $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ such that $\int_{\mathbb{R}^{m}}(|a|^{2}+|\log p(a)|)\,p(a)\,\mathrm{d}a<\infty$ , define

$$ \mathfrak{J}_{\eta}(p):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{m}}\Bigl(a^{\top}Sa+2a^{\top}\eta+\lambda\log p(a)\Bigr)p(a)\,\mathrm{d}a. $$

Note that the first two terms inside the integral can be rewritten as $a^{\top}Sa+2a^{\top}\eta=\bigl(a+S^{-1}\eta\bigr)^{\top}S\bigl(a+S^{-1}\eta\bigr)-\eta^{\top}S^{-1}\eta$ . Hence, defining

$$ g_{\eta}(a):=\frac{\sqrt{\det S}}{(\pi_{0}\lambda)^{m/2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{\lambda}\bigl(a+S^{-1}\eta\bigr)^{\top}S\bigl(a+S^{-1}\eta\bigr)\right). $$

With this definition, (123) becomes

$$ \mathfrak{J}_{\eta}(p)=-\eta^{\top}S^{-1}\eta-\frac{\lambda}{2}\Bigl(m\log(\pi_{0}\lambda)-\log\det S\Bigr)+\lambda\,\mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,g_{\eta}). $$

In particular, $\mathfrak{J}_{\eta}(p)$ is minimized uniquely at $p=g_{\eta}$ .

Step 4: Expansion of the drift term. Set $z:=s-\bar{\mu}$ and $\eta(s,\mu):=Us+(W-U)\bar{\mu}+O.$ Using (29), (30), (120)-(121), and the definitions (36)-(37), a direct computation yields

$$ \displaystyle-\beta V(s,\mu)+ \displaystyle(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}V)(s,\mu)+r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s,\mu)=-z^{\top}\Bigl(Q-\beta K+KA+A^{\top}K+D^{\top}KD\Bigr)z \displaystyle-\bar{\mu}^{\top}\Bigl(Q+\bar{Q}-\beta\Lambda+\Lambda(A+\bar{A})+(A+\bar{A})^{\top}\Lambda+(D+\bar{D})^{\top}K(D+\bar{D})\Bigr)\bar{\mu} \displaystyle-2\Bigl(M+(A^{\top}-\beta I_{d})Y+D^{\top}K\gamma\Bigr)^{\top}s-\Bigl(-\beta R+\gamma^{\top}K\gamma\Bigr) \displaystyle-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{m}}\Bigl(a^{\top}Sa+2a^{\top}\eta(s,\mu)+\lambda\log p_{\pi}(s,\mu,a)\Bigr)\pi(\mathrm{d}a\mid s,\mu). $$

Applying (124) with $\eta=\eta(s,\mu)$ and $p=p_{\pi}(s,\mu,\cdot)$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle-\beta V(s,\mu)+(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}V)(s,\mu)+r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s,\mu)=-z^{\top}\Gamma_{K}z-\bar{\mu}^{\top}\Gamma_{\Lambda}\bar{\mu}-2\Gamma_{Y}^{\top}s-\Gamma_{R}-\lambda\,\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\pi}(s,\mu,\cdot)\,\|\,g_{s,\mu}\right), $$

where $g_{s,\mu}:=g_{\eta(s,\mu)}$ and

$$ \Gamma_{K}=Q-\beta K+KA+A^{\top}K+D^{\top}KD-U^{\top}S^{-1}U, $$

$$ \Gamma_{\Lambda}=Q+\bar{Q}-\beta\Lambda+\Lambda(A+\bar{A})+(A+\bar{A})^{\top}\Lambda+(D+\bar{D})^{\top}K(D+\bar{D})-W^{\top}S^{-1}W, $$

$$ \Gamma_{Y}=M+(A^{\top}-\beta I_{d})Y+D^{\top}K\gamma-U^{\top}S^{-1}O, $$

and

$$ \Gamma_{R}=-\beta R+\gamma^{\top}K\gamma-O^{\top}S^{-1}O-\frac{\lambda}{2}\Bigl(m\log(\pi_{0}\lambda)-\log\det S\Bigr). $$

By (32)-(35), all these coefficients vanish. Hence

$$ -\beta V(s,\mu)+(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}V)(s,\mu)+r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s,\mu)=-\lambda\,\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\pi}(s,\mu,\cdot)\,\|\,g_{s,\mu}\right). $$

Step 5: Comparison for an arbitrary policy. Substituting (125) into (122) yields

$$ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{S}_{t\wedge\tau_{n}}^{\pi}\right]=V(s,\mu)-\lambda\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau_{n}}e^{-\beta r}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\pi}(s_{r},\mu_{r},\cdot)\,\|\,g_{s_{r},\mu_{r}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}r\right]\leq V(s,\mu). $$

Since $V$ has quadratic growth and, by definition of $\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ , the discounted second moments vanish at infinity, we may let $n\to\infty$ in (126) and obtain, for every $t\geq 0$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{S}_{t}^{\pi}\right]=V(s,\mu)-\lambda\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\beta r}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\pi}(s_{r},\mu_{r},\cdot)\,\|\,g_{s_{r},\mu_{r}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}r\right]\leq V(s,\mu). $$

Recalling (119), this implies

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{-\beta t}V(s_{t},\mu_{t})\right]+\mathbb{E}^{s,\mu,\pi}\!\left[\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\beta r}\Bigl(r(s_{r},\mu_{r},a_{r}^{s})-\lambda\log p_{\pi}(s_{r},\mu_{r},a_{r}^{s})\Bigr)\,\mathrm{d}r\right]\leq V(s,\mu). $$

Letting $t\to\infty$ in (128) and using the defining property of $\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ , namely

$$ \lim_{t\to\infty}e^{-\beta t}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}|s_{t}|^{2}+m_{2}(\mu_{t})\Bigr)=0, $$

together with the quadratic growth of $V$ , we conclude that

$$ V^{\pi}(s,\mu)\leq V(s,\mu)\qquad\text{for every }\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}. $$

Hence $V^{*}(s,\mu)\leq V(s,\mu)$ .

Step 6: Optimality of the candidate policy. By construction, the Gaussian kernel (38) has density $p_{\pi^{*}}(s,\mu,\cdot)=g_{s,\mu},$ so the Kullback-Leibler term in (125) vanishes identically for $\pi=\pi^{*}$ . Moreover, Lemma A.8 shows that $\pi^{*}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ . Therefore (127) becomes

$$ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{S}_{t}^{\pi^{*}}\right]=V(s,\mu),\qquad t\geq 0. $$

Letting $t\to\infty$ and using Lemma A.8 again, we obtain $V^{\pi^{*}}(s,\mu)=V(s,\mu).$ Combining this with (129), we conclude that $V^{*}(s,\mu)=V^{\pi^{*}}(s,\mu)=V(s,\mu).$

Step 7: Uniqueness of the optimal policy. Let $\hat{\pi}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ be another optimal stationary feedback policy. Then $V^{\hat{\pi}}(s,\mu)=V(s,\mu)$ for every $(s,\mu)$ , and (127) implies

$$ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta r}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\hat{\pi}}(s_{r},\mu_{r},\cdot)\,\|\,g_{s_{r},\mu_{r}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}r\right]=0. $$

Since the integrand is nonnegative, it follows that

$$ \mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\hat{\pi}}(s_{r},\mu_{r},\cdot)\,\|\,g_{s_{r},\mu_{r}}\right)=0\qquad\text{for almost every }r\geq 0,\ \text{almost surely.} $$

Hence $p_{\hat{\pi}}(s_{r},\mu_{r},\cdot)=g_{s_{r},\mu_{r}}$ for almost every $r\geq 0$ , almost surely. Since the initial condition $(s,\mu)$ is arbitrary and the minimizer in (124) is unique, we conclude that $\hat{\pi}=\pi^{*}$ as stationary feedback kernels. Therefore $\pi^{*}$ is the unique optimal stationary feedback policy in $\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}$ . ∎
